title: Production Postgres credential hardcoded in a tracked script
evidence: scripts/run_schema_migration_prod.py deleted; tests/test_migration_tooling.py::test_sec01_leaking_script_is_deleted_and_never_returns; no DSN literal remains in scripts/. ROTATION PLANNING this session: coordinated real, read-only reconnaissance with the AWS-equipped sibling session (nothing written/rotated/redeployed) to sequence the rotation safely. Findings: (1) the real secret is `vyomquant/production/database_url` (arn:aws:secretsmanager:ap-southeast-1:273709947018:secret:vyomquant/production/database_url-s7iUfF), manual rotation only (Supabase-hosted Postgres has no native AWS rotation Lambda integration), already has AWSCURRENT+AWSPREVIOUS versions so it has been updated via put-secret-value before. (2) Exactly one consumer account-wide: the vyomquant-api container of task definition vyomquant-api:214, under the single ECS service vyomquant-api-service-cjema2sl in vyomquant-cluster -- reconfirmed no worker services exist in production at all (same finding as INF-03/OPS-TRAIN-01), so nothing else needs coordinating. (3) ECS resolves secrets/valueFrom only at task LAUNCH time, never live-reloaded into a running container -- updating the secret's value alone does nothing until a force-new-deployment (same task definition revision 214, no new revision needed) launches fresh tasks that re-resolve it. (4) The service's deployment config is ROLLING (minimumHealthyPercent=100/maximumPercent=200) with the deployment circuit breaker enabled (rollback: true) -- a force-new-deployment launches a second task and waits for it to pass the ALB health check before stopping the old one, so it never goes through zero running tasks, AND if the new task's DATABASE_URL were to point at a password Supabase hasn't been updated to yet, the new task fails its readiness check and ECS automatically rolls back on its own with the old task still healthy -- no manual rollback needed for that ordering mistake. The real risk direction is the OPPOSITE order: if Supabase's password changes BEFORE the AWS secret is updated and redeployed, the currently-running task's existing pooled connections likely survive (Postgres doesn't kill live sessions on a password change, only new connection attempts need the new password) but new connection attempts from that stale task would start failing immediately -- a general Postgres fact, not independently verified against this app's specific pool/reconnect behavior. Correct sequence per this evidence: stage the new value in Secrets Manager -> flip the password in Supabase -> force-new-deployment, as close together as practical. INCIDENT, 2026-10-23 -- SEC-01 IS MATERIALLY WORSE THAN FILED AND THE REPOSITORY IS PUBLIC. This finding was scoped to one file (scripts/run_schema_migration_prod.py) and its remaining work recorded as 'rotate the password'. Scoped to that file the evidence said the exposure was ALREADY CLOSED, and that sub-conclusion is correct: the password in that file is 23 chars, the live one is 17, both name the same role (postgres.wrkexcjqnidkdrayhlsi on aws-1-ap-southeast-1.pooler.supabase.com:6543/postgres, verified), PostgreSQL stores one password per role, and the live DSN was proven to authenticate (`--verify` connected as postgres at 2026-10-23T08:26:13Z). So that file's leaked value is dead. THAT CONCLUSION WAS RIGHT ABOUT THE FILE AND WRONG ABOUT THE REPOSITORY. A full-history sweep of all 20 readable production Secrets Manager values against `git log --all -p` (481,799,695 chars) matched THREE OTHER LIVE SECRETS, in files this finding never named: (1) vyomquant/production/master_encryption_keys, WHOLE VALUE, in `aws_secrets_deploy.py`, first published 2026-07-22 (4428a4daaa) -- ~93 days public; this is the MultiFernet key protecting exchange_keys.encrypted_api_key/encrypted_secret_key/encrypted_password (2 rows live). (2) vyomquant/production/jwt_secret, WHOLE VALUE, same file and date; HMAC key for platform-minted tokens such as strategy_operations.py:5704's model-download token. (3) vyomquant/production/database_url PASSWORD COMPONENT, across 15 files under scripts/, first published 2026-08-14 (12a799e603), commits 12a799e603/8992f2eda7/659c04df77/fbaf266fdb -- the last of which is titled 'Remediate SEC-01, ...', i.e. the remediation commit MOVED the literal instead of removing it from history. All three are absent from HEAD and present in history, so a working-tree scan cannot see them and `git clone` recovers all three. gh repo view: visibility=PUBLIC, forks=0, collaborators=1, deploy keys=0. NOT AN INCIDENT, recorded so it is not conflated: supabase_anon_key also matched, but Supabase anon keys are PUBLIC BY DESIGN (shipped in the browser bundle, stored as the VITE_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY CI secret for that purpose, protected by RLS not secrecy). SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET IS CLEAN -- user logins are Supabase-issued and verified with that secret, so existing sessions are NOT forgeable from what leaked. COVERAGE CAVEAT: 20/21 secrets compared; vyomquant/production/supabase_key returned ResourceNotFound and is UNKNOWN, not clean. METHOD CORRECTION worth recording: the FIRST sweep reported 'live values loaded for comparison: 4' against 11 watched secrets and still printed a verdict -- Secrets Manager throttles rapid get-secret-value calls and the loader treated a non-zero exit as a silent skip, so 7 secrets were unchecked while the output looked complete. The replacement (sec01_full_sweep.py) retries with backoff, fails loudly on an unreadable secret, and reports per-secret OUTCOME so 'clean' is distinguishable from 'not checked'. ROTATION MECHANICS VERIFIED BEFORE RECOMMENDING: MASTER_ENCRYPTION_KEYS rotation is NON-DESTRUCTIVE because api_key_vault.py:96-99 builds a MultiFernet from a comma-separated list (first encrypts, all decrypt) and already ships generate_new_master_key() + rotate_key(); but core/credential_vault.py:285 takes ONLY the first key through PBKDF2 to derive a single Fernet, so prepending there would silently orphan its ciphertext -- it has NO production callers (its own module, tests, and test_strategy_dag_architecture.py which treats importing it as a violation) and stores to Redis not Postgres, so it carries no data today, but it is a live trap for any future rotation. Full write-up: docs/launch_readiness/SEC-01_INCIDENT.md SEVERITY CORRECTION, same day, for the master_encryption_keys component of this finding: it exposes NO customer credential. Filed VAULT-01 separately. Every one of the 4 ciphertext values in exchange_keys was tested against all 265 structurally valid Fernet keys recoverable from the full git history, and none decrypt -- the rows were encrypted 2026-06-21 under a key that exists in neither Secrets Manager nor git. So an attacker holding the leaked master key can decrypt nothing that is currently stored. It must STILL be rotated, because it is the key that would encrypt every FUTURE credential and it is public -- but the exposure is prospective, not retrospective, and calling it CRITICAL alongside the database password overstated it. The database password was the genuinely critical one and is now ROTATED AND VERIFIED: scripts/audit_secrets_in_git_history.py reports vyomquant/production/database_url as clean, a new AWSCURRENT version was created 2026-10-23T15:26:16+05:30 with the prior value retained as AWSPREVIOUS, the service rolled 232->234 and reports COMPLETED with running=1/1 HEALTHY, and the stored DSN connects as postgres. jwt_secret remains exposed and unrotated; scripts/rotate_jwt_secret.py is built and its --plan confirms the current value IS in history. ALL THREE ROTATIONS COMPLETE AND INDEPENDENTLY VERIFIED, 2026-10-23. scripts/audit_secrets_in_git_history.py now prints 'NO LIVE SECRET IS RECOVERABLE FROM GIT HISTORY' and exits 0. Per secret: (1) database_url -- rotated via scripts/rotate_database_password.py, new AWSCURRENT at 2026-10-23T15:26:16+05:30 with the prior value retained as AWSPREVIOUS, service rolled 232->234, reports clean. (2) jwt_secret -- rotated via scripts/rotate_jwt_secret.py, fingerprint 1ba08925c720 -> 69ec7601df82, version 1761003f-0031-48ec-b1da-bea0f6acea38, deployment COMPLETED, --verify confirms production-grade AND absent from history. The value was generated in-process and never printed, prompted for, pasted, or placed on a command line, so no human ever handled it -- strictly less exposure than the database rotation, which needed an operator to carry the value to the Supabase dashboard. (3) master_encryption_keys -- rotated via scripts/rotate_master_encryption_keys.py, fingerprint baff8a448794 -> bade92adbfb2 by prepend, redeploy, then retire of the old key (a second redeploy followed), ending at a single key; --verify confirms 1 key present and NOT in history. PRODUCTION HEALTH AFTER THREE CONSECUTIVE DEPLOYMENTS: ECS task RUNNING health=HEALTHY, running=1/1, rolloutState=COMPLETED on vyomquant-api:234, ALB target group state 'healthy', and the stored DSN connects as postgres. None of the three deployments failed or rolled back. The jwt_secret rotation is additionally proven by the boot itself: main.py:320 calls assert_jwt_secret_is_production_grade() and raises on a weak value, so a task that reaches RUNNING has necessarily accepted the new secret. WHAT REMAINS FOR SEC-01, AND IT IS NO LONGER A LIVE EXPOSURE: (a) two ORPHANED secrets, /vyomquant/production/MASTER_ENCRYPTION_KEYS and /vyomquant/production/JWT_SECRET, still hold the OLD published values. They are referenced by NOTHING -- confirmed against the running task definition's 11 valueFrom ARNs -- so what they contain authenticates nothing now that the secrets ECS actually reads have been rotated. Secret sprawl holding dead material; remedy is DELETE, not rotate. (b) the git-history purge of all the old literals, still a destructive action awaiting explicit instruction. (c) vyomquant/production/supabase_key returns ResourceNotFound, so sweep coverage is 20/21 and that one is UNKNOWN rather than clean. (d) repository visibility is still PUBLIC. TOOL CORRECTION made in the same pass: the sweep was reporting supabase_anon_key as an exposure and, after the rotations, the two orphans as 'LIVE SECRET(S) ... must be rotated'. Both were wrong in a way that matters -- an alert carrying known-benign entries teaches its reader to skim past the real ones. It now reads the running task definition to classify LIVE vs ORPHANED, treats Supabase anon keys as public by design (they ship in the browser bundle; safety rests on RLS, not secrecy), and exits non-zero ONLY for a live exposure so a scheduled run stays meaningful. ||| CLOSED (Kiro). THE LAST CONTROL IS NOW SCHEDULED, AND TWO OF THE FOUR RECORDED RESIDUALS WERE ALREADY RESOLVED -- measured before anything was changed. RESIDUAL (1), 'DELETE the orphaned uppercase secrets /vyomquant/production/MASTER_ENCRYPTION_KEYS and /JWT_SECRET', plus the four 'mirroring duplicates' beside it: THEY DO NOT EXIST. `list-secrets` in ap-southeast-1 returns 15 secrets and every one is lower-case. They were deleted earlier in this effort, so that item and its warning about mirrored live values are stale. RESIDUAL (3), 'RESOLVE vyomquant/production/supabase_key (ResourceNotFound) so sweep coverage is 21/21 rather than 20/21 with one UNKNOWN': the sweep now reports 'COVERAGE: 15/15 - complete' and classifies that secret as 'exists, stores no value', counted as resolved rather than as a gap -- 'a Terraform-declared secret whose value is set out of band looks exactly like this'. Verdict line: 'NO LIVE SECRET IS RECOVERABLE FROM GIT HISTORY.' Exit code 0. 11 of the 15 are referenced by the running task; supabase_anon_key is correctly in git and reported as public by design. ALSO MEASURED, because this finding's TITLE is about a tracked script: the live database password appears in ZERO tracked files and ZERO commits (compared by value, read from Secrets Manager, never printed). The project ref 'wrkexcjqnidkdrayhlsi' and 'pooler.supabase.com' DO appear, in 14 and 28 tracked files, but a project ref is not a credential -- it ships inside the browser's own Supabase URL -- and those hits are ECS task definitions, deployment docs, this ledger and SEC-01's own incident report. An earlier scan that matched 22 'credential-bearing DSNs' in tracked files was filtering on password shape rather than host; every hit was a test fixture against db.example.supabase.co, 127.0.0.1, or the literals 'host'/'user'. WHAT WAS ACTUALLY BUILT, and it is the item this entry's own closing sentence named -- 'The defect class was never one careless file; it was that nothing watched for this': a `secret-history-sweep` job in .github/workflows/04-nightly-audit.yml, running on the existing nightly schedule, which greps all of git history against the CURRENT value of every secret in Secrets Manager. IT IS A SEPARATE JOB RATHER THAN A STEP, for three reasons that would each have silently defeated it: (a) the existing audit job checks out at the default depth of 1, and this sweep greps every commit -- at depth 1 it would scan one commit, find nothing and report CLEAN, which for this question is the worst available outcome, so `fetch-depth: 0` is load-bearing and a runtime guard fails the job if the clone is shallow anyway; (b) every step in that job carries `continue-on-error: true`, which is right for a dependency report and wrong for 'a live production credential is readable from git', so this job has no such escape; (c) the sweep is only meaningful because it compares against LIVE secret values, which needs AWS credentials -- CI's existing Trivy secret scan answers the different, complementary question of whether a string LOOKS like a secret. Region pinned to ap-southeast-1 and asserted, because this session established that an AWS default of us-east-1 makes list-secrets return an unrelated account's secrets and `ecs list-task-definition-families` return empty -- which reads exactly like 'nothing is deployed' and nearly produced two wrong conclusions. 7 new tests in tests/test_nightly_audit_workflow.py pin the properties that decide whether the sweep CAN fail: scheduled and not only manual, full-history checkout, the shallow-clone guard exits 1, the sweep is not continue-on-error, credentials and region present, script still exists. Negative control: flipping fetch-depth to 1 fails exactly the load-bearing test; restoring it passes all 9. SCOPE LIMIT STATED RATHER THAN HIDDEN, and carried in the workflow's own comment: the sweep compares against secrets that exist in Secrets Manager when it runs, so a credential that leaked and was then DELETED from AWS is invisible to it. NOT DONE, DELIBERATELY -- residual (2), the git-history purge. The sweep proves no live value is recoverable, so `git filter-repo` + force-push would rewrite published history to delete strings that are already dead; it cannot reach existing clones or forks, so it would not remove the exposure it appears to; and it needs an explicit instruction this does not have. Rotation was the control that mattered and it is complete. RESIDUAL (4), repository visibility: OUT OF SCOPE by the owner's explicit instruction -- the repository is public by intention.
verification_level: PRODUCTION-VERIFIED: the sweep was run against the real account (ap-southeast-1) and exits 0 with 15/15 coverage and the verdict that no live secret is recoverable from git history; the live database password was compared by value against every tracked file and every commit and found in neither. Not verified: that the scheduled job has yet executed on its own schedule (it runs nightly at 02:00 UTC and its properties are test-pinned rather than observed), and the sweep cannot see a credential that leaked and was later deleted from Secrets Manager.
remaining_action: NONE that is blocking. Two standing notes: (1) the git-history purge remains available if the owner ever wants the dead strings gone, and needs an explicit instruction because it rewrites published history and cannot reach existing clones; (2) the sweep's blind spot is a credential deleted from Secrets Manager after leaking -- closing that would mean keeping a hash ledger of retired secrets, which is a new mechanism rather than a fix to this one. Repository visibility is intentional and out of scope.

title: Any signed-in user can grant themselves a paid plan, raise limits and unfreeze their account via Supabase REST
evidence: exploit reproduced then blocked on real Postgres; tests/test_sec07_profiles_platform_columns_postgres.py (13) VERIFICATION STRENGTHENED (this session, no code change): this finding's regression file, tests/test_sec07_profiles_platform_columns_postgres.py, was named in NO PostgreSQL lane in 01-pr-check.yml, so its assertions skipped in the SQLite lane and ran against a real server nowhere -- including in run 39695784610, where all 8 jobs were green. The evidence above ('exploit reproduced then blocked on real Postgres') was therefore true of a prior local session and had never been re-established by this repository's own pipeline. CI-11 (opened this session) wires the file into the provisioning lane, and it now passes there against real PostgreSQL 17: run 39728990457, job 119660118669 shows test_user_cannot_change_platform_columns_on_own_row PASSED for every escalation vector this finding named -- subscription_tier='enterprise', max_api_slots=99, is_frozen=false, balance=1000000, plan_limit_overrides, available_discounts, billing_currency='INR', referred_by_user_id -- plus test_user_cannot_modify_another_users_row and test_browser_roles_cannot_insert_or_delete_profiles. The P0's fix is now proven by the pipeline, not only by a session transcript. *** CRITICAL CORRECTION (Kiro, 2026-10-22): THIS P0 WAS STILL LIVE-EXPLOITABLE IN PRODUCTION while recorded VERIFIED_FIXED, and has now been closed there. *** Checked the real production database directly for the first time. `anon` AND `authenticated` both held DELETE, INSERT, REFERENCES, SELECT, TRIGGER, TRUNCATE, UPDATE on public.profiles -- table-level, so every column was writable, including all six platform-owned ones that exist there (subscription_tier, max_api_slots, is_frozen, balance, available_discounts, billing_currency). RLS was enabled but NOT forced, and its 'Update own profile' policy constrains WHICH ROW, not WHICH COLUMNS -- so a signed-in user updating their own row could set their own plan, raise their own API slots, clear their own freeze and write their own balance through the REST API with their own JWT. Exactly this finding's described exploit, unmitigated. ROOT CAUSE OF THE MISRECORD: migration 033 was written and tested but never applied to production -- `recorded_migrations` does not exist in that database at all -- and this entry's own remaining_action said so ('Apply migration 033 to staging/production (human-run)') while the status read VERIFIED_FIXED. Earlier the same day this entry's evidence was strengthened because its regression tests now pass in CI; they pass against a database provisioned from REPOSITORY SOURCE, which says nothing about the deployed one. That scope limit was stated at the time and this is what it cost. REMEDIATION APPLIED: one transaction, verified before commit, revoking INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, REFERENCES, TRIGGER from anon and authenticated; SELECT deliberately retained because RLS scopes reads to the caller's own row and the profile page depends on it; service_role and postgres untouched. Safe because the frontend never writes profiles through Supabase REST -- grepped every .js/.jsx under algo22-terminal/src for `.from('profiles')` (no matches) and for `profiles` generally (comments, docstrings and reads via the backend's own GET /api/user/profile only). Verified after: anon and authenticated hold SELECT only; UPDATE on every sensitive column reads False; ECS service healthy at 1/1 running, 0 pending. EXPOSURE ASSESSED, NOT ASSUMED: all 182 profiles are still subscription_tier='free', with 0 paid tiers, 0 max_api_slots>1, 0 available_discounts, 0 next_billing_date, 0 payment_provider, and every payment table empty (billing_invoices, invoices, payment_methods, subscriptions all 0 rows). The only non-zero values were 7 `balance` rows sharing one identical microsecond timestamp (2026-08-14 03:12:57.680311+00) -- a single batch seed, six of them exactly 1000.0 and one an obvious dev artifact. CONCLUSION: the hole was open but NOT exploited, because the platform is pre-launch with no paying users. Had it launched with that grant in place, the first user to read the anon key out of the JS bundle could have granted themselves Enterprise. *** SECOND CORRECTION (Kiro, 2026-10-22, same session): THE FIX I APPLIED EARLIER TODAY OVERSHOT AND BROKE THREE USER-FACING FEATURES IN PRODUCTION. Now repaired. *** My earlier production fix revoked INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, REFERENCES and TRIGGER on public.profiles from anon and authenticated. Migration 033 -- the fix actually designed for this finding -- revokes only INSERT and DELETE, and column-scopes UPDATE with a BEFORE INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE trigger (guard_profiles_platform_columns) that rejects any change outside an allowlist of username, display_name, avatar_url, bio, telegram_id, full_name, preferred_currency, updated_at. It keeps UPDATE deliberately, because three user-facing writes reach profiles as the `authenticated` role -- they use a Supabase client built from the ANON key carrying the end user's JWT (core/dependencies.py: create_request_supabase:148, create_request_supabase_async:242, and the get_request_supabase dependency at :389): routers/user.py:93 update_profile, core/pricing_service.py:324 set_user_currency_preference, backend/account_lifecycle.py:215 delete_account. MEASURED, not inferred: with table-wide UPDATE revoked, all three failed in production with 'permission denied for table profiles'. So the escalation was closed and profile editing, currency preference and account deletion were all broken at the same time. REPAIRED in one verified transaction: installed migration 033's trigger function and trigger, then GRANT UPDATE ON public.profiles TO authenticated (anon deliberately NOT restored -- no path-(A) write is ever the anon role). INSERT, DELETE, TRUNCATE, REFERENCES and TRIGGER remain revoked from both browser roles. Re-verified on a fresh connection afterwards: authenticated CAN update full_name and preferred_currency (1 row each); authenticated CANNOT set subscription_tier, flip is_frozen, set balance, or DELETE a profile row -- each refused with 'platform-controlled columns cannot be modified by role authenticated' (SQLSTATE 42501). ECS service healthy throughout (task vyomquant-api:224, 1/1 RUNNING, healthStatus HEALTHY, rolloutState COMPLETED). ONE RESIDUAL, FIXED IN CODE: delete_account writes `email` and `is_frozen`, which are correctly NOT in the allowlist -- a role that can SET is_frozen can also CLEAR it, which is precisely this finding's 'unfreeze their account' vector, so an account cannot be frozen with the credentials of the account being frozen. account_lifecycle.delete_account now takes an optional service_supabase and uses it for step 4 only, while steps 1-3 keep the user-scoped client because RLS is what confines them to the caller's own rows; routers/user.py resolves it via get_service_supabase_async(). Pinned by tests/test_priv01_account_export_and_deletion.py::test_the_profile_anonymisation_uses_the_service_client_not_the_users and ::test_delete_account_still_works_when_no_service_client_is_supplied (11/11 passing, was 9). NOTE on the trigger's semantics, verified deliberately: it compares to_jsonb(NEW) - allowlist against to_jsonb(OLD) - allowlist, i.e. VALUES not column lists, so writing a platform column to the value it already holds is permitted. A first verification run asserted 'SET is_frozen = false' must be refused and failed the assertion -- the profile was already unfrozen, making the write a no-op. The change set correctly rolled itself back on that failed assertion; the test was corrected to flip the value (SET is_frozen = NOT is_frozen) and then passed.
verification_level: production (escalation re-attempted and refused on a fresh connection AFTER the repair; the three path-(A) writes re-attempted and two confirmed working, the third intentionally blocked and fixed in code with tests) + code+test
remaining_action: Migration 033 is now applied to production as a trigger, but production still has no migration ledger (see DEPLOY-05), so nothing in the database records that. Reconcile when recorded_migrations is created.

title: Paper Sessions (the persisted, canonical paper-trading path) can never start
evidence: Built the missing persistence layer for the measurement that Requirement 14.4's correctness floor (already real) was never given anywhere to read: backend_app/backend/market_data_measurement_store.py (record_measurement, latest_measurements, MeasurementStoreUnavailable; service-role only) + migration 039_market_data_source_measurements.sql (append-only, RLS enabled, no browser-role policy, explicit REVOKE/GRANT). market_data_latency.py gained from_dict on LatencySummary and SourceMeasurement (exact inverses of to_dict, explicitly skipping derived properties) so a stored row round-trips byte-for-byte. routers/paper_trading.py's _recorded_measurements() now reads the store instead of hardcoded None. scripts/record_market_data_measurement.py is the operator CLI that runs the existing tests/perf/test_market_data_latency.py::run_experiment() and persists whatever it actually measured (never an invented/unmeasured result). tests/test_rt04_measurement_store_round_trips.py (6 tests, fake-Supabase double): round-trip fidelity, newest-row-wins per source, unknown source refused before any write, no-rows-yet is an empty dict not a fabricated pair, an unreadable store raises rather than reading as silently unmeasured. tests/test_task_28_1_session_routes.py updated for the new async seam. Full regression this session: targeted RT-04/RT-16/RT-21 suite (45 passed/1 skipped) + a broader paper/market_data pass (1676 passed, 50 skipped, 0 failed) + full validation_sweep/schema_drift/session_routes (584 passed, 2 failed -- confirmed pre-existing, unrelated billing-route findings present on the clean tree before this change). Commit 838a0ed. *** RT-04's BLOCKER IS NOT WALL-CLOCK TIME (Kiro, 2026-10-23). *** This was recorded as EXTERNAL_BLOCKED pending 'roughly a week of continuous measurement against the real production feed with real outbound network access'. Both halves of that turned out to be wrong, and the real blocker is a platform defect now recorded as DATA-03. FIRST, the network access was available. Candidate B's probe needs only TCP reachability to the venue (`probe_candidate_b` -> api.binance.com:443) -- NOT Redis and NOT the MDS process, which only Candidate A requires. Verified from this machine: the venue is reachable, CCXT connected and loaded 4,697 markets, and a direct klines fetch returns bars. So the measurement did not need INF-03's workers at all, and could have been started at any point. SECOND, the operator tool had NEVER WORKED. `scripts/record_market_data_measurement.py` ran `asyncio.run(_main(...))` and called the synchronous `run_experiment()` from inside it -- but `run_experiment` drives its own coroutines with `asyncio.run()` internally (`observe_ingest_processing_cost`, tests/perf/test_market_data_latency.py:616, and `_measure_candidate_b`'s poll loop), and asyncio refuses to start a loop inside a running one: 'RuntimeError: asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop'. The script therefore raised before reaching the persistence step and had never recorded a measurement. On the prescribed window that failure would have surfaced at the END of a multi-day run with nothing persisted. Found by running a 60-second window first; fixed structurally -- the experiment now runs at top level with no loop running, and only the genuinely async persistence gets its own asyncio.run. ALSO FIXED: `--resolve-config-from-aws` reads SUPABASE_URL/EXCHANGE_ID from the deployed vyomquant-api task definition and SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY/REDIS_URL from Secrets Manager, printing names only and never values. Persisting a measurement needs the service-role credential, and requiring an operator to hand-export four values correctly first was part of why this had not been run. It warns before a long window if the persistence credentials are still missing, rather than letting the run discover it at the end. THIRD, AND THE ACTUAL BLOCKER: with the tool fixed and the venue reachable, the run still produced NOT_MEASURED -- because the platform's OWN validator refused real exchange data: 'DATA_QUALITY: ... Found 1 outliers in close log-returns using z_score for UNKNOWN. Dataset rejected'. Measured against 12,000 live BTC/USDT 1m bars, 100% of 10,000-bar windows are rejected at every threshold from 3.0 to 10.0 because the whole window is refused on any single exceedance. See DATA-03. Running the prescribed window would not have closed this finding; it would have burned a week and produced the same NOT_MEASURED. ||| CLOSED (Kiro). A MEASUREMENT NOW EXISTS, PASSES THE FLOOR, AND IS PERSISTED IN PRODUCTION. This entry recorded 'No measurement has ever produced a result'; that was confirmed empirically first -- a read-only query of production found market_data_source_measurements present (migration 039 applied) with ZERO rows. STEP 1, DATA-03 resolved (see that entry). STEP 2, the prescribed 60s smoke run, which is what this entry asked for next: Candidate B went from NOT_MEASURED with 'DATA_QUALITY: Found 1 outliers in close log-returns ... Dataset rejected' to delivering validated windows -- 'Validation complete for BTC/USDT 1m: score=95.0, issues=1', repeatedly -- with measured=True and completeness=1.0. So DATA-03 was the whole of the blocker this entry named. THE 'THEN 7 DAYS WALL-CLOCK' WAS AN ARTEFACT OF THE HARNESS, NOT THE REQUIREMENT, and that is the finding that let this close today. The smoke run returned expected_bars=999 against a floor of >=10,000, so completeness_sample could never pass. The cause: _measure_candidate_b called `fetch_historical_ohlcv(..., limit=1000)` -- a HARDCODED 1,000 against a floor requiring DEFAULT_FLOOR.min_completeness_sample_bars = 10,000 (itself derived from 1/(1-0.9999)). Completeness here is computed from the BAR TIMESTAMPS ('a closed 1m bar is due every 60s between the oldest and the newest bar delivered'), so with a 1,000-bar request the delivered grid saturated at ~999 whatever the window length, and only NEW bars closing during the run could widen it -- ~9,000 more minutes, which is precisely the 'roughly seven days of continuous measurement' this entry and migration 039 both record. That is now fixed, and it was three defects compounding, not one. (1) STATUS. `execute_with_idempotency` wrote ExecutionStatus.COMPLETED whenever `_execute_trade_internal` reported success, and success at a venue means ACCEPTED, not FILLED -- a resting limit order and a genuine fill took the same branch. COMPLETED is operationally terminal: `OrderWatchdog._find_open_orders`, `_find_stale_orders` and `ExchangeReconciliation._get_active_orders` all select only PENDING/EXECUTING, so the row left every reconciliation population at the exact moment it most needed watching. (2) QUANTITY, and this is the one the finding's own description understated. `execution_engine.py` built the result with `float(result.filled_size or size)`. `0` is falsy in Python, so whenever the venue reported `filled=0` this substituted THE FULL REQUESTED SIZE as filled -- and `master_executor.settle_exposure` reads exactly that field to credit `recovered_exposure_coins`, the bot's only record of what it holds, while the fee row is computed from the same number. One falsy zero turned an unfilled order into phantom exposure AND a phantom fee. `float(result.avg_price or price)` had the identical bug, reporting the price we ASKED for as a price we GOT. (3) THE ROW WAS NOT WATCHABLE ANYWAY, so fixing the status alone would have been inert -- it would have swapped 'marked complete and never checked' for 'marked executing and never checked', which is worse. Every venue call in OrderWatchdog passed `order.order_id` and both population queries required `order_id IS NOT NULL`, but TRADE-12 deliberately moved the venue's identifier to `venue_order_id` (because `order_id` carries FOREIGN KEY -> orders(id)) and the engine leaves `order_id` NULL. So EVERY row the live engine created was invisible to the watchdog on both counts. Worse, `EventRouter._find_execution_by_order_id` matched the venue id taken from the exchange's own WebSocket event against `order_id` -- the platform column that never holds one -- so the fastest and most authoritative fill-confirmation path in the system resolved to None every time and the event was dropped as an unknown order. THE FIX. `classify_venue_fill` (core/models/execution_record.py) reads the venue's own status word and its own filled quantity and returns filled / partially_filled / accepted, resolving every ambiguous case to `accepted` -- under-reporting is self-correcting because the row stays EXECUTING and therefore stays in the watchdog's population, while over-reporting is not. `None` (the venue did not say) and `0` (the venue said none) are now distinguished, which is the whole defect. Only a confirmed full fill persists COMPLETED; `update_status` gained optional filled_size / avg_price / remaining_size / filled_at / exchange_status so the fill columns are actually written (they never were, so a COMPLETED row carried filled_size IS NULL and the watchdog's `fill_delta = new_filled - Decimal(order.filled_size or "0")` re-credited the entire quantity on the next poll). The engine returns 'accepted'/'partially_filled' instead of 'completed', so settle_exposure credits nothing for an unfilled order and the fee is 0. `settle_exposure` learned `partially_filled` (a real part fill is real exposure). master_executor's signal-trail write stopped being binary FILLED/FAILED, which would have recorded a LIVE resting order as FAILED. OrderWatchdog and EventRouter now resolve the venue id from `venue_order_id`, falling back to `order_id` for older recovery rows. NO NEW ExecutionStatus MEMBER, deliberately: `executionstatus` is a PostgreSQL enum (alembic d97ffff9c3bb) so SUBMITTED would need an ALTER TYPE, and EXECUTING already carries exactly this meaning everywhere else -- `_update_order_from_status` maps a venue partial fill onto it and `resolve_stale_execution` defaults its CAS to from_status=EXECUTING. ONE CORRECTION TO MY OWN WORK, recorded because the test caught it and not me: I first made `settle_exposure` REFUSE to credit a `completed` result that carried no quantity, which broke tests/test_rt06_exposure_follows_completed_fills_only.py::test_completed_without_a_reported_size_uses_the_requested_quantity. The test is right and I was wrong. `previous_exposure` gates position limits, so OVER-stating it makes the bot trade less than it could, while UNDER-stating it makes the bot believe it has room it does not have and buy again -- refusing to credit a confirmed fill is the DANGEROUS direction. The phantom exposure came from the STATUS, not that fallback; with the status corrected an accepted order never reaches the crediting branch at all. Reverted, and the reasoning is now recorded at the fallback so it is not 'fixed' again. VERIFICATION. tests/test_rt16_completed_requires_a_confirmed_fill.py -- 29 tests, real engine, real repository, real in-memory SQLite execution_records, recording double for the venue. Includes a POSITIVE CONTROL (a confirmed fill still reaches COMPLETED, so the 'not completed' assertions cannot be passing because the harness cannot complete anything) and two NEGATIVE CONTROLS that assert the PRE-FIX watchdog filter and pre-fix EventRouter lookup find nothing, so those tests fail if the engine ever starts writing order_id and silently stops proving anything. FIRST, THE CHAIN WAS MAPPED, AND ALL THREE LINKS ARE OPEN -- the entry said 'nothing feeds it', which understated it. (1) `ExchangeWebSocketListener._listen_for_orders` (watch_orders -> _handle_order_update): `start()` and `start_listening()` have no caller. (2) `EventListener._on_exchange_event` (enqueue -> _event_processing_loop): `start(event_router)` -- the ONLY code that sets `_event_router` and drains the queue -- has no caller. (3) `EventRouter.route_event` -> `_handle_filled` -> the DB: `EventRouter` and `get_event_router` have no caller and main.py imports neither. So starting link 1 alone would deliver nothing: events would be built and handed to a listener with no router. DEFECT A, FIXED: `_listen_for_orders` called `get_or_create_exchange(user_id=tenant_id, exchange_id=exchange_id)` with NO api_key, secret or password and then awaited `watch_orders()` -- an authenticated, per-account channel. Two consequences, the second worse than the first. It could not work; and because the enclosing loop is `except Exception: await asyncio.sleep(1)`, it would not fail loudly either -- it would spin once per second forever, logging what reads as a transient network error while no fill was ever delivered. And it POISONS THE SHARED POOL: the pool is keyed on (user, exchange), and CONN-01 already records this exact file by name -- 'Whichever caller populated the pool key first won, so if one of those won the race an UNAUTHENTICATED client was pooled' -- so this listener winning the race hands an unauthenticated client to every credentialed caller for that pair. Now credentials are resolved first, through the same `get_vault().load_decrypted_keys` + positional `get_or_create_exchange` shape that `api_ws/ws_routes.py::ws_user` (:813-817) already uses, and the listener REFUSES to open the stream when they are unavailable rather than connecting unauthenticated. `_load_keys` fails closed on every path -- no vault, no stored pair, undecryptable ciphertext -- which is the EXPECTED state today, not an edge case, because VAULT-01 records every stored exchange_keys ciphertext as currently undecryptable. DEFECT B, FIXED: `_on_exchange_event` added the event to `_processed_event_ids` and then queued it, with no check that anything drains the queue. On an unstarted listener that is the worst of the three possible behaviours simultaneously -- the fill is lost, the memory is not (an unbounded PriorityQueue grows for the life of the process), a later REDELIVERY of the same fill is suppressed as a duplicate because the dedup set was written first, and nothing reports any of it. It now refuses, says so at ERROR, and un-records the event so a redelivery can still arrive. Also replaced `asyncio.create_task(queue.put(...))` with `put_nowait`: the queue is unbounded so `put` never blocks, the task was overhead, and it detached the enqueue from the call so the order of two events in one tick depended on task scheduling rather than on the sequence key that exists to decide it -- and any exception vanished into an un-awaited task. That form also meant the callback could only be invoked from inside a running event loop, which the negative control below demonstrates. Residual (3), live-venue certification, is unchanged and external. ONE OBSERVATION WORTH CARRYING, measured here: `api_ws/ws_routes.py::ws_user` ALREADY runs an authenticated private stream -- watch_my_trades, watch_orders and watch_balance through DataEngine -- and broadcasts all of it to the browser. The platform therefore already READS the venue's private fill stream; it just never records it. That is the most promising wiring point AND the trap: it is per-connected-browser, created and cancelled with one websocket, so recording fills from it would make the ledger depend on whether a user happened to have a tab open -- a partial ledger that looks complete, which is worse than the current honest gap. The design degrades SAFELY rather than wrongly -- Requirement 18.15 and the key's TTL exist precisely so a dead feed reads as "no fresh price" instead of serving a stale one forever, so PAPER-02's correctness property (never silently substitute a stale figure) holds whether or not mds runs. Its task definition, command and sizing are correct and committed, and it is one command from live; it is left off because training_jobs holds 0 rows and it costs ~$98/month at 2048 cpu / 8192 MB. Start it when a job exists; until then it would be paying for an empty queue. title: Load-balancer health check cannot fail on dependency outage
evidence: Confirmed the exact mechanism before fixing it: backend_app/main.py's health() handler always returns HTTP 200 from /health -- it computes 'status': 'ok'/'degraded' from Redis/Supabase/QuestDB probes, but that result lives only in the JSON body. terraform/alb.tf's aws_lb_target_group.api health_check is a bare status-code matcher (matcher = "200"), which never reads the body, so a target with no reachable database or Redis still passed every ALB health check and kept receiving production traffic. backend_app/core/readiness.py's evaluate_readiness (added under OBS-01, confirmed by reading its module docstring and the /health/ready route) actually measures the database (every authenticated request resolves identity and RLS through it) and Redis (backs the rate limiter and the distributed execution locks outside a declared local environment) and returns a real 503 when either is down -- QuestDB/telemetry deliberately excluded, since it degrades to a mock by design and must not turn a metrics outage into a total one. Changed aws_lb_target_group.api's health_check.path from /health to /health/ready; left timeout at 5s (readiness.py's own PROBE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS is 3.0s per dependency, comfortably inside it) and matcher at "200" unchanged (503 correctly fails it). Left the websocket target group's /health/live (a different service, ws_server.py, already covered by WS-01) and the frontend target group's "/" untouched -- only the API target group's path was wrong. New tests/test_inf01_alb_health_check_targets_readiness.py (2 tests, direct text parsing of terraform/alb.tf since no terraform binary is available in this sandbox): the API target group's health_check.path is exactly /health/ready (not a substring check -- /health is itself a substring of /health/ready, so a naive check would be satisfied by the very regression this guards against) and matcher stays "200"; a second test pins the timeout staying >= 5s against readiness.py's own probe budget. Verified as a real regression test: git-stashed just the terraform/alb.tf change and reran, got the exact expected failure ('expected ... /health/ready, got /health instead'); restored and reran, green. Full regression: tests/test_inf01_alb_health_check_targets_readiness.py (2 passed) + tests/test_validation_sweep.py (376 passed, 2 skipped). terraform/alb.tf parses as valid HCL (python-hcl2; no terraform binary available in this sandbox for a real plan/validate). ADDENDUM (discovered while fixing OPS-02, commit fd6cbb2): infra/alb.sh -- a raw-AWS-CLI provisioning script, not terraform -- independently creates/reasserts the SAME API target group's health-check path on EVERY run via an unconditional `aws elbv2 modify-target-group --health-check-path "/health"`. Per INF-02 (terraform does not describe the production deployment), this script is most likely what actually configured production, meaning this finding's terraform-only fix (commit 2762ac3) would have been silently re-clobbered back to /health the next time anyone ran infra/alb.sh. Applied the same /health -> /health/ready change there too (part of the OPS-02 commit, since that is where it was found), so the two mechanisms cannot drift back out of sync.
remaining_action: APPLIED AND VERIFIED AGAINST REAL PRODUCTION AWS this session, with explicit user confirmation obtained first (relayed authorization from a prior-session message was deliberately NOT acted on by itself -- held until the user confirmed directly in this session's own conversation). BEFORE: `elbv2 DescribeTargetGroups` on target group `vyomquant-api-tg` (arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:ap-southeast-1:273709947018:targetgroup/vyomquant-api-tg/9e93b22862870f31) showed HealthCheckPath=/health. ACTION: `elbv2 ModifyTargetGroup` with HealthCheckPath=/health/ready; the API response echoed the new value immediately. AFTER: re-ran DescribeTargetGroups -- HealthCheckPath is now /health/ready. Checked DescribeTargetHealth twice, once immediately after the change and once after a longer interval spanning several of the target group's own HealthCheckIntervalSeconds=15 (so the health check logic/HealthyThresholdCount=2 had genuinely re-evaluated against the new path, not just reported a stale cached state): the single running target (10.0.10.14, ap-southeast-1a) was `healthy` both times, with no AdministrativeOverride -- production traffic was not interrupted. Also confirmed infra/alb.sh (the raw-AWS-CLI script, not terraform, that per INF-02 most likely configures production) already asserts /health/ready in its own source (both the create path and its idempotent `modify-target-group` call), so the next operator run of that script will not re-clobber this back to /health -- source and live reality now agree. terraform/alb.tf also already has the correct path (this entry's own earlier fix, commit 2762ac3), so all three of (terraform source, infra/alb.sh source, live AWS) are now consistent. Follow-up noted but out of scope, unchanged from before: /health itself still always returns 200 with a 'degraded' body for any OTHER consumer that treats 200 as proof of health (a dashboard, a synthetic monitor) -- this fix only changes what the ALB specifically checks.

title: Terraform does not describe the production deployment
evidence: This finding's remaining_action has two halves; investigated both. (1) 'Remove dead files': grepped every .tf file for `file(`/`templatefile(` and literal filenames; found terraform/route53-policy.json (a bare IAM policy JSON, no project-specific resource IDs) referenced nowhere -- not by terraform, not by any script/workflow/doc except a historical git-ls-tree-style inventory snapshot in staging/p11b22_entry_staged.txt that is itself just a listing. Removed in commit bfec458 as unambiguous dead weight. Also checked terraform/redis-only/main.tf, which LOOKS like a second dead-file candidate (a whole directory alongside the root module's own redis.tf) but is almost certainly the OPPOSITE: it is a SEPARATE, standalone root module (its own terraform{}/provider{} blocks) with hardcoded real resource identifiers (vpc-0f3e7b3f243fbc133, a real security group ID sg-0262aed02d8df0356, real subnet CIDRs) and an explicit `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true; ignore_changes = all }` guard on a replication group it calls 'deprecated' -- exactly the kind of guard someone writes around a REAL, already-existing production resource, not a throwaway file. It most likely IS the one accurate terraform description of how production Redis was actually provisioned (hardcoded against the real existing VPC/SG, applied as its own standalone `terraform apply` from a different working directory/state), predating and never consolidated into the root module's own generic, environment-parameterized redis.tf -- itself likely never actually applied to real production. This is a direct, concrete illustration of the finding's own title ('terraform does not describe the production deployment' -- there are TWO different terraform descriptions of Redis in this repository, and nothing says which one, if either, matches what AWS actually runs). Did NOT delete it -- confirming which file (if either) is accurate needs real AWS access this sandbox does not have, and deleting on a wrong guess would destroy the only record this repo has of real infrastructure. (2) 'Import live resources into Terraform state': needs real AWS credentials to run `terraform import` against the actual account -- genuinely unreachable from this sandbox.
remaining_action: The one confidently-dead file is removed. EXTERNAL_BLOCKED on the substantive half: a session with real AWS access must (1) determine whether terraform/redis-only/main.tf's resources (vyomquant-redis-production / vyomquant-redis-production-cmd) or terraform/redis.tf's resource (vyomquant-redis-${var.environment}) -- or neither -- matches what ElastiCache actually runs today; (2) consolidate to one accurate description (most likely: `terraform import` the real resource's real ID into the root module under redis.tf's resource address, then delete terraform/redis-only/ once state is confirmed to track the real thing); (3) do the same reconciliation for every other resource type in terraform/ this session did not have reason to inspect (ALB target groups and ECS services are already known, per this session's own OPS-02 finding, to be actually managed by infra/alb.sh's raw AWS CLI calls rather than by terraform at all -- the same class of drift, a different resource type). A full `terraform plan` against the real account's actual state would surface the rest precisely; guessing further from source inspection alone, without that plan output, risks the same wrong-guess-destroys-real-infra failure mode this session avoided for redis-only/main.tf. QUESTION (1) ABOVE NOW ANSWERED with real evidence this session (read-only `elasticache DescribeReplicationGroups` via the live, scoped CI credential, ap-southeast-1): exactly one real ElastiCache replication group exists account-wide -- ARN arn:aws:elasticache:ap-southeast-1:273709947018:replicationgroup:vyomquant-redis-production, ClusterMode=enabled, node_type cache.t4g.micro, config endpoint clustercfg.vyomquant-redis-production.4lf97k.apse1.cache.amazonaws.com -- which matches terraform/redis-only/main.tf's hardcoded resource (same replication_group_id, same node_type, same cluster-mode-enabled shape) exactly. terraform/redis.tf's generic vyomquant-redis-${var.environment} resource corresponds to NOTHING real; it was never applied. So: redis-only/main.tf is the accurate description; redis.tf's redis resource is dead/aspirational and should eventually be removed once (2)'s import is done. (2) and (3): the tooling gap is now closed -- terraform 1.9.8 installed into this sandbox this session (checksum-verified download), `terraform init -backend=false` + `terraform validate` both succeed against the real `~> 5.0` AWS provider for both terraform/ root and terraform/redis-only/. Still EXTERNAL_BLOCKED on the credentials-scope + state-backend side: `terraform import` needs the real state backend initialized first, and the terraform remote-state backend itself (s3://vyomquant-terraform-state, providers.tf) does not exist yet (`GetBucketLocation` -> NoSuchBucket) -- so `terraform init` against this backend would fail account-wide, for any resource type, until that bucket + the DynamoDB lock table (vyomquant-terraform-lock) are created first. That bootstrap step is itself a prerequisite for (2) and (3), not something this pass attempted (bucket/table creation is a separate, deliberate infra decision needing explicit confirmation, not a read-only check). UPDATE (AWS-equipped session, this effort): attempted the state-backend bootstrap (s3://vyomquant-terraform-state + the vyomquant-terraform-lock DynamoDB table) with real, user-confirmed AWS access. Both s3:CreateBucket and dynamodb:CreateTable are implicitDeny for this credential, confirmed via iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy (not guessed by probing with the real call). The same check revealed this credential's attached policies are actually broader than CI-02's own fix assumed -- IAMFullAccess, AmazonEC2FullAccess, AmazonECS_FullAccess, SecretsManagerReadWrite -- but S3/DynamoDB bucket/table *creation* specifically is not among them. So this is now a confirmed credential-scope gap, not an unattempted step: unblocking (2)/(3) below needs either a credential with s3:CreateBucket+dynamodb:CreateTable (or broader admin) granted to it, or someone with console/root access to create the bucket and table once, by hand, after which this same credential can very likely proceed with `terraform init`/`import` against them. FURTHER PROGRESS (this session, independently re-confirmed the same redis-only/main.tf-is-accurate / redis.tf-is-dead conclusion via a fresh `elasticache describe-replication-groups` call before reading this entry's own prior text): rather than wait on the state-backend bootstrap to formally `terraform import` and delete redis.tf, converted its dead MANAGED resource into a read-only `data "aws_elasticache_replication_group" "redis"` lookup of the real replication_group_id (vyomquant-redis-production-cmd, the cluster-mode-DISABLED one REDIS_URL/REDIS_REPLICA_URL actually point at -- note this session's own live env-var read found this to be the operative one, not the cluster-mode-enabled vyomquant-redis-production the prior session's DescribeReplicationGroups call happened to return first). terraform/outputs.tf's redis_endpoint output repointed at the data source. A `data` block has no lifecycle to protect and can never create/modify/destroy anything, so this needed no state backend, no import, and no additional credential -- it closes the 'dead/aspirational resource sitting in the applyable root module' risk immediately rather than waiting on the bootstrap. Left unresolved: the orphaned `aws_security_group.redis` in the root module's security_groups.tf (nothing in this root references it anymore); the broader resource-type reconciliation (ALB/ECS vs infra/alb.sh drift, per item (3) above) is unchanged and still needs the same state-backend bootstrap.

title: Background schedulers run in every web worker
evidence: Confirmed in main.py: start_reconciliation_scheduler() is called from the FastAPI lifespan startup hook, which every uvicorn/gunicorn web worker process runs independently -- so every worker built its own ReconciliationScheduler (core/reconciliation_scheduler.py) and polled the shared reconciliation_mismatches table every POLL_INTERVAL_SECONDS (30s) from N processes at once, each attempting to escalate the same mismatches and trigger the same kill switch redundantly. Checked RECON-01 first to confirm this is a DIFFERENT, already-running scheduler from ExchangeReconciliationService (RECON-01's subject, never started anywhere) -- did not touch RECON-01's deliberately-deferred leader-election/tenant-enumeration work, only this already-running one. Neither duplicated action was itself corrupted (the kill switch and the 'already-escalated' DB check are each idempotent on their own), so the real cost was DB/alerting load multiplied by N for no benefit. Fixed by adding _try_become_leader: a renewable Redis lease using the exact same primitive master_executor's execution lock and IdempotentExchangeSubmission.claim_submission already use (SET key value NX EX to win an unheld lease; a plain SET to renew one still held by the SAME instance id, checked via GET first, since a one-shot NX-only lock would make even the current leader lose and re-win the role every cycle). Fails CLOSED the same way those two already do -- redis_manager.get_client() returning None or raising answers 'not leader' rather than letting a per-process mock stand in for Redis outside development and silently reintroduce the N-way fan-out, exactly the failure mode tests/test_redis_fallback_does_not_fake_a_distributed_lock.py already guards the other two locks against. _loop now calls _poll_and_escalate only when leader. New tests/test_inf04_reconciliation_scheduler_leader_election.py (8 tests) against a fake Redis client backed by a store SHARED across instances (unlike MockRedisClient's per-process dict): exactly one of two schedulers wins leadership in the same cycle; the same leader renews rather than losing the role every cycle; a different instance cannot steal an active lease; a crashed leader's expired lease is picked up by another instance; Redis unreachable/erroring both fail closed; a non-leader cycle skips _poll_and_escalate entirely while a leader cycle runs it. Full regression: 6 existing reconciliation/health test files + test_redis_fallback_does_not_fake_a_distributed_lock.py (75 passed); test_validation_sweep.py (373 passed, 2 skipped).
remaining_action: None identified for ReconciliationScheduler, the scheduler this finding's own evidence names as actually running in every worker today. RECON-01's ExchangeReconciliationService remains separately, deliberately OPEN (not started anywhere at all yet, and its own leader-election + tenant-enumeration design is explicitly deferred to a dedicated session per that finding's own remaining_action) -- this fix does not close RECON-01 and was not intended to. If another in-process scheduler is added later that also runs via the FastAPI lifespan hook, it will need its own leader check; this fix is scoped to ReconciliationScheduler alone, not a generic one-leader-per-process framework.

title: Long-lived AWS keys in CI; mutable :latest tag pushed; digest fallback
evidence: Confirmed all three sub-issues directly in .github/workflows/02-build.yml and 03-deploy.yml before changing anything. (1) Mutable :latest: 02-build.yml built and pushed both $ECR_REGISTRY/$ECR_REPOSITORY:$IMAGE_TAG (the commit SHA) AND $ECR_REGISTRY/$ECR_REPOSITORY:latest. Confirmed via grep that the live deploy path never reads :latest -- scripts/ecs_deploy_and_diagnose.py builds its own image_uri as f'{ECR_REGISTRY}/vyomquant-api:{IMAGE_TAG}' where IMAGE_TAG is 03-deploy.yml's own '${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_sha || github.sha }}', i.e. always the commit SHA -- so :latest was a standing mutable pointer in the registry with no current reader, but a live risk for the first future thing that pulls by tag instead of digest/SHA. Removed the :latest build+push; only the immutable SHA tag is pushed now. (2) Digest fallback: the same step computed DIGEST via `aws ecr describe-images ... || echo "$IMAGE_TAG"` -- on a describe failure this silently set image_digest to a TAG, not a digest, with no error. Grepped every workflow and script for image_digest/outputs.image_digest: nothing currently consumes it, so this had no live blast radius, but fixed it anyway since an output that lies about its own contents on failure is a trap for whatever becomes its first reader -- now fails the step with ::error:: instead of echoing a fake digest. (3) Long-lived AWS keys: both workflows authenticate via secrets.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID/AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY through aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4 -- a standing IAM user credential, not scoped to GitHub Actions, with no expiry. NOT flipped live this pass (see remaining_action) but terraform/iam.tf now defines the OIDC provider + role a dedicated session with real AWS access needs to complete the fix: aws_iam_openid_connect_provider.github_actions (token.actions.githubusercontent.com, aud=sts.amazonaws.com) and aws_iam_role.github_actions_deploy, trusted only for this repo's main/master branches via the OIDC sub claim (terraform/variables.tf gained github_repository, default 'Narendra2212/vyomquant-saas', for that condition), with an attached policy scoped to exactly the ecr:*/ecs:*/logs:*/iam:PassRole calls 02-build.yml and scripts/ecs_deploy_and_diagnose.py actually make (enumerated by grepping every `aws ecs`/`aws ecr`/`aws logs` subcommand in both). Verified .github/workflows/02-build.yml as valid YAML (python yaml.safe_load) and terraform/iam.tf + variables.tf as valid HCL (python-hcl2 -- no terraform binary available in this sandbox for a real `terraform validate`/`plan`). Full regression: tests/test_validation_sweep.py (376 passed, 2 skipped) -- a CI/infra-config-only change touching no application code.
remaining_action: Two of three sub-issues are fully fixed and need nothing further (:latest push removed; digest fallback now fails loudly instead of lying). The long-lived-keys sub-issue is NOT flipped live: the terraform role exists only as unapplied source, and 02-build.yml/03-deploy.yml still authenticate with the static IAM user keys. This was a deliberate sequencing decision, not an oversight -- switching either workflow's configure-aws-credentials step to role-to-assume before the role actually exists in AWS would break every build and deploy outright, and this sandbox has no real AWS credentials to terraform apply it with first. title: Refunds do not revoke plan entitlement; webhook idempotency lives only in Redis for 24h
evidence: This finding has two halves; confirmed the first was already closed. (1) 'Refunds do not revoke plan entitlement': backend_app/routers/billing.py::_revoke_plan_for_refunded_razorpay_payment (BILL-01, VERIFIED_FIXED earlier this session) is called from the Razorpay refund.processed handler and revokes a fully-refunded plan, gateway-confirmed. Razorpay is the only live payment provider this deployment bills plans through (src/pages/Billing.jsx documents no live Stripe secret exists; every Stripe-only endpoint 500s by design), so BILL-01 already covers the real production path; not re-done here. (2) 'Webhook idempotency lives only in Redis for 24h': confirmed by reading both webhook handlers in billing.py: a 'processing' key (60s TTL) transitioning to 'completed' (86400s TTL) was the SOLE idempotency record. core/cache/redis_manager.py is deliberately fail-soft (every method swallows its own exception and returns a falsy default), so a Redis outage during the initial check silently read as 'not a duplicate' and the handler proceeded to reprocess a real duplicate delivery undetected -- and even with Redis healthy, a redelivery more than 24h after the first (both providers redeliver for days; an operator can manually resend an old webhook from either dashboard for reconciliation) found no record at all once the 'completed' key expired. Fixed by adding a DURABLE claim layered UNDERNEATH the existing Redis fast path (not a replacement -- preserves every existing Redis-based test's assertions unchanged): new migration backend_app/migrations/045_sec03_durable_webhook_events.sql creates public.webhook_events (UNIQUE (provider, event_id), service-role only, RLS enabled, no anon/authenticated grants), applied and verified idempotent against a real local PostgreSQL 16 instance (CREATE then re-CREATE, both clean). New core/webhook_idempotency.py (acquire_webhook_processing/mark_webhook_completed/release_webhook_processing) uses Postgres's own unique-constraint enforcement as the atomicity primitive -- no TTL to outlive. A 'processing' row older than PROCESSING_STALE_AFTER_SECONDS (60s, matching the old Redis TTL) is reclaimable, preserving the original crash-safety property. Wired into BOTH webhook handlers (Stripe and Razorpay) at every existing acquire/complete/release point, additively: Redis's own check still runs and still refuses first (unchanged, so the pre-existing tests/test_webhook_duplicate_delivery_real_redis.py -- 646 lines of real-Redis keyspace-split-proof engineering -- needed zero changes and still passes, gated as before on AERORA_TEST_REDIS_URL); the durable claim is a second, independent gate immediately after. Not configured (get_service_supabase_async() returns None -- the normal DEV_MODE/local/test shape) defers entirely to Redis rather than refusing every webhook; configured but a call raising (a real outage) fails closed. New tests/test_sec03_durable_webhook_idempotency.py (9 tests, against a fake PostgREST table reproducing real unique-constraint conflict/filter semantics): fresh acquire succeeds; a second concurrent acquire is refused; a completed delivery is refused with NO TTL (re-checked 3 times); a stale processing row is reclaimed (the crash-recovery property); release deletes a processing row (immediate retry, no staleness wait) but never touches an already-completed row (a bug this test caught and that was fixed in the test's own fake, not application code); not-configured defers to Redis rather than refusing everything; configured-but-unreachable fails closed; a static source check confirms billing.py calls all three functions at both handlers. Full regression (migration_tooling, db01_provisioning_order, webhook_duplicate_delivery_real_redis, billing_e2e, sec02_razorpay_webhook_reconciles_order, billing_hardening_and_failure_recovery_audit, validation_sweep, route_contract -- 545 tests) clean except the 2 unrelated pre-existing billing failures already confirmed earlier this session.

title: No account deletion or data export
evidence: Confirmed by grep (delete_account/account_deletion/data_export/export_user_data/anonymize) that neither feature existed anywhere in this codebase. New backend/account_lifecycle.py adds both, deliberately scoped to what can be built and verified safely from this sandbox without a real Postgres instance. export_account_data(supabase, user_id) reads every category this module knows how to read directly through the request-scoped (RLS-respecting) client -- profile, strategies, backtests, marketplace subscriptions/listings, settlements, and paper trading sessions (via the existing paper_repository.list_sessions) -- with connected exchange NAMES listed via APIKeyVault.list_connected_exchanges but decrypted API credentials themselves never exported. Each category reports its own ok/error so one failing table does not abort the export. delete_account(supabase, user_id, user) is deliberately NOT a physical cascade-delete across this repository's ~58 tables -- auditing which may legally and safely be hard-deleted without a real Postgres instance to verify against is exactly the kind of repo-wide change this session has consistently declined to improvise (the same reasoning TENANT-01's FORCE RLS wiring and RECON-01's leader election were left to a dedicated session over, cross-referenced directly in the module's own docstring). Instead it composes existing, already-tested primitives: stops every live deployment (strategy_lifecycle.stop_deployments_for_reason, the same Requirement 20.9 path the kill switch already uses), stops every RUNNING/PAUSED paper session (paper_session_service.stop_session, called the way it is already designed to be called without a live feed/task handle), revokes every connected exchange's API keys (APIKeyVault.delete_exchange_keys), and anonymises the profile's PII fields while setting is_frozen=True -- the same flag core.dependencies.get_current_user already enforces as a 403 everywhere, achieving the functional equivalent of account deletion with no new column and no migration. The profile anonymisation step is the one allowed to raise (a row that cannot be updated means the account is not deleted); the other three steps are best-effort and individually reported. Two new routes: GET /api/user/account/export and DELETE /api/user/account, the latter requiring an exact confirmation phrase in the body (422 otherwise) since there is no undo for the PII anonymisation. New tests/test_priv01_account_export_and_deletion.py (9 tests): export reads every direct table scoped to the user and never includes decrypted credentials; a failing category does not abort the export; deletion stops deployments, stops only RUNNING/PAUSED sessions (not CREATED/STOPPED), revokes every connected exchange's keys, anonymises the profile; deletion raises when the profile update matches no row; one exchange failing to revoke does not stop profile anonymisation; the export route requires auth; the delete route rejects a wrong confirmation phrase and succeeds with the exact one. Registered the new DELETE route in test_validation_sweep.py's exhaustive MUTATING_ROUTES list (its own self-enforcing coverage check caught the omission on first run). Full regression: test_user_router.py + test_validation_sweep.py (387 passed, 2 skipped). ADDITIONALLY this session: used this session's own newly-provisioned real Postgres replica (see TENANT-01's entry) to audit, for the first time with an actual schema rather than source inspection alone, exactly what a literal `DELETE FROM profiles WHERE id = ...` would do. Querying information_schema for every foreign key referencing profiles(id) found 27 referencing columns across 26 tables: 20 CASCADE (dag_tasks, exchange_connections, exchange_keys, execution_records, fills, notification_settings, orders, positions, referral_codes/_commissions/_payouts/_profiles/_relationships/_wallets, referrals, risk_settings, strategy_limits), 1 SET NULL (profiles.referred_by_user_id, a self-reference), and -- the finding that matters here -- 6 RESTRICT: billing_invoices, invoices, payment_methods, risk_settings_audit, security_logs, subscriptions. A real physical delete of the profiles row would FAIL OUTRIGHT on any of those 6 while a single row remains, by the database's own constraint, not silently leave orphans. This confirms the current anonymise-and-revoke implementation's reasoning is not merely 'safe because this sandbox lacked Postgres to verify against' -- it is the ARCHITECTURALLY CORRECT choice independent of that: making a real hard-delete work would mean either resolving those 6 tables' own rows first (destroying exactly the audit/financial history BILL-01, AUD-01 and SEC-xx's own findings in this same ledger depend on existing durably -- security_logs and risk_settings_audit by name) or relaxing their RESTRICT constraints (which would re-open exactly the kind of accidental data loss those constraints exist to prevent). If the product's actual legal/compliance requirement is physical erasure rather than anonymisation + access revocation, the real design question a future session should resolve is narrower than before: not 'can we cascade-delete 58 tables' but specifically 'what should happen to these 6 financial/audit tables' historical rows under an erasure request' -- a business/legal policy question (does erasure override retention?), not a technical blocker, and one this sandbox does not have the authority to answer on its own. RESOLVED this session: asked the product owner directly whether the real legal/compliance obligation requires physical erasure of historical data on account deletion, or whether anonymising PII + revoking access while retaining financial/audit history (this entry's existing implementation) is sufficient. Answer: anonymisation + access revocation IS sufficient. This was the one open question this entry's own remaining_action named as blocking closure -- with it answered, the existing implementation (export_account_data / delete_account in backend/account_lifecycle.py, 9 tests in tests/test_priv01_account_export_and_deletion.py, both already built and tested in an earlier pass this remediation effort) meets the real requirement as designed. The FK-constraint audit against this session's own real Postgres replica (see above) independently confirmed the same conclusion from the schema side: 6 tables RESTRICT a physical delete outright while they hold financial/audit history for that user, so a hard-delete implementation would have had to either destroy that history or fight those constraints -- neither necessary now that anonymisation is confirmed sufficient.
remaining_action: None. The one open question (does the real legal/compliance requirement exceed anonymisation + access revocation) has been answered by the product owner: no, the current implementation already meets the real requirement. No further action needed.

title: Privilege-hardening backstop does not detect RLS-disabled customer tables
evidence: Confirmed the defect by reading scripts/post_migration_validation.py section 3 ("VALIDATING RLS STATUS"): it checked rowsecurity only for tables already named in the required_tables list defined at the top of the same function -- the same list section 1 checks for existence. A table a later migration grants anon or authenticated a privilege on (Supabase grants most new tables a default privilege shape automatically) but never gets ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY would not be examined at all unless someone also remembered to add its name to this list -- the exact gap the title names. Separately, the script never called sys.exit(1) despite importing sys, so even a FAILED line printed to stdout left the process exiting 0. Fixed both: fetch_privileged_tables_without_rls(cur) now asks the catalog directly (pg_tables joined against information_schema.table_privileges for grantee IN ('anon','authenticated')) for every table either role can touch, with no table name hardcoded anywhere; evaluate_privilege_hardening(rows) is the pure decision half (same fetch/evaluate split already used in scripts/verify_rls.py), and validate_production_db() now returns that result, with __main__ calling sys.exit(1) when it fails. VERIFIED AGAINST A REAL POSTGRESQL 16 SERVER (this session's own local instance): created a table named db03_brand_new_customer_table_not_on_any_list -- confirmed absent from required_tables by inspecting validate_production_db's own source -- granted authenticated SELECT on it with RLS left disabled, and proved the new check finds it anyway (fetch_privileged_tables_without_rls returns it; evaluate_privilege_hardening fails). Negative controls: enabling RLS on that same table makes the check pass; a table with no anon/authenticated grant at all is never flagged even with RLS disabled (service-only tables are a normal, intentional configuration). New tests/test_db03_privilege_hardening_detects_untracked_tables_postgres.py (4 tests, real Postgres) and tests/test_db03_privilege_hardening_pure_logic.py (5 tests, no database) all passed. tests/test_migration_tooling.py (36 tests, pre-existing, covers this same file's import-of-os regression) still passes.

All six now read SUPABASE_ANON_KEY from the environment (test_currency_repro.py via setdefault on SUPABASE_URL plus a presence check on SUPABASE_ANON_KEY, so a caller's own value still wins) and exit with a clear message naming the missing variable when it is unset, rather than silently falling back to the committed credential. New tests/test_sec06_no_hardcoded_supabase_jwt_in_scripts.py (187 tests): a JWT-shaped-literal regex scan across every file in scripts/ (not just the six named, so a seventh script reintroducing the pattern is caught the same way) finds none; each of the six named scripts is executed as a subprocess with SUPABASE_ANON_KEY unset and asserted to exit non-zero naming that variable (three of the six import playwright at module level before anything this fix touches -- those three skip gracefully, not fail, in an environment where playwright is not installed, rather than reporting a false negative about the env-var guard); and a static source check confirms each reads os.environ.get("SUPABASE_ANON_KEY") rather than some other hardcoded source. remaining_action: SUPABASE_URL (the project's own Supabase domain, not a secret -- it is also decodable from inside the JWT's own claims, which is what made this an anon-key finding and not a URL-confidentiality one) was deliberately left hardcoded in the five scripts that had it as a bare constant; SEC-06 and its remediation note ("Read from env") name the JWT specifically. Credential rotation for the leaked anon key itself (now that it has been in git history) is an operator action this sandboxed session cannot perform; anon keys are designed to be client-exposed and are gated entirely by RLS, so this is a hygiene/policy fix, not a live-exploit fix.

WHY 2.0.1 BREAKS THE DEADLOCK, AND WHY A GREP WOULD MISS IT: razorpay 2.0.x STILL CONTAINS the string pkg_resources, so searching for it says nothing changed. The import MOVED. In 1.4.1 it is at client.py:4, unconditional, module level. In 2.0.1 it is at client.py:109, inside `_get_version()`, in the `except ImportError` arm of a try that reaches for importlib.metadata first. importlib.metadata is stdlib from Python 3.8, so on this project's 3.11 the fallback CANNOT fire. 2.0.1's module-level imports are os, json, requests, warnings, random, time and types -- nothing from setuptools. PROVEN BY CONSTRUCTION, NOT BY READING.
