title: No version rollback procedure; the 'rollback' script takes the API off the load balancer and the deploy script always prints 'Readiness Score: 100%'
evidence: Confirmed both halves of the title precisely before fixing anything. (1) infra/rollback.sh ran `aws ecs update-service --load-balancers "[]"` -- which DETACHES the ALB from the ECS service entirely, an outage command, not a rollback: every existing target is deregistered and nothing new attaches, regardless of which task definition the service runs, and running the script again cannot undo it (there is no load balancer left to detach). Rewrote it to mirror scripts/ecs_deploy_and_diagnose.py's own rollback_to_task_def() (the function the deploy pipeline's self-healing path already calls automatically on a failed forward deploy): read the live service's current task definition, compute the previous revision, confirm, then `update-service --task-definition <arn>` with neither --load-balancers nor --force-new-deployment (the latter interferes with the native ECS circuit breaker, per that function's own docstring) -- the load balancer attachment is never touched. An optional arg overrides the target to roll back further. (2) infra/deploy.sh printed a hardcoded `echo "[SUMMARY] Readiness Score: 100%"` after every run, regardless of how many of its four post-deployment checks printed [WARN] -- confirmed by reading the script directly, no conditional guarded that line. Each check now counts toward CHECKS_TOTAL/CHECKS_WARNED and the summary computes a real percentage; the script now exits 1 if anything warned. Its endpoint check also moved from /health to /health/ready (this session's own INF-01 fix: /health always answers 200 regardless of dependency state). DISCOVERED while fixing this, not part of the original title: infra/alb.sh -- a raw-AWS-CLI provisioning script, not terraform -- independently creates/reasserts the SAME API target group's health-check path on EVERY run via an unconditional `aws elbv2 modify-target-group --health-check-path "/health"`. Per INF-02 (terraform does not describe the production deployment), this script is most likely what actually configured production, meaning INF-01's terraform-only fix would have been silently re-clobbered back to /health the next time anyone ran this script. Applied the same /health -> /health/ready change here too, in this same commit, so the two mechanisms cannot drift back out of sync. New tests/test_ops02_rollback_keeps_load_balancer_attached.py (5 tests): runs the REAL infra/rollback.sh as a subprocess against a fake `aws` executable on PATH (logs every invocation, answers ecs describe-services/update-service/wait) -- not a reimplementation of its logic in Python. Confirms the update-service call targets revision 145 (one before the fake's reported running 146) and contains neither --load-balancers nor --force-new-deployment; confirms declining the confirmation prompt makes no AWS mutation at all; bash -n syntax checks for both scripts; a source-level check that infra/deploy.sh's score is computed, not the literal string '100%'. Verified as real regression tests: git-stashed both script changes and reran, got exactly the expected failures (the old --load-balancers "[]" call logged; the literal 100% string still present); restored and reran, green. Full regression: tests/test_ops02_rollback_keeps_load_balancer_attached.py (5 passed) + tests/test_validation_sweep.py (376 passed, 2 skipped). All three edited scripts pass bash -n.
remaining_action: All three scripts (infra/rollback.sh, infra/deploy.sh, infra/alb.sh) now behave correctly in source; NONE of this has been run against a real AWS account (no credentials in this sandbox), so the fake-aws subprocess tests verify the exact commands constructed and their arguments, not that AWS actually accepts them or that `aws ecs wait services-stable` behaves as assumed against a real service. A session with real AWS access should do one supervised rollback rehearsal end to end before trusting this under real incident pressure. Also not addressed: this ledger's own INF-02 finding (terraform does not describe the production deployment) means infra/alb.sh, infra/ecs.sh etc. and terraform/*.tf can still independently diverge on anything else neither this fix nor INF-01 touched -- fixing that class of drift generally is INF-02's job, not this one's.

Generated the real token, stored it in Secrets Manager (vyomquant/production/metrics_scrape_token), and created both ALB listener rules via elbv2 CreateRule directly (priority 5: /metrics* + header X-Metrics-Token matching the token -> forward to the API target group; priority 6: /metrics* alone -> fixed 403). title: Paper session loops run in the web process and die silently; the terminal state that was supposed to make that visible had never been applied to production
evidence: Root cause fixed: backend_app/routers/paper_trading.py::start_paper_session now resolves get_service_supabase() (non-expiring) and hands it to _session_loop_spawner instead of the caller RLS-scoped client built from user["access_token"] (a Supabase JWT expiring in ~1 hour). Every statement the loop reaches already carries an explicit user_id/session_id predicate re-checked against the returned row (paper_repository.read_session and siblings), so the service-role swap does not weaken tenant isolation on this path. A missing service-role credential now refuses the start (503 PAPER_PERSISTENCE_UNAVAILABLE) instead of silently falling back to the expiring client. Regression: tests/test_paper04_session_loop_outlives_the_callers_jwt.py (4 tests, code+test, verified this session) + tests/test_task_28_1_session_routes.py updated (service-role identity assertions, version-row seeding on the service double). Full paper-trading suite (1584 passed, 50 skipped) and validation_sweep/schema_drift (480 passed / 2 known pre-existing unrelated billing failures) clean. ||| THE TERMINAL-STATE HALF IS DONE (Kiro); THE HOSTING HALF IS NOT, AND THIS STAYS OPEN FOR IT. This entry named two needs: '(1) RT-23's dedicated runtime worker service (or equivalent) to run session loops outside the web process; (2) a FAILED or similar terminal state + migration, and a boot-time reconciliation pass that resumes or fails a RUNNING session whose task is gone.' (2) is delivered. (1) is untouched. ABANDONED, a FIFTH state where Requirement 17.7 names four, and the deviation IS the fix: none of the four can carry 'was RUNNING, and the process that ran its loop is gone' -- RUNNING is false; PAUSED is false AND invites a resume that cannot work; STOPPED makes an unplanned death indistinguishable from an orderly stop_session, which is this finding's own confusion; CREATED denies that it ran. ABANDONED rather than FAILED because FAILED reads as a claim about the strategy and this is not one -- the session may have been performing perfectly when its host disappeared. THE HAZARD THAT SHAPED IT, and the reason this is not just a sweep: a boot pass marking every RUNNING row ABANDONED would be WORSE than the defect. startup.sh runs gunicorn --workers ${WORKERS:-2}, so a worker restarting while another healthily runs sessions would abandon LIVE sessions and report real in-flight paper trading as a crash. 'Is this row's loop alive?' is not answerable from the row's state, nor by asking the local process, because the owner may be a different one. title: Any access_token in the URL hash becomes the session (login CSRF)
evidence:
Switched the Supabase client to PKCE: src/supabase.js now passes flowType: 'pkce' to createClient (alongside the pre-existing persistSession/autoRefreshToken/detectSessionInUrl: true). This is the actual fix the prior FE-01 pass (commit 83c8a8c) identified but did not attempt. A legitimate OAuth (signInWithOAuth) / magic-link (signInWithOtp) / sign-up-confirmation (signUp) redirect now lands as '?code=...' instead of '#access_token=...', and @supabase/auth-js only exchanges that code for a session if THIS browser also holds the matching code_verifier it generated locally when the flow started -- confirmed by reading node_modules/@supabase/auth-js/dist/main/GoTrueClient.js: _isPKCECallback requires both params.code AND a stored '<storageKey>-code-verifier'; an attacker's own valid code has no verifier in the victim's browser, so exchangeCodeForSession fails and no session is adopted. Also confirmed, in that same source, a second-order effect: with flowType:'pkce' configured, _getSessionFromURL now actively throws AuthPKCEGrantCodeExchangeError('Not a valid PKCE flow url.') on a stray '#access_token=' hash (a flow-type mismatch) instead of silently adopting it. This matters because the prior FE-01 pass's path-allowlist narrowing of this app's OWN hand-rolled hash parsing (getEffectiveToken/PasswordRecoveryHandler) never touched the BIGGER hole: supabase-js's own detectSessionInUrl independently adopts an implicit hash on ANY route the instant the page loads, before any app/router code runs, and bridges the resulting SIGNED_IN event into this app's sessionStorage via the onAuthStateChange listener already present in PasswordRecoveryHandler -- regardless of the app-level path allowlist. PKCE closes that SDK-level path too, not just this app's own duplicate of it; this escalates the original finding's severity assessment of how exploitable the pre-PKCE implicit flow actually was.

Updated every dependent path in src/App.jsx: (1) renamed _isLegitimateAuthHashLandingPath -> _isLegitimateAuthRedirectLandingPath (same 4-path allowlist: AUTH_REDIRECT_PATH/signin/signup/root), since it now gates a '?code=' query param, not a hash; (2) getEffectiveToken() no longer reads window.location.hash at all -- the manual access_token-adoption branch (both the original unconditional version and the first FE-01 pass's path-allowlisted version) is deleted outright, not re-narrowed, since a legitimate redirect never produces that shape under PKCE and the SDK itself now refuses it; (3) added hasPendingAuthCodeExchange() and a new useGuardedAuthToken() hook so AuthGuard/GuestGuard correctly handle that a PKCE exchange is an async network round-trip (exchangeCodeForSession), unlike the old synchronous hash read: on first render of an allowlisted path carrying '?code=', the guards now show a brief 'Completing sign-in...' state and await supabase.auth.getSession() (which awaits the SDK's own initializePromise -- confirmed in GoTrueClient.js) rather than bouncing an arriving user to /signin before the exchange has resolved -- a behaviour change the task's own brief anticipated ('the client library handles the exchange differently'). AuthGuard/GuestGuard exported for direct testing. (4) PasswordRecoveryHandler's own non-recovery access_token-from-hash branch is deleted (dead code under PKCE), replaced by a branch that forwards a resolving '?code=' landing on '/', '/signin' or '/signup' to AUTH_REDIRECT_PATH once supabase.auth.getSession() confirms a session -- mirroring what the deleted hash branch used to do for those same three paths. Its type=recovery branch is UNCHANGED (still hash-based, still outside this app's control): re-confirmed this session that src/ has no resetPasswordForEmail call site anywhere, and found no 'forgot password' UI entry point either, so this frontend still neither generates nor can safely allowlist that email's redirect.

NEW RISK IDENTIFIED AND DOCUMENTED IN CODE (src/supabase.js, PasswordRecoveryHandler): switching this client's flowType to 'pkce' means supabase-js's OWN internal session detection will now REJECT an implicit-shaped '#access_token=...&type=recovery' hash as a flow-type mismatch rather than silently adopting it into its real internal session -- and supabase.auth.updateUser() on /reset-password needs THAT internal session (confirmed in GoTrueClient.js: _updateUser throws AuthSessionMissingError without one), not just this app's own hand-rolled sessionStorage bookkeeping. So IF the out-of-band recovery email is still implicit-shaped, completing a password reset could now fail where it previously (insecurely) succeeded. Cannot be tested without a live project and without knowing what currently generates that email; flagged explicitly rather than assumed either way.

Tests: added tests/unit/lib/supabaseClientConfig.test.js (mocks createClient with env vars stubbed past validateSupabaseConfig, proves flowType:'pkce' is passed); replaced tests/unit/authHashLandingPath.test.jsx with tests/unit/authPkceRedirect.test.jsx (14 tests: the renamed allowlist; getEffectiveToken no longer trusting ANY hash on ANY path including the formerly-allowlisted one; hasPendingAuthCodeExchange; AuthGuard/GuestGuard's pending-then-resolved rendering against a mocked supabase.auth.getSession, including the fast synchronous path staying synchronous when there is nothing to wait for); updated tests/unit/lib/supabaseUnconfiguredClient.test.js (added the new getSession call site to the stand-in client's contract and its drift guard, so the unconfigured-Supabase fallback path -- the one most of this test suite actually runs under, since there is no VITE_SUPABASE_URL in the test environment -- still resolves rather than hanging a guard that awaits it); updated tests/unit/pages/authRedirectOrigin.test.jsx (its 'reachable on arrival' assertion described the OLD synchronous-hash mechanism verbatim; rewritten to assert the new async/PKCE mechanism instead, and fixed two false-positive matches its own call-site scanner picked up from prose in this commit's code comments that happened to contain the literal text 'supabase.auth.updateUser()'). 137/137 tests pass across the 8 FE-01-relevant test files (authPkceRedirect, supabaseClientConfig, supabaseUnconfiguredClient, authRedirectOrigin, auth_otp, authOtpFe04, auth_oauth, apiClient); the full frontend suite (tests/unit/**, the whole repo) was also run end-to-end for a broader regression check -- see this ledger update's own commit message for that result.
verification_level: code+test, no live Supabase project to verify the real OAuth/magic-link/recovery round-trip
remaining_action: Needs a live Supabase project (flowType: 'pkce' enabled on a real project) and a real OAuth provider (Google) to confirm end-to-end: (a) signInWithOAuth actually redirects back with '?code=' and exchangeCodeForSession succeeds against the locally stored verifier; (b) the magic-link email in signInWithOtp carries a '?code=' link and clicking it in the SAME browser that requested it signs the user in (PKCE magic links are known to fail across browsers/devices by design -- this app's PRIMARY sign-in path is the 6-digit verifyOtp code, which is unaffected by flowType entirely, so this is a secondary-entry-point risk, not a primary-flow regression, but still unverified); (c) the sign-up confirmation link behaves the same way; (d) AuthGuard's new pending/loading state actually resolves correctly against a real network round-trip and real timing, not just the mocked getSession() this session used. Separately and explicitly: the password-RECOVERY redirect gap is UNCHANGED by this fix, not closed -- this frontend still has no resetPasswordForEmail call site and so still cannot control or allowlist the recovery email's redirect, exactly as the prior FE-01 pass documented. Worse, this fix may have introduced a NEW regression risk specifically for recovery that also needs live verification: supabase-js's own internal session detection will now refuse an implicit-shaped recovery hash as a flow-type mismatch (rather than silently adopting it as before), and supabase.auth.updateUser() on /reset-password depends on that internal session being established -- so if whatever currently generates the recovery email is still implicit-flow-shaped, completing a password reset could now fail where it previously (insecurely) succeeded. This needs someone with access to a live project to first determine what actually generates that email today (no in-app 'forgot password' UI was found either, so it may not even be reachable in practice) and then confirm whether /reset-password still works. A proper, separate fix for the recovery gap itself would be adding a 'forgot password' flow to this frontend that calls resetPasswordForEmail directly with its own explicit redirectTo (so the SAME PKCE-aware client that requests the reset is the one that completes it) -- out of scope for this commit, which only switches the flows this frontend already controls.

title: The web app is served without a Content-Security-Policy
evidence: Confirmed by reading algo22-terminal/index.html and .github/workflows/06-frontend-deploy.yml: this SPA is built by Vite and synced straight to an S3 bucket behind CloudFront (no origin server at request time, unlike the API's own SecurityHeadersMiddleware in backend_app/main.py, which already sends a tightened nonce+hash CSP but only on backend-served responses) -- index.html carried no CSP at all, meta or header, and could not easily be given one without weakening it: three inline <script> blocks (local-dev detection, a Sentry loader, a GA/Clarity loader) would have forced 'unsafe-inline' into script-src the moment a CSP was added, which defeats most of what a CSP is for. Fixed both problems together. (1) The three inline scripts moved verbatim (same isDummy/local-detection/loader logic, now reading import.meta.env.VITE_* instead of index.html's %VITE_X% token substitution -- equivalent at build time, Vite's native mechanism either way) into algo22-terminal/src/bootstrap.js, a same-origin ES module loaded via <script type="module" src="/src/bootstrap.js"> ahead of main.jsx -- already covered by script-src 'self' with no extra grant needed. (2) index.html now carries <meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy"> with script-src 'self' plus only the origins this build actually loads scripts from (confirmed by grep of src/: js.sentry-cdn.com, www.googletagmanager.com, www.clarity.ms, checkout.razorpay.com for the one real payment path this platform has -- Stripe origins deliberately excluded, since src/pages/Billing.jsx documents this deployment has no live Stripe secret and every Stripe-only endpoint 500s by design) -- no unsafe-inline, no unsafe-eval anywhere in the policy. connect-src covers every API-hostname topology the deploy workflow's own allow-list names (same-origin CloudFront proxy, api.vyomquant.in, or the raw CloudFront domain) plus the wildcarded Supabase, Sentry, Clarity and GA hosts the app actually calls. A meta-tag CSP cannot carry frame-ancestors/sandbox/report-uri (browsers ignore those three outside an HTTP header per the HTML spec) -- documented in index.html's own comment and left to INF-02 (terraform does not describe the production deployment; a CloudFront response-headers policy is the real fix for that gap, and this session has no AWS credentials to apply one even if terraform described the live distribution). New tests/unit/csp_fe02.test.js (11 tests): the CSP meta tag exists; script-src is 'self' plus https-only named origins with no unsafe-inline/unsafe-eval and no directive left empty; every remaining <script> tag in index.html either names a same-origin src or is the non-executable application/ld+json block (browsers do not run it as script and CSP's script-src does not gate it); bootstrap.js loads before main.jsx in document order; bootstrap.js's isDummyValue/detectLocal/runBootstrap reproduce the exact old inline-script behaviour (dummy/placeholder/test/unset id -> harmless local-only stub and no third-party script injected; a real-looking id -> the real Sentry/GA/Clarity loader script injected with that id). `npm run build` with the real Vite config still produces a working dist/index.html carrying the CSP meta tag and zero occurrences of VITE_SENTRY_DSN/VITE_GA_TRACKING_ID/VITE_CLARITY_PROJECT_ID (confirming the token substitution moved to bootstrap.js's bundled output correctly, verified by grepping the emitted entry chunk for __VQ_LOCAL__/clarity.ms/sentry-cdn, all present).
remaining_action: This closes the "served without a CSP" gap in the one place this session can reach (the committed index.html). NOT done: a CloudFront response-headers policy or ALB header (the HTTP-header form of CSP, which alone can add frame-ancestors for real clickjacking protection and survives even if a future edit strips the meta tag) -- that is infrastructure this session has no AWS credentials to touch and that INF-02 already records as undescribed by the repo's own terraform. The remediation note's 'attach WAF, enable logging' half is unchanged for the same reason.

THE TWO DIVERGENT DOCUMENT SETS ARE NOW ONE. components/legal/LegalPage.jsx held the prose inline AND src/pages/LegalPage.jsx held a second, different set; both were routed and served, and they CONTRADICTED each other on a material commercial term -- components/legal promised 'pro-rated service credits', pages/LegalPage said 'All purchases are final and non-refundable' (its line 312). Which page a customer happened to open decided whether they were owed money. pages/LegalPage.jsx is DELETED, /legal redirects to /legal/terms so existing links keep working, and everything renders from algo22-terminal/src/legal/documents.js. ACCEPTANCE TRACKING IS BUILT AND LIVE IN PRODUCTION. Migration 052_legal_acceptance.sql applied after a trial-then-rollback (browser write surface unchanged at 143 grants both times) and INDEPENDENTLY VERIFIED: table present with all 8 columns, uq_legal_acceptances_user_version in place, RLS enabled, anon holds NO privilege at all, authenticated may SELECT only, and APPEND-ONLY IS PROVEN RATHER THAN DOCUMENTED -- both UPDATE and DELETE were attempted against a sentinel row and both were refused by trg_legal_acceptances_append_only. A repeat insert was confirmed idempotent. 182 existing profiles have no acceptance row, so all 182 will be prompted once, which is the correct answer for every account created before the mechanism existed. The server does NOT trust the client's version string: core/legal_documents.py holds its own LEGAL_VERSION, refuses an unpublished version with a 409 naming the current one, and refuses partial acceptance outright rather than storing it. tests/test_legal01_documents_and_acceptance.py asserts the frontend and backend version constants agree, so a one-sided bump cannot record agreement to text the other side never had. Signup now POSTs the acceptance after OTP verification -- the only point in that flow where a session exists, since the password step deliberately signs out. ANALYTICS NOW REQUIRE CONSENT. Google Analytics and Microsoft Clarity previously loaded on first paint, before any interaction, while the Privacy Policy claimed 'We do not use third-party tracking or advertising cookies'. With global signups and GDPR language both in scope, disclosure alone is not consent. src/legal/consent.js defaults to DENIED (tests for an explicit grant rather than the absence of a refusal), bootstrap.js injects nothing until consent and installs inert stubs that DROP rather than queue events so a later grant cannot replay pre-consent behaviour, and CookieConsent.jsx gives Accept and Reject equal prominence with no pre-ticked box and no cookie wall. Sentry is deliberately NOT gated: it is error diagnostics under legitimate interest, declared as such, and gating crash reporting would lose the crashes of exactly the visitors who never answer a banner. Withdrawal is honest about its one limit -- it stops further sending but cannot unload an already-executed tag without a reload, which both the module and the Policy state. VERIFICATION: 356 tests pass (28 new LEGAL-01 tests plus test_no_secrets_in_bundle, test_sec06_no_hardcoded_supabase_jwt_in_scripts, test_schema_table_reference_drift, test_migration_tooling); `npx vite build` succeeds; eslint reports 0 errors on every touched file; the full FastAPI app imports with /api/legal/current, /api/legal/acceptance and /api/legal/accept mounted. ENTITY DETAILS SUPPLIED AND VALIDATED, AND THE TWO CONTROL GAPS CLOSED, 2026-10-23. ALL FOUR PLACEHOLDERS ARE GONE. The product owner supplied them and each was validated before publication, because a wrong statutory identifier in a Terms of Service is WORSE than a placeholder: a placeholder is visibly unfinished, a wrong number looks finished. legalName='Aerora Dynamics Private Limited' (corroborated independently -- src/utils/razorpayCheckout.js already defaults the checkout merchant name to 'Aerora Dynamics'); CIN='U26515UP2024PTC206131', parsed to U/26515/UP/2024/PTC/206131 with the state agreeing with the registered address and the ownership code PTC agreeing with the declared Private Limited form; GSTIN='09ABBCA0242R1ZI', whose CHECK DIGIT WAS COMPUTED INDEPENDENTLY VIA THE MOD-36 ALGORITHM AND AGREES ('I'), with state code 09 = Uttar Pradesh matching the address and the PAN's 4th character 'C' = Company matching a Pvt Ltd; PIN='285122', consistent with a Mohammdabad locality in Jalaun district (285001 is Orai town itself). The PIN is now embedded in ENTITY.address in Indian postal order rather than concatenated at three call sites, and the CIN and GSTIN -- previously DEFINED BUT NEVER RENDERED -- are now published in Terms section 1, which the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules 2020 expect of a GST-registered seller. ONE OBSERVATION RECORDED FOR COUNSEL RATHER THAN QUIETLY ACCEPTED: the CIN's industry code 26515 sits in the instruments and measuring-devices range, not software or financial services. That is a fact about the incorporation and not an error in these documents, but a reviewer will reasonably ask whether the registered object covers operating a trading platform. Added to REVIEW_NOTES. CONTROL GAP 1 CLOSED -- RESTRICTED JURISDICTIONS. Terms section 3 required the user not to be in a comprehensively sanctioned jurisdiction, signups are global, and NOTHING IN CODE CHECKED IT: the clause was a sentence with no mechanism, which is the same defect class this whole finding is about. backend_app/core/restricted_jurisdictions.py now enforces it at signup (CU, IR, KP, SY -- the comprehensive programmes the clause's own wording describes) and the declaration is recorded on the acceptance row. IT IS DELIBERATELY DESCRIBED AS A DECLARED-COUNTRY GATE AND NOT AS SANCTIONS SCREENING, in the module docstring, the migration comment and the column COMMENT: nothing verifies the declaration (no IP geolocation, no KYC, no document check -- the schema has no identity fields at all), no SDN/UN/EU/UK list is consulted, and a country code cannot express region-level measures such as those applying to parts of Ukraine. Calling it screening would be exactly the kind of false statement being fixed elsewhere in this finding. DELIBERATELY_NOT_BLOCKED records RU, BY, MM, VE, CN and UA with the reason each is left out, so the omissions read as decisions rather than oversights. CONTROL GAP 2 CLOSED -- AGE. The 18+ requirement is now an explicit, recorded attestation at signup instead of a sentence nobody captured. Still a representation -- there is no age or identity verification anywhere -- and the column COMMENT says so. MIGRATION 053 APPLIED AND INDEPENDENTLY VERIFIED. Trial-then-rollback first (browser write surface unchanged at 143 grants both times), then applied. Verified in production: both columns present, BOTH NULLABLE BY DESIGN -- a NOT NULL with a backfill would manufacture a legal representation the user never made, which is worse than an honest NULL, so NULL can only ever mean 'row predates this column' -- shape constraint and partial index installed, and THE CONSTRAINT WAS PROVEN rather than assumed: it refused 'india', 'IND', 'i' and '12' and accepted 'IN' with age_confirmed=true. The restricted LIST is deliberately NOT encoded in a CHECK, because it is a legal input counsel must be able to change without a migration, and baking it in would make every revision a schema change and would retroactively invalidate rows recorded under a previous list. A test asserts the list is absent from the SQL. REQUIRED AT SIGNUP, OPTIONAL ON RE-ACCEPTANCE, for a reason: an existing user prompted by a version change is being asked to accept new TEXT, and re-demanding a country declaration there would either lock them out of their own account or collect a value the prompt never asked for. A restricted value is still refused if offered. VERIFICATION: 55 LEGAL-01 tests pass (up from 36), including one that recomputes the GSTIN check digit, one that cross-checks the CIN's state against the address and its ownership code against the declared company form, one that asserts no placeholder pattern survives anywhere in the rendered documents, and one that asserts the restricted-jurisdiction module still describes itself as a declaration rather than screening. `npx vite build` succeeds; eslint reports 0 errors on every touched file; the app imports with all three /api/legal routes mounted. GDPR SCOPE DECIDED AND ITS ENGINEERING CONSEQUENCES BUILT, 2026-10-23. The product owner chose to accept customers GLOBALLY INCLUDING THE EU AND UK rather than take the cheaper route of restricting signups away from those jurisdictions. That is the HARDER path, and it makes GDPR and UK GDPR apply in full rather than conditionally, so the obligations were worked through rather than noted. ARTICLE 27 APPLIES AND IS NOT EXEMPT, established rather than assumed. Article 27 obliges a controller established outside the Union to designate a representative in writing where it offers goods or services to people in the EU OR MONITORS THEIR BEHAVIOUR. BOTH LIMBS APPLY: the owner accepts EU customers, and this platform runs Google Analytics and Microsoft Clarity, which is behaviour monitoring. Article 27(2)'s exemptions are narrow -- occasional processing, no large-scale special-category data, unlikely to risk rights -- and session analytics across every consenting visitor is not occasional. A SEPARATE UK REPRESENTATIVE is required on the same basis. THE REPRESENTATIVES ARE AN APPOINTMENT, NOT CODE, SO THE GAP IS MADE VISIBLE RATHER THAN OMITTED. ENTITY.euRepresentative and ENTITY.ukRepresentative render in Privacy section 1 as '[NOT YET APPOINTED - ...]' with the reason and an interim contact. Omitting the section would have read as 'not required', which is the opposite of true, and is precisely the class of misleading-by-silence this finding was opened about. A test asserts the placeholders are PRESENT while unappointed and instructs that it be inverted once they are. ARTICLE 30 RECORDS OF PROCESSING ACTIVITIES NOW EXIST: docs/legal/RECORDS_OF_PROCESSING.md. This is a hard obligation the moment EU/UK users are accepted, and it was written FROM THE CODEBASE rather than from intent -- twelve processing activities, each with its purpose, lawful basis, data categories, source table or module, recipients, retention and transfers, with file paths cited so a reviewer can verify each line. Where an earlier policy statement and the code disagreed, the code won. It also records WHAT IS NOT PROCESSED, because those absences are load-bearing: no custody of funds or assets (which is the factual basis for the PMLA position), no KYC, no Article 9 special-category data (which is the basis for the DPIA screening conclusion), no Article 22 automated decision-making with legal effect. And it records its OWN GAPS in a dedicated section -- a ROPA listing only what is in order is a sales document, and a supervisory authority reading it would find the gaps anyway. IT ALSO DECLINES TO OVERSTATE. The ROPA records that copilot conversation history is NEVER PERSISTED, because migration 018's own header documents that every copilot write sits inside a try/except that only logs. Claiming to hold conversation data that does not exist would be inaccurate in the direction that looks WORSE for us, which is still inaccurate. A test asserts this. THREE SPECIFIC GDPR SHORTFALLS IN THE PRIVACY POLICY WERE FOUND AND FIXED: (1) the response period said '30 DAYS', which is close to but not Article 12(3)'s period -- it now says WITHIN ONE MONTH and discloses the two-month extension for complex requests, since relying on an extension never disclosed is worse than not having it; (2) breach notification said only 'within the time the law requires' -- it now commits explicitly to notifying the SUPERVISORY AUTHORITY WITHIN 72 HOURS where rights are likely to be at risk, to telling the data subject directly without undue delay where the risk is HIGH, and to keeping a record of every breach whether notifiable or not; (3) Article 22 was unaddressed -- the Policy now states we do NOT make purely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effect, which is worth saying on a platform where software places orders because a reader could reasonably assume otherwise. The right to object to legitimate-interest processing and the route to a named supervisory authority (the ICO for the UK) are now explicit as well. VERIFICATION: 63 LEGAL-01 tests pass, up from 55. The new ones assert the Article 27 gap is visible, the 72-hour commitment is present, the one-month period and its extension are stated, Article 22 is addressed, the ROPA exists and names every processor the Policy names, the ROPA records its own gaps and the non-processing facts, and the ROPA does not overstate the copilot. `npx vite build` succeeds; eslint 0 errors. ENGINEERING COMPLETE, 2026-10-23. The remaining 5% was three items, and one of them did not need to be asked for. SUPABASE REGION ESTABLISHED WITHOUT ASKING: ap-southeast-1 (Singapore). The ROPA recorded this as an open gap on the grounds that every reference in the repository is the placeholder your-project-ref.supabase.co -- which was true of the REPOSITORY and not of the running system. The Supavisor pooler hostname in Secrets Manager is aws-1-ap-southeast-1.pooler.supabase.com, which encodes the region directly, and the project ref lives in the DSN username. It is the SAME region the application's own compute runs in, so the database and the app are co-located and there is no additional cross-border hop between them. For an EEA/UK data subject the transfer is EEA/UK -> Singapore, with the controller in India: two third countries, no adequacy decision, which is exactly what Privacy section 7 discloses and what the processor SCCs have to cover. A ROPA that cannot say where the primary database sits is missing one of the things a ROPA exists for, so this mattered. ARTICLE 33/34 BREACH RESPONSE RUNBOOK WRITTEN: docs/legal/BREACH_RESPONSE_RUNBOOK.md. Privacy section 10 commits to 72-hour notification, and a commitment with no procedure behind it is the precise pattern this finding was opened about -- 72 hours is not long enough to invent a process in. It records that THE CLOCK STARTS ON AWARENESS rather than on completing the investigation (getting that wrong is how an organisation misses the deadline while believing it has time left), that Article 33(4) permits phased notification so a partial notice inside 72h beats a complete one after, the Article 33(3) and 34(2) content requirements, and the containment tooling THAT ALREADY EXISTS on this platform mapped to each incident type. It cites the platform's OWN incidents rather than hypotheticals: SEC-01 (three live secrets public for 70-93 days) and VAULT-01 (two customers' credentials irrecoverable because a key was lost -- recorded because IRRECOVERABLE LOSS IS A BREACH even though nobody gained access, which a runbook written only around intrusions would miss). It also records its own standing gaps, including that the unappointed Article 27 representatives BLOCK ITS OWN NOTIFICATION STEP -- there is no designated route to an EEA/UK supervisory authority today, so a notifiable breach would have to be improvised under a legal deadline. ARTICLE 35 DPIA SCREENING WRITTEN: docs/legal/DPIA_SCREENING.md. Conclusion: a full DPIA is NOT MANDATORY, with each of the three Article 35(3) triggers assessed separately rather than waved at. 35(3)(a) is not met because the automated processing evaluates MARKET DATA, not people -- there is no scoring, ranking, categorising or prediction about the user, and the decisions that affect them financially are their own instructions being executed; this is the limb where the intuitive answer on an algo-trading platform is the wrong one. 35(3)(b) is not met because FINANCIAL DATA IS NOT AN ARTICLE 9 SPECIAL CATEGORY -- a trap that would have produced a wrong mandatory-DPIA conclusion in the cautious-looking direction. 35(3)(c) is not met because a signed-in session is not a publicly accessible area. Against the authority criteria one is clearly met (systematic monitoring) and one is arguable (highly personal data), and the screening SAYS THE RESULT IS BORDERLINE RATHER THAN COMFORTABLE, recommending a focused DPIA on the session-replay processing anyway. AND THE SCREENING FOUND A REAL DEFECT, WHICH IS WHY IT WAS WORTH WRITING: MICROSOFT CLARITY WAS RECORDING AUTHENTICATED SESSIONS WITH NO MASKING. Clarity's default masking covers form inputs but NOT page text, and on a trading platform the text is the sensitive part -- account balances, position sizes, P&L, strategy logic and exchange-connection screens all render as ordinary text and would have appeared in a replay. That is an Article 5(1)(c) data-minimisation problem independent of Article 35, and it was fixable with configuration rather than legal argument. FIXED: data-clarity-mask="true" now applies to the single <main> landmark wrapping every authenticated route in App.jsx, so every signed-in page is masked BY DEFAULT rather than relying on each new page remembering. The public marketing pages render outside that element and stay unmasked, which is deliberate -- they carry no personal data and are where the analytics are actually useful. Disclosed in Privacy section 6, naming specifically what is not captured, because 'we mask sensitive data' is a claim a reader cannot check. NOT OVER-CLAIMED: the fix does not change the account-wide masking mode in the Clarity dashboard (owner-side, would be defence in depth) and does not retroactively mask recordings already captured, which should be purged on the Clarity side. Both limits are stated in the screening document. VERIFICATION: 71 LEGAL-01 tests pass, up from 63. New ones assert the runbook carries the 72-hour clock and the awareness-not-investigation rule, names the real containment tooling, cites VAULT-01 and SEC-01, and records that Article 27 blocks its own notification step; that the DPIA screening addresses all three 35(3) limbs, reaches a conclusion, calls it borderline, and does NOT claim financial data is special-category; that Clarity masking sits on the authenticated <main> landmark rather than a leaf component; that the Privacy Policy discloses the masking; and that the ROPA records the region. TWO OF MY OWN TESTS WENT STALE AND WERE CORRECTED RATHER THAN THE DOCUMENTS BENT TO FIT: one asserted the Supabase region was unknown and failed the moment it was established -- a closed gap reading as a regression -- and one broke on a markdown line wrap inside a blockquote. Both now assert content via a whitespace-squashing helper instead of raw text, so a rewrapped paragraph cannot fail a test about substance. `npx vite build` succeeds; eslint 0 errors.
remaining_action: CLOSED ON THE PRODUCT OWNER'S EXPLICIT INSTRUCTION, NOT ON COUNSEL REVIEW. THIS DISTINCTION IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THIS ENTRY AND MUST NOT BE READ PAST. WHY THE STATUS IS ACCEPTED_NONBLOCKING AND NOT VERIFIED_FIXED: this finding's text names 'counsel-drafted ToS/Privacy/Risk-disclosure/Refund policy, versioned, with per-user acceptance recorded at the version they agreed to'. Versioned: TRUE and tested. Per-user acceptance recorded: TRUE, live in production, append-only proven by attempting UPDATE and DELETE against a real row. Counsel-drafted: FALSE. No lawyer has drafted or reviewed these documents. Marking VERIFIED_FIXED would assert in the permanent record that counsel review happened, and a false record on a legal finding is worse than an open one. WHAT THE OWNER HAS ACCEPTED, ITEMISED SO THE ACCEPTANCE IS INFORMED: (1) ARTICLE 27 REPRESENTATIVES ARE NOT APPOINTED, for either the EU or the UK. The owner has chosen to accept customers globally INCLUDING the EU and UK. Article 27 obliges a non-EU controller to designate a representative where it offers services to people in the EU OR monitors their behaviour, and BOTH limbs apply here because this platform runs Google Analytics and Microsoft Clarity. THIS IS A LIVE NON-COMPLIANCE FOR THE OWNER'S OWN CHOSEN MARKET, not a drafting nicety, and it additionally blocks the breach-notification route in BREACH_RESPONSE_RUNBOOK.md section 4. It is normally bought as a service for a few hundred euros per jurisdiction per year -- the cheapest open item anywhere in this audit relative to what it closes. It renders as a VISIBLE placeholder in Privacy section 1 so a user is told rather than misled by silence, and a test asserts that placeholder stays present while unappointed. (2) PROCESSOR DPAs AND SCCs ARE NOT CONFIRMED EXECUTED with Supabase, AWS, Google, Microsoft and Sentry. Privacy section 7 states we rely on them. All five publish them and most are click-through, so this is minutes of work rather than a negotiation. (3) FOUR CLAUSES ARE UNREVIEWED BY COUNSEL: the DPIA screening's conclusion (the reasoning is recorded and the premises are verifiable; only the conclusion needs a lawyer); the PMLA/FIU-IND position (factual premises verifiable in code -- no custody, no exchange, no transfer on behalf of another -- only the legal conclusion needs counsel); the liability cap (Indian consumer law limits exclusion against a consumer); and whether the CIN's registered object, industry code 26515 for instruments and measuring devices, covers operating a trading platform. (4) TWO CONTROLS ARE REPRESENTATIONS RATHER THAN VERIFICATION, by design and stated as such in the documents, the migration and the column comments: the restricted-jurisdiction check is a declared-country gate, not screening against a licensed list, and cannot express region-level measures; the 18+ requirement is an attestation, not age verification. IF ANY OF THESE IS LATER ACTED ON, REOPEN THIS FINDING RATHER THAN AMENDING IT. In particular, when the Article 27 representatives are appointed, ENTITY.euRepresentative and ENTITY.ukRepresentative in algo22-terminal/src/legal/documents.js must be replaced with real contact details, LEGAL_VERSION must be bumped (which re-prompts every user by design), and tests/test_legal01_documents_and_acceptance.py::test_the_article_27_gap_is_visible_rather_than_omitted must be INVERTED to assert the real details are present -- its docstring says so. NOTHING ENGINEERING REMAINS. Every obligation that is code or a document has been built and tested, and the one obligation that is neither has been made impossible to overlook rather than quietly omitted.

title: A settlement retried after a partial failure can leave money recorded as settled while the buyer's subscription stays unpaid
evidence: The prior pass's own remaining_action named exactly what this pass does: 'the broader architectural alternative (performing the entire settle() as one SQL function/transaction)... judged lower-risk... than restructuring it into an RPC, and that larger redesign is not attempted here.' Confirmed the real schema of marketplace_settlements, library_subscriptions and library_subscription_transitions against this session's own fully-provisioned disposable Postgres replica before writing anything, including reading trg_subscription_transition_guard's and trg_lib_subs_period_mirror's own installed bodies directly (pg_get_functiondef) rather than assuming the migration files describe the live triggers: confirmed the transition guard requires a matching non-reversal marketplace_settlements row to ALREADY EXIST (visible to it because Postgres triggers see uncommitted writes from earlier in the SAME transaction) before admitting a move to 'active' -- which is exactly why the ledger insert and the transition have to be in the same function and in that order, not a redesign choice. Added backend_app/migrations/050_mkt03_settlement_atomic_transition.sql: one SECURITY DEFINER function, record_and_transition_settlement, performing the idempotent (ON CONFLICT ON CONSTRAINT uq_settlement_reference_reversal DO NOTHING) ledger insert and the guarded (.eq-equivalent WHERE status = expected_from_status) subscription UPDATE plus its library_subscription_transitions history row in ONE transaction, scoped NARROWLY to the two writes whose separation is the actual defect. The transition DECISION ITSELF -- ELIGIBLE_FOR_ACTIVATION, can_transition, the renewal-in-place carve-out, period_for_activation/period_for_renewal's date arithmetic -- is extracted UNCHANGED from the old write-performing _apply_transition into a new pure function, _decide_transition, with no I/O of its own; the existing property-test suite (test_subscription_state_machine.py, test_entitlement_expiry_boundary.py) exercises it exactly as before, because it is the same code. The entitlement grant (step 4) is DELIBERATELY left outside this function, still invoked through settle()'s existing injectable grant_permission parameter: folding it in would remove the test seam several existing tests use to observe or fail that one step in isolation, for no correctness gain, since the prior pass already independently verified (against this session's own disposable Postgres replica) that deployment_permissions carries a real UNIQUE (user_id, library_id, is_active) constraint making a duplicate grant structurally impossible regardless of timing. _insert_settlement, _apply_transition and _write_transition_row -- the three functions whose separate PostgREST statements WERE the defect -- are removed outright (ported, not left dead); grepped the whole backend_app/ tree first and confirmed nothing else references them (a second, module-local _write_transition_row in subscription_reinstatement.py is unrelated and untouched). settle()'s outer Requirement 10.11 retry budget, and _Attempt's cross-attempt WITHIN-one-call resumption, are unchanged; MK001 (raised when the subscription moved under the caller) is caught and re-raised as the same SettlementPersistenceError that retry budget already retries today. Updated the FakeSupabase test doubles in tests/test_settlement_service.py (the shared double several other suites import) and tests/test_marketplace_concurrency.py to simulate the real function's all-or-nothing semantics -- every sub-write staged and committed only once every fault check (the same raise_on/fail_times/error_on injection every other statement already used) has passed, including a new between_ledger_and_transition test seam replacing a now-impossible monkeypatch of the old separate .table() calls for the 'a concurrent writer moves the row' race test. tests/test_mkt03_settlement_resumes_across_redeliveries.py's own two tests, whose premise was a FRESH settle() call producing 'ledger written, transition not' by exhausting its retry budget on the UPDATE step, were rewritten: that state is now structurally unreachable for a fresh call (proved directly by test_a_ledger_insert_that_never_completes_leaves_the_ledger_unchanged and its UPDATE-step sibling in test_settlement_service.py, both of which already passed and still do), so both tests now seed that exact row shape directly, AS legacy data predating this migration, and prove the existing DUPLICATE_RESUMED fallback still repairs it -- which is precisely the residual case that fallback is now for. Full regression: test_settlement_service.py (60), test_mkt03_settlement_resumes_across_redeliveries.py (5), test_marketplace_concurrency.py (45), test_subscription_renewal_regression.py (32), test_subscription_reinstatement_regression.py (40), property/test_settlement_idempotence.py (2), property/test_settlement_ledger.py (2), property/test_subscription_state_machine.py (7), property/test_entitlement_expiry_boundary.py (8), test_aud02_order_audit_trail_is_durable.py + test_audit_trail_events.py (14 passed, 8 skipped), test_validation_sweep.py (376 passed, 2 skipped) -- all passed, zero failures. ||| MIGRATION 050 COULD NEVER HAVE BEEN APPLIED TO PRODUCTION, AND THAT IS NOW FIXED (Kiro, 2026-10-24). This entry's remaining_action said to 'apply backend_app/migrations/050_mkt03_settlement_atomic_transition.sql to staging first, then production'. Attempting exactly that against real production failed: the file's own self-exercise block inserts a library_strategies row with category = 'trend', and library_strategies carries CONSTRAINT valid_category CHECK (category IN ('mean_reversion','trend_following','market_making','arbitrage','momentum','ml_hybrid','other')) -- read off the real constraint with pg_get_constraintdef, and declared in repository source at archived_migrations/root_migrations/001_create_library_strategies.sql. 'trend' is in neither. So the seed raised check_violation, the handler around it caught only undefined_table / undefined_column / not_null_violation, and the exception propagated and took the whole migration down -- with the function itself already correctly installed and then rolled back along with everything else. WHY REVIEW AND CI MISSED IT: the from-source provisioning path does not build library_strategies with that constraint, so in CI the seed hit undefined_table/undefined_column, the handler caught it, and the self-test SKIPPED. A self-test that always skips reports success either way. TWO FIXES, both in the migration: the category is now 'trend_following', and the handler also catches check_violation and foreign_key_violation -- which is what the handler's own message ('not in the expected shape on this database') always meant, and a self-exercise must never be the reason a correct function cannot be installed. New tests/test_mkt03_migration_050_self_test_vocabulary.py parses the migration and the constraint's own declaration and fails if they disagree, plus asserts the handler catches a constraint refusal; negative-control verified by restoring both halves of the defect, which failed 3 of 6 tests with the exact predicted messages, then restoring the fix (6 passed). ||| APPLIED AND VERIFIED IN REAL PRODUCTION (Kiro, 2026-10-24). Every statement went through one explicit transaction on the Supabase SESSION-mode pooler (port 5432, not the stored DSN's 6543 transaction pooler -- see the note on MKT-04 for why that distinction was load-bearing), with row counts of 27 watched tables, the full pg_policies set and the full RLS-enabled table set captured before and after INSIDE the transaction and the commit REFUSED on any divergence. Invariants held across all four applies: policies 148 -> 148, RLS-enabled tables 83 -> 83, profiles 182 -> 182, zero row-count delta on any watched table, and zero self-test residue (048 and 050 both seed auth.users/profiles/paper_*/library_* rows in their postflight blocks and roll them back; that rollback was verified by measurement rather than trusted). Re-checked afterwards on a FRESH connection so the verdict is not read from the session that wrote it. MKT-03 SPECIFICALLY: after the fix, 050 applied with its preflight passing and its self-exercise reporting 'a stale from_status raised MK001 and left no ledger row committed'; record_and_transition_settlement is confirmed present and SECURITY DEFINER on a fresh connection.
verification_level: production (record_and_transition_settlement installed and confirmed SECURITY DEFINER on a fresh connection, its own self-exercise passing against the real schema) + code+test
remaining_action: Two items, both narrower than before. (1) A live settlement smoke test against production -- a real Stripe/Razorpay test-mode webhook redelivery -- has NOT been run; the function's own MK001-and-rollback property is now proven against the real production schema by its postflight, which is strictly more than the repo-source evidence this entry previously rested on, but it is not the same as a real redelivery. (2) The dedicated tests/test_mkt03_settlement_atomic_transition_postgres.py exercising the installed function directly over psycopg2 (rather than through the FakeSupabase simulation) is STILL NOT WRITTEN -- the migration's own postflight now covers the MK001 path against a real server, but not the happy path or the concurrent-redelivery race. title: A unique index keyed on strategy_id blocks every subscriber after the first from ever deploying a marketplace listing

title: The market-data quality validator's default thresholds reject almost all real-shaped market data
evidence: Confirmed the defect exactly as named, and traced its real blast radius: OutlierDetector._z_score_filter/_iqr_filter (reached by default -- ValidationConfig.outlier_method defaults to Z_SCORE) computed their test against the RAW price/volume LEVEL of the whole window, then rejected the ENTIRE window on a single violation. market_data_contract.quality_report, strategy_operations, strategy_service and training_worker all REUSE this exact validator per their own docstrings -- this is not dead code, it sits on real production paths. Confirmed empirically (not just by reading): a realistic trending-price + log-normal-volume series (900 bars, the platform's typical window size) was rejected by the pre-fix z-score-on-levels check on every one of several random seeds tried, while the existing test suite's own 'clean, accepted' fixture (tests/test_feed_state_and_data_quality.py's _pool()) is explicitly documented as a bounded SINE WAVE rather than anything resembling real market data, specifically to dodge this exact bug -- independent confirmation the defect is real and already known-about well enough to be worked around rather than fixed. Root cause: price and volume levels are both non-stationary (price trends/drifts, volume is approximately log-normal) by construction, so a z-score/IQR test against a non-stationary series' own mean/quantiles measures 'how far this point is from a mean the trend/burst itself moved', unrelated to whether any individual bar is actually anomalous. FIX: switched both _z_score_filter and _iqr_filter to bar-to-bar LOG-RETURNS (log(x_t/x_(t-1))) for close AND volume -- the standard transform that makes a trending/multiplicative series approximately stationary, which these tests require to mean anything. Percent-change returns were tried first and empirically still left volume's heavy right tail (ordinary volume bursts are large MULTIPLICATIVE swings) fat enough to trip the z-score on realistic data (2 violations in 30 seeds); log-returns resolved it completely (0/30). Also raised z_score_threshold 3.0->5.0 and iqr_multiplier 1.5->3.0 (both env-overridable via MARKET_DATA_Z_SCORE_THRESHOLD / MARKET_DATA_IQR_MULTIPLIER): rejecting a whole window on ANY single point beyond a per-comparison threshold has a false-positive rate that RISES WITH WINDOW SIZE regardless of what it's computed over -- for a 900-bar window, a per-point threshold calibrated for a single comparison (3 sigma / 1.5xIQR) is tripped by chance alone far more often than not; this is a general multiple-comparisons argument, not a dataset-specific calibration, and both new values were empirically verified (across 25-30 independent random seeds per method) to clear realistic trending+bursty-volume windows while STILL catching a genuine single-bar 50x price spike. Investigated the third remediation item ('make the gap threshold interval-aware') and found it already true of the current code, just not of what the ledger note assumed: GapHandler.handle's actual gap DETECTION already derives its threshold from the timeframe (`expected_diff = timedelta(minutes=_timeframe_to_minutes(timeframe)); gaps = time_diffs > expected_diff * 1.5`) -- the `max_gap_minutes` PARAMETER the caller passes in (ValidationConfig.max_gap_minutes, fixed at 5.0) is dead code, immediately overwritten by the measured gap value before it is ever read. Not a gap in this codebase's current behaviour, just an unused/confusingly-named parameter; left as-is since removing a dead parameter is outside this finding's scope and touches a shared signature. New tests/test_data02_outlier_detection_on_returns_not_levels.py (39 tests): 25 independent random seeds of realistic trending-price + bursty-volume data accepted (previously rejected); a genuine single-bar 50x spike still rejected; the existing sine-wave clean/spike fixtures still behave exactly as before (both directions, independently re-verified here); the same two properties for the non-default IQR method. Full regression: new suite + tests/test_feed_state_and_data_quality.py + tests/test_market_data_contract.py + tests/test_validation_sweep.py (542 tests) clean except pre-existing, unrelated EmptyCategoryError collection errors (confirmed pre-existing/unrelated repeatedly this session) and the 2 pre-existing billing failures already confirmed earlier this session.
remaining_action: The two threshold VALUES (z_score_threshold=5.0, iqr_multiplier=3.0) are principled, empirically-verified-against-synthetic-data defaults, not a fit against this platform's own real historical return distributions -- this sandbox has no such data. The original audit's own remediation note separated 'validate on returns/log-returns' (done, this session) from 'widen or recalibrate thresholds against real historical distributions' (NOT done -- needs a session with access to real market data to fine-tune beyond the general multiple-comparisons correction applied here). Both new constants are env-overridable so this can happen without a code change.

title: Walk-forward analysis does not actually fit per-window parameters, and several of its reported figures are hardcoded placeholders
evidence: Confirmed by reading run_walk_forward_analysis: self._get_best_parameters(self._optimization_history) was called ONCE before the loop and the resulting fixed parameter set was evaluated on every window's train AND test period -- a fixed strategy re-run on rolling windows, not walk-forward analysis. Investigating this surfaced a more fundamental, previously untracked defect (filed and fixed separately as BT-02, commit 29e319d): BacktestRuntime.run_backtest never used start_date/end_date to select data at all, so every window's backtest ran on byte-identical 'most recent bars' regardless of its own dates, which would have made even a correct per-window fit numerically meaningless. Fixed run_walk_forward_analysis (depends on BT-02) by adding _optimize_on_window: a copy of the caller's config with parameters[start_date/end_date] overridden to the window's own train period, dispatched through the same search method (_grid_search/_random_search/_bayesian_optimization/_genetic_algorithm) the caller chose, with the window's own trials kept OUT of self._optimization_history so one window cannot leak into another's fit or into the whole-period benchmark (the OPT-03-shaped cross-contamination, reintroduced inside one engine instance if not guarded against). Also fixed the three hardcoded report figures the finding names: _run_buy_hold_benchmark (was the literal total_return_pct=50.0/sharpe_ratio=1.0/max_drawdown=20.0 for every call) now fetches the strategy's own symbol/timeframe over the same window via BT-02's since_ms/until_ms and computes all three from the closes actually fetched, reporting computed=False/None rather than a fabricated number when the fetch fails; _calculate_beta (was the literal 1.0) now computes cov(strategy_returns, benchmark_returns)/var(benchmark_returns) from both backtests' own return series, returning None rather than 0.0/1.0 when there are too few paired observations or the benchmark has zero variance; complexity score (was the literal 0.8) now scales with the strategy's own tunable-parameter count (1.0 at zero parameters, 0.0 at a documented 10-parameter cap), matching the 'higher is better' convention every other component of the weighted score already uses. New tests/test_opt02_walk_forward_fits_per_window_and_report_figures_are_real.py (10 tests) against a deterministic, parameter- and window-dependent fake backtest_runtime: different windows provably choose different winning parameters (not merely 'ran without crashing'); the fitted parameters carry unchanged from train to test; two windows' calls carry two different date ranges (the BT-02 dependency, checked directly); buy & hold computes a real return/Sharpe/drawdown from a controlled price series and reports not-computed on empty data; beta computes exactly (2.0 for a strategy whose returns are exactly 2x the benchmark's) and is None on zero variance or too few observations; alpha/beta are both None together when the benchmark could not be measured; complexity varies from 1.0 to 0.0 with parameter count. One real bug the test suite itself caught before commit: the first _calculate_beta draft mixed np.cov's sample covariance (ddof=1) with np.var's population variance (ddof=0), scaling every beta by N/(N-1) for no reason -- caught because the exactly-2.0 test came back 2.4, fixed by aligning both to ddof=1. Full regression: test_save_performs_no_backtest.py + test_opt01_optimize_config_field_name.py + test_strategy_analysis_endpoint_accuracy.py + test_opt03_optimization_engine_is_not_a_shared_singleton.py + test_bt02_backtest_honors_requested_date_range.py (100 passed, 1 pre-existing unrelated import-pin failure confirmed via git-stash comparison to predate this change entirely); test_validation_sweep.py (373 passed, 2 skipped).
remaining_action: None identified at the code level for the two defects this finding names. The fix credits two commits: 29e319d (BT-02, the data-range prerequisite) and be82e3d (this finding's own per-window fitting and report-figure fixes). The validation_method field on OptimizationConfig (TIME_SERIES_CV/BLOCKED_CV/ROLLING_VALIDATION/WALK_FORWARD) is still read only for a log line in run_walk_forward_analysis and does not select a different windowing or fitting strategy -- that is a separate, smaller gap this pass did not scope in, since the finding's own title and remaining_action named only the per-window fitting and the hardcoded figures.

title: Optimization engine is a process-wide singleton that leaks one tenant's best parameters into another tenant's walk-forward/sensitivity results
evidence: Confirmed by reading backend_app/backend/optimization_engine.py::get_optimization_engine and backend_app/backend/backtest_runtime.py::get_backtest_runtime: both are plain module-level singletons (global _x; if _x is None: _x = X(); return _x). Grepped every call site in the repo (exactly two): backend_app/routers/strategy_operations.py's POST /strategies/{id}/optimize and backend_app/routers/strategies.py's POST /walk-forward both called them directly, so every tenant's call shared the SAME OptimizationEngine instance and therefore the SAME _optimization_history list -- every one of run_walk_forward_analysis/run_sensitivity_analysis/run_monte_carlo_simulation/run_benchmark_comparison reads its 'best parameters' back via self._get_best_parameters(self._optimization_history), so a tenant whose call overlapped or ran back-to-back with another tenant's in the same process could have had that tenant's optimization results folded into their own. The shared backtest_runtime singleton compounded it: constructed once with the class defaults ($10,000 capital, 0.1% fees, 0.05% slippage), so both endpoints' submitted capital/fee/slippage/risk fields were accepted and then silently ignored -- confirmed this is the EXACT SAME bug class backend_app/routers/strategy_operations.py::_backtest_runtime_for's own docstring already names and fixes for the plain (non-optimization) backtest endpoint (that fix's own comment explicitly calls out get_backtest_runtime() by name as the thing it is NOT calling, for this exact reason) -- the optimize/walk-forward endpoints had simply not received the same fix. Fixed both call sites the same way: new backend_app/routers/strategy_operations.py::_optimization_engine_for(body) constructs a fresh OptimizationEngine() and a fresh BacktestRuntime(...) (from the request's own initial_capital/commission/slippage/risk_per_trade/max_drawdown/daily_loss_limit fields) per request; backend_app/routers/strategies.py's /walk-forward closure does the equivalent inline, reusing the values already read into its OptimizationConfig (so no duplicate payload.get() calls). get_optimization_engine()/get_backtest_runtime() themselves are UNCHANGED -- kept, not deleted, since tests/test_save_performs_no_backtest.py's Requirement-22.1 tripwire still needs to patch get_backtest_runtime by name in both router modules to prove a strategy SAVE never starts a backtest. Removed a redundant local re-import of OptimizationEngine/BacktestRuntime inside /walk-forward's closure that would otherwise have shadowed the module-level names and silently defeated test patching at the new injection points. New tests/test_opt03_optimization_engine_is_not_a_shared_singleton.py (6 tests, direct construction, no mocking -- mirrors tests/test_task_6_1_backtest_execute.py's existing proof pattern for the sibling bug): two calls return two different engine instances with independent _optimization_history (the concrete cross-tenant leak, reproduced then shown closed); the runtime carries the SUBMITTED capital/fee/slippage/risk values, not the class defaults; two different configurations produce two differently-configured runtimes; the engine returned is wired to THIS call's own runtime; the singleton accessors themselves are unchanged and still work (negative control). Updated tests/test_strategy_analysis_endpoint_accuracy.py's two walk-forward tests, which mocked get_optimization_engine/get_backtest_runtime by name, to patch the new injection points (OptimizationEngine/BacktestRuntime class constructors) instead -- both still pass. Full regression (opt03 + endpoint_accuracy + backtest_execute + validation_sweep + route_contract + router_registration_completeness, 441 tests) clean except the 2 unrelated pre-existing billing failures already confirmed earlier this session; tests/test_save_performs_no_backtest.py's pre-existing 10 failed/10 errored (an unrelated environment gap, confirmed identical on the pre-change baseline via git stash) are untouched by this fix.
remaining_action: This closes the isolation half (OPT-03's own title and remediation note) for both call sites that exist. NOT attempted: OPT-02's separate, deeper finding that walk-forward analysis does not actually fit per-window parameters and reports several hardcoded placeholder figures -- a correctness question about the ALGORITHM, independent of this finding's isolation question, and out of this fix's scope.

title: Per-deployment execution-config limits (notional cap, position cap, slippage tolerance) are validated and stored but no execution path reads them
evidence: SECOND PASS (this session): real enforcement for two of the five fields, replacing the prior pass's blanket deploy-time refusal for those two. max_order_notional and max_open_positions are now genuinely consulted by master_executor.evaluate_deployment_execution_limits, called from BotRunner._inner_loop immediately before the risk-manager check on every tick -- the real order-construction path for both paper and live deployments. max_order_notional REFUSES (does not clamp) an order whose notional exceeds the deployment's own cap, the same disposition ExecutionGuard._validate_order_size already applies for its own process-wide ceiling. max_open_positions refuses opening a new position once the deployment already holds this many; measured against the architecture (one BotRunner is one (user, symbol, strategy) and deployment_binding.resolve_binding_market's own MARKET_AMBIGUOUS gate forbids more than one market per version, so a deployment can hold at most ONE net position) this cap genuinely binds only at max_open_positions=0 -- stated plainly in the function's own docstring and in this entry rather than oversold. slippage_tolerance_bps, order_timeout_seconds and retry_policy remain refused (UNENFORCED_EXECUTION_CONFIG_FIELDS): this platform's order path (ExecutionEngine.execute_with_idempotency / exchange_executor.place_order, market orders only per deployment_runtime.EXECUTABLE_ORDER_TYPES) has no slippage-tolerance check, no per-order timeout and no retry policy for a value to apply to, so wiring them would have been cosmetic. normalise_execution_config's EXECUTION_CONFIG_NOT_ENFORCED refusal now fires for exactly those three (UNENFORCED_EXECUTION_CONFIG_FIELDS), not all five; the two enforced fields (ENFORCED_EXECUTION_CONFIG_FIELDS) are instead validated for a usable value (positive finite number / non-negative whole number; EXECUTION_CONFIG_INVALID_FIELD otherwise) so an unusable value is refused at deploy time rather than discovered as a silent no-op at the first tick. DESIGN, AND WHY ExecutionGuard WAS NOT TOUCHED: traced every call site of ExecutionGuard.validate_trade in the real repository (routers/orders.py's cancel and cancel-all, routers/portfolio.py's close-all) and confirmed -- consistent with this same remediation effort's own POST_LAUNCH_IMPROVEMENTS.md finding and with core/execution_engine.py's own comment at the live-path notional-ceiling check -- that ExecutionGuard.validate_trade is reached ONLY from those three risk-REDUCING control endpoints, never from the signal-driven order-opening path. Threading execution_config into ExecutionGuard would therefore have changed nothing a real order passes through; the real order-construction path for a strategy deployment is BotRunner._inner_loop (risk_manager.validate_trade_request, then ExecutionEngine.execute_with_idempotency), so that is where this fix lives. The config reaches it via the SAME per-deployment object BotRunner already receives at construction (strategy_blueprint, which already carries deployment_id/exchange_id/mode) rather than a new deployment-id-keyed cache: deployment_runtime.build_runtime_blueprint now also carries execution_config, populated from deployment_binding.evaluate_binding's DeploymentBinding.execution_config at deploy time and from the strategy_deployments row itself on resume after a restart (rebuild_for_resume) -- this is design option (b) in the original remediation note: the config threaded explicitly through an existing call chain, not a new lookup. BLAST RADIUS, CONFIRMED BEFORE STARTING: read core/live_execution_gate.py (RT-15/TRADE-04) -- live trading is gated at the venue-write boundary (require_live_authorization, called from CCXTExchangeExecutor.place_order) and remains OFF regardless of this change; this fix only affects orders reaching BotRunner's gate, which today means paper-mode orders (and whatever a live order would do if RT-15 were later lifted, since the gate sits downstream of this one and is unaffected by it). TESTS: tests/test_deploy01_execution_config_enforcement.py (new, 18 tests) -- the pure gate function (empty config is a complete no-op; oversized order refused; order within cap allowed; reduce-only skips the notional cap; max_open_positions=0 refuses the deployment's one possible entry; cap>=1 allows it; adding to an existing position is never blocked; both caps compose), build_runtime_blueprint/rebuild_for_resume carrying execution_config, BotRunner.__init__ reading it off the blueprint (and defaulting to {} when absent, so every pre-DEPLOY-01 blueprint is unaffected), and TWO full paper-mode end-to-end BotRunner runs (real compiled plan, fake keyless exchange, recording execution engine, the same fixture-driven boot test_rt02_builder_strategy_runs_on_deployment_runtime.py uses) proving a tight max_order_notional / max_open_positions=0 produces NO order on a tick that, with no execution_config at all, DOES produce one. Updated test_deploy01_execution_config_fields_not_enforced.py, test_task_8_2_deployment_binding.py and test_task_8_2_deploy_preflight.py for the transition: the refusal no longer fires for the two now-enforced fields; preflight now reports max_order_notional as a PASSING condition instead of EXECUTION_CONFIG_NOT_ENFORCED. Regression: the full set of execution-guard/bot-runner/deploy/paper-trading/RT-15/TRADE-04 suites named in this remediation pass (2208 tests, this session) plus every deployment-binding/preflight/deploy-strategy test in the repo -- all green after one fix to this file's own new docstring (a literal substring collided with an unrelated source-order assertion in test_rt08_deployment_state_is_durable.py; reworded, re-ran, green).
verification_level: code+test (verified this session, local suite only; no production access)
remaining_action: Three of the five fields are STILL refused-not-enforced by design, not oversight: slippage_tolerance_bps, order_timeout_seconds and retry_policy have no corresponding mechanism anywhere on this platform's order-submission path (no slippage-tolerance check, no per-order timeout, no retry policy), so wiring them would mean storing a value nothing reads -- exactly the defect this finding exists to close. Closing them for real needs a structural addition to ExecutionEngine.execute_with_idempotency / exchange_executor.place_order (a retry/timeout wrapper and a slippage-vs-fill check), which is a materially larger change to the hot order-submission path than the two fields fixed this pass and deserves its own dedicated review rather than being rushed in alongside this fix. max_open_positions is real but narrow given the current one-symbol-per-deployment architecture (binds only at 0); widening it to a meaningful range above zero would need a multi-position execution model (tracking more than one net position per deployment) this codebase does not have. NONE of this has been applied to, deployed against, or exercised on the real running production backend -- this session has no production or Supabase/AWS access; verification is code + a local test suite only (production_verified: false). The next deploy to staging/production should confirm a live deployment with a real max_order_notional actually refuses an oversized paper order end to end, through the real fleet/BotRunner boot path rather than this session's fixture-driven one.

title: Marketplace browse builds a PostgREST filter from raw user input
evidence: Confirmed by reading backend_app/routers/library.py::browse_library: the `q` search parameter was interpolated raw into a PostgREST or() filter string -- query.or_(f"name.ilike.%{q}%,description.ilike.%{q}%") -- and PostgREST's filter mini-language treats `,`, `.`, `(`, `)` as syntax, so a search term containing any of them could close the current clause and open a new one against an unrelated column. Separately, the handler fetched ALL matching rows via query.execute() and sliced [offset:offset+limit] in Python, so every browse request transferred the entire matching catalogue regardless of page size. Fixed both. (1) Extracted _postgrest_quoted_ilike_pattern(term): wraps the term in double quotes (PostgREST's own escaping rule), backslash-escaping \ and " themselves FIRST -- in that order, deliberately, since escaping quotes before doubling backslashes would let a trailing backslash absorb its own escaping backslash and leave the closing quote unescaped. (2) Switched to count="exact" on .select() plus .range(offset, offset+limit-1) on the query, pushing LIMIT/OFFSET and the total-match count to PostgREST instead of this process. Extended two existing fake-Supabase test doubles (tests/test_marketplace_pipeline.py::FakeTable, tests/test_library_detail_projection_regression.py::_Query/_Resp) with .range()/count="exact" support, since neither had it before this fix and both are exercised by this same handler's existing regression suite. title: Notifications are kept in an unbounded per-process dict with an O(n) idempotency scan
evidence: Confirmed the defect exactly as named: backend_app/routers/notifications.py's _in_memory_notifications was a plain, unbounded module-level dict -- one entry retained forever for every notification ever created in this process's lifetime, across every tenant, whether or not it was ALSO durably persisted to Supabase (list_notifications always tries Supabase first and only falls back to this dict when Supabase has nothing, confirmed by reading it -- so a persisted entry's in-memory copy was pure, unbounded-growth dead weight). The idempotency check also did a full scan (`for existing_id, existing_data in _in_memory_notifications.items(): ...`) on every single create, so it got slower, not just memory-hungrier, as the dict grew. Fixed with (1) _MAX_IN_MEMORY_NOTIFICATIONS (env-overridable via MAX_IN_MEMORY_NOTIFICATIONS, default 5000) -- once exceeded, the OLDEST entries are evicted (plain dicts preserve insertion order in Python 3.7+, and no code here ever re-inserts an existing key, so the first key is reliably the oldest); (2) an O(1) idempotency index (_idempotency_index, keyed by (user_id, idempotency_key)) replacing the full-dict scan, kept in sync on insert, eviction, AND delete (both delete_notification and delete_all_notifications now route through a shared _forget_notification_locked helper instead of a bare `del`, so a deleted or evicted notification's idempotency key is freed for reuse rather than left dangling). New tests/test_hy04_notifications_memory_bounded.py (6 tests, using a shrunk cap via monkeypatch rather than actually inserting 5000+ rows) proves: exceeding the cap evicts the oldest entries first; a duplicate idempotency key for the SAME user returns the existing id without growing the store; the SAME key for DIFFERENT users does not collide; delete_notification and delete_all_notifications both clean the idempotency index, not just the dict; an evicted entry's idempotency key is freed for reuse. Updated tests/test_notifications_feature_e2e.py's state-cleanup fixture to also clear the new _idempotency_index between tests (it only cleared _in_memory_notifications before, which would have let the new index leak across runs in that file's own autouse fixture -- a miniature version of the exact unbounded-growth problem this finding is about). Full regression (new HY-04 suite + existing notifications e2e suite, 1 file/23+ tests + tests/test_validation_sweep.py, 388+ tests) clean except the 2 unrelated pre-existing billing failures already confirmed earlier this session (missing real Supabase service credentials in this sandbox).
remaining_action: The finding's remediation note offered TWO options joined by 'and/or': cap the in-memory structure, OR make Supabase the source of truth with a visible degraded-mode indicator. This fix takes the first option in full (bounded growth, O(1) idempotency) -- the second option's 'visible degraded-mode indicator' (e.g. surfacing to the user or to ops when notifications are running on the in-memory fallback rather than Supabase) was NOT attempted; Supabase was already and remains the primary store attempted first on every write and read, so this is an observability nice-to-have on top of an already-correct fallback, not a remaining correctness gap.
