title: The API client overwrites caller-supplied Idempotency-Key headers with its own weak hash
evidence: Confirmed by reading algo22-terminal/src/apiClient.js's request interceptor: it called generateIdempotencyKey(config.url, data), which hashed sessionId_url_payloadStr with a weak 32-bit simpleHash into the Idempotency-Key header UNCONDITIONALLY -- even when the caller (api/modules/strategies.js::deploy's options.idempotencyKey, a prepared but not-yet-wired-to-any-UI call site) had already set its own Idempotency-Key header, it was overwritten. The deeper bug: the hash was deterministic over (session, url, payload), so two SEPARATE, deliberately-identical submissions (placing the same order twice in a row on purpose) collided onto the identical key, and the backend's own idempotency check would then treat the second legitimate order as a duplicate retry of the first. Fixed: the interceptor now checks config.headers['Idempotency-Key'] for an existing value first and only falls back to its own generator when the caller supplied none; the fallback itself (generateIdempotencyKey) no longer takes url/data at all -- it is now idemp_${crypto.randomUUID()}, content-independent, so two identical submissions never collide. Removed simpleHash (now unused) and getSessionId (now unused -- confirmed no other call site anywhere in algo22-terminal/src or tests references either name). New algo22-terminal/tests/unit/apiClientIdempotencyFe05.test.js (4 tests, same axios-mock convention as the existing ATTACK 3 idempotency test it extends): a caller-supplied key is honoured verbatim, not overwritten; a request with no caller key still gets a defined idemp_-prefixed key; two identical submissions with no caller key get DIFFERENT keys (the collision bug, proven fixed); a GET request still never receives the header. The pre-existing tests/unit/attack_frontend_full.test.js (8 tests, whose ATTACK 3 only asserted the idemp_ prefix and definedness, not hash-determinism) still passes.
remaining_action: No current UI call site actually passes options.idempotencyKey to strategies.deploy (or any other caller-supplied-key path) yet -- this fix makes the mechanism correct for when one is wired up, consistent with how this session treated other prepared-but-unused mechanisms (e.g. SEC-11). A future session adding a 'Deploy' button's retry/resubmit handling should generate one UUID per click and pass it through, rather than relying on this interceptor's own per-request fallback, if intentional retry-coalescing is wanted.

title: Terraform does not describe the running production infrastructure: state is empty, names match nothing live, and a plan proposes a second production
evidence: Found by actually running terraform for the first time, after INF-03's route (A) made the remote backend exist (see that entry for the backend work and its verification). `terraform init` succeeds; the plan that follows is the finding. MEASURED with terraform v1.17.0 / aws provider 5.100.0 against arn:aws:iam::273709947018:user/github-actions in ap-southeast-1: `Plan: 91 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy`. `0 to change` IS THE WHOLE PROBLEM. Production is running -- one ECS cluster, `vyomquant-cluster`, with one service, `vyomquant-api-service-cjema2sl`, on task definition vyomquant-api:237, behind an ALB and CloudFront, with 8 secrets, a Redis replication group and ~84 resources in total. Terraform proposes to change none of it, because its state is empty and its NAMES MATCH NOTHING THAT EXISTS: the config declares cluster `vyomquant-cluster-production` (which returns ClusterNotFoundException) and service `vyomquant-api-service-production`. So the plan is not an adoption of production, it is a proposal to build a SECOND one alongside it: a new VPC, 6 subnets, 3 NAT gateways, 3 EIPs, an internet gateway, 4 route tables, a new ALB with 2 target groups, a new CloudFront distribution, a new WAF web ACL, a new ECS cluster, 7 services, 8 task definitions, 8 Secrets Manager secrets, CloudTrail with its S3 bucket, and 7 metric alarms. Applying it would begin billing 3 NAT gateways and a second ALB and CloudFront distribution immediately, then fail partway on the 8 secret names and the 3 IAM role names (ecsTaskExecutionRole, VyomQuantEcsTaskExecutionRole-production, VyomQuantEcsTaskRole-production) that already exist -- leaving a half-built parallel stack and a state file describing some of it. IT DOES NOT CURRENTLY PRODUCE AN APPLYABLE PLAN AT ALL, which is the one piece of luck here: the plan exits non-zero on alb.tf line 100's own precondition -- `var.enable_custom_domain || !contains(["prod","production"], var.environment)` -- because enable_custom_domain defaults to false and environment defaults to "production". That guard was added to stop a plaintext listener reaching production and it incidentally blocks this. THE NARROW ESCAPE DOES NOT WORK EITHER: `-target`ing just the workers, to get INF-03's processes running without the rest, pulls in the new network anyway, because aws_ecs_service.workers sets subnets = aws_subnet.private[*].id and security_groups = [aws_security_group.ecs_tasks.id] -- both resources of the unbuilt VPC, not the live one. Workers created that way would sit in a fresh VPC with no route to the live database or Redis. Note existing_vpc.tf already contains data sources for the REAL network (vpc-0f3e7b3f243fbc133, two private subnets, sg-0262aed02d8df0356) and only redis.tf uses them; ecs.tf, alb.tf and vpc.tf describe a parallel one. SECOND DEFECT, independent of state: every container definition in ecs.tf uses a BARE image reference -- 'vyomquant-api:latest', 'vyomquant-mds:latest', 'vyomquant-simulator:latest', each carrying a '# ECR URL goes here' comment. With no registry host, ECS resolves these against Docker Hub and never consults ECR, so any apply of this config produces tasks that cannot pull. This is precisely why the three vyomquant-worker-*-production:1 revisions are INACTIVE and never ran. Qualifying the URI fixes api, mds and the workers; it CANNOT fix simulator, because there is no vyomquant-simulator repository in ECR at all -- the account holds vyomquant-api, vyomquant-tee, vyomquant-mds, vyomquant-worker and vyomquant-frontend. WHY THIS IS FILED SEPARATELY rather than absorbed into INF-03: INF-03 is 'the workers are not deployed', and it has a working answer that does not touch any of this (scripts/deploy_worker_services.py, which uses the cluster and network that actually exist). Adopting production into terraform is a different, much larger job -- import ~84 live resources, reconcile every name, supply real custom-domain configuration, and reconcile ecs.tf and vpc.tf against existing_vpc.tf -- with production blast radius throughout. Folding it into INF-03 would have meant either doing all of it under a finding about workers, or quietly leaving it undescribed once the workers ran.
verification_level: The plan output is real terraform output from a real credential against the real account, saved and read in full (2993 lines), not a prediction from reading the config. The resource counts come from parsing the plan's own 'will be created' lines. The name mismatches, the missing cluster, the ECR repository inventory and the live service's network configuration were each confirmed by separate AWS API calls. NOTHING WAS APPLIED and no terraform state was written: plan is read-only, and the state object in the new bucket is still absent. The precondition failure is the plan's own error, quoted verbatim.
remaining_action: A DECISION FIRST, THEN A PROJECT. The decision: should production be brought under terraform at all, or should the committed terraform be treated as aspirational and the real infrastructure managed another way? Both are defensible; what is not defensible is the current position, where a repository contains 83 managed resources that look authoritative, are scanned by CI (05-security.yml runs Trivy over terraform/), and describe something that has never existed -- so anyone who reads them to understand production is misled, and anyone who runs `terraform apply` to change production builds a second one instead. IF THE ANSWER IS YES, the order that keeps blast radius down: (1) fix the bare image references, and decide what simulator should point at given it has no ECR repository -- cheap, and it is the one change that is purely a defect fix; (2) reconcile ecs.tf/alb.tf/vpc.tf against the live names and against existing_vpc.tf's data sources, so the config describes the real cluster, the real service and the real network instead of a parallel one; (3) supply real values for enable_custom_domain and domain_name, since the committed defaults (false, 'example.com') cannot plan in a production environment; (4) `terraform import` the live resources incrementally, re-planning after each group and requiring '0 to change' before moving on -- importing is itself safe, since it only writes state, so the risk is entirely in what the first apply afterwards does; (5) only then consider an apply, and read it. DO NOT run `terraform apply` from the current configuration under any circumstances. The remote backend created under INF-03 is safe to keep either way -- it holds no state yet, costs approximately nothing, and an empty versioned bucket is the right place for state to land if step (4) ever happens.

title: backend_app.backend.dag_worker has no process entry point, so the dag worker command in the committed deployment exits 0 on import
evidence: Found by deploying it. INF-03 created vyomquant-worker-dag-service from terraform/ecs.tf's own declaration -- `command = ["python", "-m", "backend_app.backend.dag_worker"]` -- and the task exited 0 within seconds, twice, with ECS dutifully restarting it: tasks c247dbe435aa43d8ad123a4368211763 and 517076dbe99543009d5deb6354c1fd95, both `lastStatus: STOPPED`, both `stoppedReason: "Essential container in task exited"`, both container `exitCode: 0`. Each produced exactly one log line, a pydantic protected-namespace UserWarning, and nothing else -- no startup message, no traceback. THE CAUSE IS SIMPLE AND IS IN THE MODULE: backend_app/backend/dag_worker.py defines DagWorker and WorkerPool and ends with a module-level global, `worker_pool = WorkerPool(num_workers=4)`. There is NO `if __name__ == "__main__":` block and no run_worker() coroutine. So `python -m backend_app.backend.dag_worker` imports the module, constructs that global, reaches the end of the file and exits successfully. Nothing is started, nothing is awaited, and the exit code is 0, so ECS cannot tell it from a job that completed. Compare backend_app/workers/command_worker.py and backend_app/workers/marketplace_expiry_worker.py, which both end with a run_worker() and an `asyncio.run(run_worker())` under __main__, and both of which started and stayed up in the same deployment. WHY NOBODY KNEW: tests/test_worker_deployment_coverage.py asserts that every WorkerBase subclass is NAMED in a deployment entry point, by regex-matching `python -m <module>` strings in terraform/ecs.tf. dag_worker satisfies that test while being unable to run, so the test reports the worker as hosted and the config reports it as deployed. The assurance was about the string, not the process. No worker had ever actually been started in production (INF-03), so the gap between the two had never been observable. CURRENT STATE: the service exists at desiredCount=0, set immediately on diagnosis to stop the restart loop. It is not deleted, so the finding stays visible and so that raising it to 1 is the whole deployment step once the module has an entry point. ||| VERIFIED IN PRODUCTION 2026-10-26. vyomquant-worker-dag-service was rolled onto vyomquant-worker-dag:2 (image 77b71dbc563ab703b8ff187b0797443d846aabd1, confirmed to contain the entry-point commit) and raised to desiredCount=1. Its own log now shows the entry point executing: 'Worker registered: dag-1', 'DAG worker process starting with 1 in-process worker(s): dag-1', 'Starting worker: dag-1', 'DAG worker process ready; 1 worker(s) running', followed by '[RedisManager] Connected to 3 databases'. Where the task previously emitted one pydantic warning and exited 0, it now starts and stays up: ZERO stopped tasks for the service since the roll, against two exit-0 lifecycles before it. Independently corroborated by OBS-02's verification, which found worker:health:dag-1 heartbeating with status='healthy' -- a key only a running worker writes. CONFIRMED FROM LOGS AND TASK HISTORY, NOT runningCount, which is the trap this finding is named for: the service reported running=1 while exit-looping between polls. The first stream checked was an older task's and showed only the pydantic warning; reading the CURRENT task's stream is what established the fix.
verification_level: Verified in production from the worker's own log and from task history: the entry point's four startup lines appear, and the service has zero stopped tasks since the roll where it previously accumulated exit-0 lifecycles every ~90 seconds. Corroborated independently by worker:health:dag-1 appearing in Redis with status='healthy', which only a running worker writes. Deliberately NOT argued from runningCount, which read 1 for this service while it was exit-looping. The static guard (tests/test_inf07_declared_workers_are_runnable.py) was separately proved to discriminate: it passes the four runnable workers and fails all three of RT-16's class-only modules.
remaining_action: NOTHING FOR THE ENTRY POINT. Two things the running worker revealed, both pre-existing and both small: (1) dag_worker.py:134 calls `redis_manager.sadd(...)` without awaiting it, so `_register_worker` never actually writes the worker-registry entry -- the process logs 'Worker registered: dag-1' while registering nothing, and Python says so at runtime ('RuntimeWarning: coroutine SharedRedisManager.sadd was never awaited'). Anything reading TaskQueueKeyBuilder.worker_registry() to enumerate live workers sees an empty set. (2) A startup race: the cache manager logged 'Redis is unavailable and this is not a development environment' twice before connecting 106ms later. It fails closed, so no lock is wrongly granted, but a caller in that window gets a refusal on a healthy deployment. ALSO STILL TRUE: DAG_WORKER_CONCURRENCY defaults to 1 and ecs.tf sizes this worker at 256 cpu / 512 MB. Raising one without the other is the mistake the constant's comment warns about, since core/database_pool.py budgets connections per worker PROCESS.

title: The shared Redis manager swallows every error and returns neutral values, so counters and membership checks silently fail open when Redis degrades
evidence: The 'remove the duplicate method definitions' half is done (commit 0357897). MockRedisClient and SharedRedisManager each defined several of their own methods twice (9 pairs, 19 dead method bodies total); Python keeps only the LAST def, so the first copy of each pair never ran. At least one pair (incr/decr) had a DIFFERENT signature in its dead copy than the one actually executing. Removed every dead (shadowed) definition after diffing each pair by hand to confirm zero behavioural change (several byte-identical copy-paste; a few an older implementation style shadowed by a newer, more complete one -- e.g. xadd gaining retries + PublishError-raising for TRADING_CRITICAL_STREAMS in its winning definition). incrby/decrby were genuinely single-definition but sat inside the same dead line range as the real duplicates -- a first pass deleted them by accident, caught by running their real caller's (subscription_engine.py) tests before committing; restored and pinned by name in the new test file. tests/test_red01_no_duplicate_redis_manager_methods.py (4 tests, AST-based): neither class defines any method name twice; incrby/decrby still exist exactly once and work end-to-end. Regression: a ~2500-test sweep across quota/idempotency/billing/paper-trading/rate-limiting/dashboard suites + full validation_sweep/schema_drift (484 passed, 2 failed -- same pre-existing, unrelated billing findings) both clean. ADDITIONALLY this session (commit 44bf0a7): rather than leaving the full 'enumerate every call site' task undifferentiated, individually traced the three categories this entry's own remaining_action named as safety-relevant (quota reservation, idempotency claims, kill-switch reads) to find out how many genuinely still rely on SharedRedisManager's fail-open contract. Confirmed the plain proxy methods (incrby/decrby/get/etc.) do swallow a connection error and return a neutral value by design (read SharedRedisManager.incrby/decrby directly) -- but found every safety-critical caller already has its OWN independent protection against that, built in earlier, separate fixes: the kill switch (KILL-01, GlobalKillSwitch.is_active's own RedisUnavailable-based local-latch fail-closed path, which does not go through the shared manager's fail-open methods at all), quota enforcement (SubscriptionEngine.reserve_quota's new_usage < amount inference -- a healthy INCRBY of a positive amount cannot return less than that amount, so a neutral 0 is distinguishable and refused -- and subscription_dependencies.enforce_quota's own explicit UsageReadFailed -> 503 'not a pass' handling), and this same module's own start_processing (already raises in production on a Redis failure). title: The secret-redacting log filter is installed on only 13 marketplace/paper logger names; billing, exchange, execution and auth loggers are unfiltered
evidence: Confirmed by reading backend_app/core/observability.py: RedactingLogFilter was attached only to the 13 logger names in GUARDED_LOGGER_NAMES (task 33.4's own scope: marketplace and paper) -- billing, exchange, execution and auth loggers carried no secret redaction at all. A Logger's own filters apply only to records it originates (Logger.handle checks self.filters, never an ancestor's), which is why attaching to 13 named loggers protected only those 13 and nothing else, however many other loggers exist in the codebase. Added install_root_log_redaction(), which attaches RedactingLogFilter to every HANDLER on the root logger instead -- a Handler's filters run for every record that propagates to it, whatever logger originated it, which is the mechanism the remediation note ("Install RedactingLogFilter at the root logging handler") names precisely. main.py calls it immediately after its own logging.basicConfig(...), which is what gives the root logger a handler to attach to. The original module's own docstring explains WHY root-handler attachment was avoided for task 33.4 ("redact the whole process's output, which the task forbids") -- that was a deliberate narrow scope for that task, not a permanent prohibition, and LOG-01 is exactly the later finding asking for the wider behavior that task declined. New tests/test_log01_root_redaction_covers_every_logger.py (4 tests, using a standalone logger/handler pair, never the real process root): an arbitrary, never-individually-guarded logger name is redacted once the handler it propagates to carries the filter; a record from an ALREADY-guarded logger (PaperRepository) is proven not to be double-mangled by passing through both its own logger filter and the root handler filter (the second pass on already-redacted text is a no-op); the installer is idempotent; a handler-less logger (the real root before basicConfig runs) returns 0 rather than raising. tests/test_log_redaction.py (362 tests, pre-existing) still passes; confirmed main.py still imports and boots with the root handler now carrying the filter.
remaining_action: Covers the single root handler logging.basicConfig installs, the dominant real log path for this process (every logger with propagate=True, the default, eventually reaches it). Does not retroactively cover a handler some other module attaches directly to a non-root logger and removes from the propagation chain (propagate=False), nor a handler uvicorn or another framework might attach to the root AFTER main.py's own install_root_log_redaction() call runs -- neither case was found by reading main.py, but a dedicated audit of every logging.basicConfig/addHandler call site was not performed. title: The admin-only portfolio-management API is largely non-functional (unawaited coroutines, nested-lock deadlock risk)
evidence: The three asks in the original remaining_action (add missing awaits; fix the non-reentrant lock being re-entered; fix forced_reduction's close percentage) were the tip of a much deeper problem: this module (admin-only, mounted at /api/internal/portfolio-mgmt behind get_admin_user, confirmed separate from the real live-trading routers/portfolio.py) had ZERO prior behavioral test coverage anywhere in the repo, and crashed or hung at nearly every call site once actually exercised. Found and fixed, layer by layer, by actually calling the code rather than reading it: (1) validate_consistency() was called from both open_position and close_position but was never defined ANYWHERE on PortfolioManager -- AttributeError on every single open or close, before any other bug was even reached. Implemented it for real: checks each strategy's used_capital+available_capital==allocated_capital invariant and that open_positions/strategy_positions only reference live, correctly-filed positions. (2) Missing awaits on get_margin_metrics/_check_exposure_limits/register_strategy and several GET endpoints (exposure/margin/margin/health/margin/status/pnl/detailed-summary/prices/update) -- all returned unexecuted coroutine objects instead of data. (3) asyncio.Lock is not re-entrant: get_portfolio_summary held its own lock and then called three other lock-acquiring methods; open_position's conflict-cancellation step called the lock-acquiring close_position while already holding that lock; update_prices did the same into margin_monitor.check_margin_health -> _forced_position_reduction -> close_position. All three are guaranteed deadlocks the moment missing-await bug #2 is fixed first (which is presumably why nobody had hit this in whatever manual testing existed). Fixed by splitting get_margin_metrics/get_exposure_metrics/get_pnl_summary/_check_exposure_limits/close_position into `_locked` bodies the caller can invoke directly while already holding the lock, with public async wrappers that acquire it fresh; narrowed update_prices' own lock scope so the margin check and any resulting forced liquidation run after the price-update lock is released. (4) get_exposure_metrics built an ExposureMetrics() instance and then read/wrote MarginMetrics-shaped fields on it (margin_used, margin_level, margin_call_threshold...) that ExposureMetrics does not declare as fields at all -- AttributeError on every call where margin_used<=0, i.e. an EMPTY portfolio, the ordinary starting state. This was a copy-paste of the margin calculation onto the wrong dataclass; rewrote it to populate ExposureMetrics' own real fields (symbol/strategy exposure breakdown, gross/net/long/short exposure, leverage, concentration), which is also the shape every caller (get_portfolio_summary, create_snapshot) already assumed when reading .symbol_exposure/.gross_exposure off the result. (5) create_snapshot (called from inside open_position/close_position, i.e. on every trade) read self.pm.available_capital/self.pm.used_capital, neither of which exists on PortfolioManager at all (only per-strategy StrategyAllocation.available_capital/used_capital do) -- AttributeError on every single snapshot. Fixed to sum across self.pm.allocations.values(). Also fixed create_snapshot's exposure_metrics.total_exposure read (ExposureMetrics has no such field either) to use the real gross_exposure field. (6) MarginMonitor's forced-liquidation path called self.pm.close_position(position_id=..., close_price=..., reason=...) -- but close_position's parameter is named exit_price, not close_price -- TypeError on every forced liquidation. Fixed, and made check_margin_health/_forced_position_reduction/get_margin_status async so they can properly await the manager calls they depend on (they were plain sync methods calling async methods, which can never actually run the async body). (7) the liquidation log said 'reducing by 25%' while the code's own comment admits there is no partial-close method and it always closes the entire position -- an operator reading logs during a real margin event would see a false 'only trimmed 25%' when 100% was actually liquidated. The log and the result's 'action' field now both say 'full_close', matching what actually happens. New tests/test_pm01_portfolio_manager_is_functional.py (8 tests, every call that used to deadlock wrapped in asyncio.wait_for with a 5s timeout so a regression times out loudly instead of hanging the whole suite) exercises register_strategy, open_position (including the real conflict-cancellation path with two opposing positions), close_position, update_prices, a real forced-liquidation scenario (drives an actual margin_level under the 110% threshold and asserts the position is actually closed, not just logged about), and get_portfolio_summary/get_margin_status end to end. Full regression (new suite + every other portfolio-management test in the repo + validation_sweep, 450+ tests) clean except the 2 unrelated pre-existing billing failures already confirmed earlier this session.
remaining_action: True partial position reduction (closing e.g. 25% of a position's size rather than always closing 100%) is NOT implemented -- PortfolioManager has no partial-close primitive (resizing a Position's quantity while keeping it open and correctly re-deriving its realized/unrealized PnL split) and adding one is a real feature, not a bug fix, with its own design and test surface. This pass fixed the DISHONESTY (claiming 25% while doing 100%) and the crashes/deadlocks around it, not the missing feature -- always closing fully on a liquidation-risk margin event is a conservative, safe behavior, not an unsafe one, so this is a legitimate deferral rather than a masked defect.

title: Alembic's baseline migration DROPs core trading tables; running it against an existing, unstamped production database would destroy data
evidence: Confirmed by reading backend_app/alembic/versions/4ef23035a692_baseline.py: it has no down_revision -- the first thing alembic upgrade head runs against an unstamped database -- and its upgrade() unconditionally DROP TABLE ... CASCADEs orders, positions, fills, transaction_records, transaction_checkpoints, transaction_rollbacks and idempotency_keys. On a fresh database this is a no-op; against an EXISTING, unstamped production database (this platform's own parallel raw-SQL migration system, backend_app/migrations/*.sql, already creates orders/positions/fills independently of Alembic, with real rows), running it would silently destroy every one of them. Added _refuse_if_any_target_table_has_rows(bind), called as the FIRST statement in upgrade() before any DROP: checks all seven target tables for even one row (EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM ... title: Two independent sequence allocators for paper session events can collide and drop a bar on feed disconnect
evidence: Confirmed the collision mechanism exactly as named: paper_market_feed.FeedHandle._emit_feed_disconnected allocated its sequence from paper_repository.next_session_event_sequence (max(paper_events.sequence) + 1, read off the LOG), while every other Paper_Channel event (paper_events.record_event -> next_sequence -> paper_repository.allocate_session_event_sequence) allocates from an atomic compare-and-swap on the paper_sessions.event_sequence COUNTER. Traced the actual failure mode: the feed writer's INSERT (via insert_session_event) advances the LOG but never touches the COUNTER, so a subsequent ordinary event's counter-based allocation can read a stale, lower number and collide with the sequence the feed writer already used; uq_paper_event_seq then refuses that ordinary event's INSERT with PaperDuplicateSessionEvent, and neither paper_session_service._emit nor the bar-stepping loop that calls it catches or retries that exception -- so the bar is dropped, not merely delayed. Fixed by routing _emit_feed_disconnected through allocate_session_event_sequence instead, so there is only one source of truth for the next sequence number and the race cannot happen at all. next_session_event_sequence itself is kept (it has its own direct test coverage and tests/property/test_paper_channel_sequence.py reuses it as a synthetic log-based second writer to stress-test the counter allocator's retry logic in general) -- only its one production caller moved. Along the way, fixed a stale property test harness bug this change exposed: tests/test_paper_market_feed_selection.py's shared _session_row() fixture never carried an event_sequence key at all, and the fake client's eq-filter compares str(row.get(col)) against the literal given -- an ABSENT key reads back as 'None', which never equals '0', so allocate_session_event_sequence's own compare-and-swap would lose all three attempts against this fixture even though the real column defaults the row to exactly the value the swap expects. Seeded it at 0 (the column's real DEFAULT per migration 009), which is behaviourally transparent to every other reader (the allocator's own code already treats an absent/NULL value as 0) and only matters for this exact-string-equality fake match. Updated the two stale docstring claims in test_paper_channel_sequence.py that called next_session_event_sequence 'task 24.4's feed writer's allocator ... a real production path', which is no longer true after this fix. New tests/test_paper06_feed_disconnect_shares_the_allocator.py (3 tests): an AST check that the feed-disconnect writer's own source calls allocate_session_event_sequence and not next_session_event_sequence (catches a revert even without a live collision); a real disconnect advances the counter to exactly match the log's own highest sequence (they can no longer diverge); and the exact scenario this finding describes -- a disconnect immediately followed by an ordinary event -- allocates consecutive, non-colliding sequence numbers end to end, with both rows landing. title: Backtests, optimization trials and walk-forward windows ran on the most recent bars regardless of the requested start_date/end_date
evidence: Discovered while investigating OPT-02 (walk-forward does not fit per-window parameters): confirmed the root cause is upstream of optimization_engine.py entirely. backend_app/backend/backtest_runtime.py::run_backtest logs start_date/end_date and stamps them onto the backtests row's metadata, then calls self.data_engine.fetch_historical_ohlcv(symbol=symbol, timeframe=timeframe, limit=10_000, max_retries=3) with NO date-range argument at all. backend_app/backend/data_seeking_engine.py::fetch_historical_ohlcv had no date-range parameter to pass -- with since=None it always answers 'the most recent N bars', per its own docstring. Grepped every start_date/end_date usage in backtest_runtime.py and confirmed neither is used to filter/select data anywhere. Consequence: a backtest requested over 2020 and one requested over 2023 fetched and ran on byte-identical data (whatever was most recent when called); every optimization trial, Monte Carlo run, sensitivity run and benchmark comparison inherited the same defect through the one shared run_backtest call; and a walk-forward window's train and test periods -- different date ranges by construction -- ran on that same identical data, which is what made genuine per-window parameter differentiation (OPT-02) structurally impossible regardless of how the optimization logic itself was fixed. Fixed by adding a second, optional since_ms/until_ms mode to fetch_historical_ohlcv (a new _fetch_ohlcv_bounded that pages FORWARD from since_ms, trimming rather than rounding past a page straddling until_ms) while leaving the existing no-argument 'most recent' mode completely untouched -- the existing DATA-01 regression suite (7 tests) still passes unmodified. Wired run_backtest to use it via a new _requested_window_ms(start_date, end_date) helper that converts the two ISO strings already received into (since_ms, until_ms), with an unreadable/blank date falling back to (None, None) -- the prior 'most recent' behaviour -- rather than a new failure mode. New tests/test_bt02_backtest_honors_requested_date_range.py (13 tests): the bounded fetch's exact-window, multi-page, mid-page-trim and open-vs-closed-window-warning behaviour; _requested_window_ms's ISO/naive-UTC/blank handling; and two end-to-end wiring tests proving run_backtest actually calls fetch_historical_ohlcv with the window implied by start_date/end_date, including that two DIFFERENT requested windows are passed two DIFFERENT bounds -- the exact guarantee OPT-02's per-window fit now depends on. Full regression: the untouched-path DATA-01 suite plus 10 other backtest/optimization test files (224 passed total).
remaining_action: None at the code level for the data-fetch mechanism itself. This finding only makes per-window / per-date-range backtesting POSSIBLE; it does not itself change optimization_engine.py's walk-forward logic to actually use different windows for fitting -- that is OPT-02's own remaining scope, tracked separately. Also not addressed: fetch_historical_ohlcv's 10,000-bar cap could still truncate a very wide requested window silently (it already warns via the existing under-coverage path when the window is open-ended, but a closed window wider than the cap is trimmed to its first bars with no warning, by design, since a closed window's own date bound is what the caller asked for) -- not flagged separately since it matches the existing cap-and-warn contract this function already had for the no-range mode.

title: _handle_ccxt_error misclassifies a network/timeout failure as a non-retryable InsufficientFundsError when its message mentions an unrelated operation name (e.g. fetch_balance)
evidence: Surfaced by this session's EXT-01 corpus synthesis (staging/PHASE11B_*.md), left explicitly unverified and without its own ledger row at that time ('a future pass should read core's _handle_ccxt_error directly and decide whether to track it'). Independently re-verified against current source this session, not taken on faith: backend_app/backend/exchange_executor.py's CCXTExchangeExecutor._handle_ccxt_error classified errors by a fixed-order substring match that checked 'insufficient'/'balance' BEFORE 'network'/'timeout'/'connection' -- so a transient network error from an operation literally named fetch_balance (ccxt's own message text for a failed balance call, e.g. 'Request timeout fetching balance') matched the funds check first and was returned as InsufficientFundsError (retryable=False) instead of NetworkError (retryable=True). That fallback (for anything not a recognised ccxt type: a raw asyncio.TimeoutError, an aiohttp/OS error, or ccxt unavailable) is itself reordered -- network/timeout checked before insufficient/balance -- for the same reason. New tests/test_w6_ccxt_error_classification.py (9 tests): the exact W-6 scenario (a real ccxt.RequestTimeout/NetworkError mentioning 'balance'/'insufficient' is still classified NetworkError, retryable); a genuine InsufficientFunds/RateLimitExceeded/BadSymbol/AuthenticationError still classified correctly (no overcorrection); three non-ccxt fallback cases unchanged. Full regression: tests/test_exchange_credential_log_redaction.py + test_dup02_ambiguous_submission_is_not_retried.py + tests/test_validation_sweep.py (410 passed, 2 skipped, 1 pre-existing unrelated failure confirmed via git stash to predate this change -- an EXCH-01 sandbox-verification log line, not this classifier).
remaining_action: None identified. This closes the finding as the corpus originally scoped it (telemetry/alerting accuracy for a misclassified error type) -- it does not claim to have found or fixed every possible substring collision in the fallback path (still string-based for non-ccxt exceptions), only the specific balance/timeout collision the corpus named and the symmetric insufficient/network collision found while verifying it.

title: The ALB's own public DNS name serves plaintext HTTP directly, bypassing CloudFront's TLS entirely, with the security group open to 0.0.0.0/0
evidence: Surfaced this session by running checkov (a local, pip-installable Trivy-equivalent IaC scanner; CI-03's own remaining_action named Trivy CRITICAL findings that could not be reproduced for lack of a reachable binary -- checkov closes that gap) against terraform/, then independently verifying the flagged resources in source rather than trusting the scanner's framing alone. title: RedactingLogFilter destroyed a lazy %-format placeholder in a denied-key-shaped label, crashing the kill-switch's 'audit write failed, never raise' fallback and turning a successful halt into a false 500
evidence: Found root-causing a real CI failure (tests/test_role_granularity_and_audit.py::TestHighBlastRadiusEndpoints::test_kill_switch_succeeds_for_operator_with_valid_reason, assert 500 == 200) by reproducing the real exception with a full traceback rather than assuming the test was stale. The 500's message was 'Kill switch error: not all arguments converted during string formatting' -- a classic %-format arg-count mismatch, not the DB error it looked like at first. Traced it to core/observability.py's RedactingLogFilter, attached to every root logging handler by install_root_log_redaction() (LOG-01) and therefore reached by every logger in the process, SafetyAudit included. _redact_key_values_in_text() runs against record.msg BEFORE Python's lazy %-logging substitutes record.args into it, so for a %-style call it sees the literal, unsubstituted template text, placeholders and all. core/safety_audit.py:record_safety_transition()'s own 'audit write failed, log the record for recovery' critical call logs '...authorization_source=%s reason=%r detail=%s'. 'authorization_source' matches the deny-list's 'authorization' entry (SECRET_KEY_NAMES) as a contiguous token subsequence, so the filter treated the literal text '%s' immediately after 'authorization_source=' as the value to redact and replaced it with '[redacted]' -- deleting one of the format string's 11 conversion specifiers while record.args (redacted separately, per item, never shortened) stayed at 11 elements. record.getMessage()'s msg %% self.args then raised TypeError the instant any handler tried to render the line. This is exactly the failure mode core/safety_audit.py's module docstring says record_safety_transition() exists to prevent: 'A safety control must not fail to engage because its audit row could not be written... never raises into the caller.' The kill switch HAD already engaged by this point (GlobalKillSwitch.activate()'s local latch is set before the DB write is attempted) -- the crash was purely in the best-effort logging fallback for a failed audit write, but because routers/admin.py:global_kill_switch() wraps the whole body in a bare 'except Exception: raise HTTPException(500, ...)', that logging crash propagated all the way out as a 500 telling the operator the halt failed, when it had actually succeeded. The DB write itself failed in this test only because the SQLite test-lane fallback has no safety_control_audit table (it is accessed via raw SQL, not an ORM model, so the sqlite-lane Base.metadata.create_all() bootstrap fixture never creates it) -- but the SAME crash would hit a real production DB outage during a real kill-switch activation, which is precisely the scenario the 'never raises' contract is written for.
verification_level: root-caused with a real, unmodified traceback captured by temporarily logging traceback.format_exc() in the route's except block (removed before commit), then confirmed character-for-character via a standalone script that the unpatched redact_text() deletes the %s after 'authorization_source=' (11 specifiers -> 10) while the patched version preserves the template exactly (11 -> 11) and still redacts a real literal secret value. Full test suite re-run after the fix: tests/test_role_granularity_and_audit.py 11/11 (was 10/11), tests/test_log01_root_redaction_covers_every_logger.py, tests/test_log_redaction.py (370 tests total, all passing before and after except one pre-existing, unrelated failure in test_exchange_credential_log_redaction.py -- confirmed via git stash to fail identically with and without this change), tests/test_trade02_kill_switch_fails_closed.py, tests/test_kill03_authoritative_global_halt.py.
remaining_action: Not yet exercised against a real deployed backend with a real database outage induced during a live kill-switch activation -- the fix is verified at the function level (redact_text() preserves %-format templates) and via the existing test suite, not end-to-end against production infrastructure. Separately, the SQLite test lane still has no safety_control_audit table at all (it is raw-SQL-only, no ORM model), so this unit test only exercises the 'DB write fails' branch by accident of the test lane's schema gap rather than by deliberate fault injection -- worth a dedicated test that injects a DB failure on purpose, but out of scope for this fix.

title: ConnectionSharder.get_shard_for_user used Python's per-process-randomized hash(), breaking its own 'a user always connects to the same shard' guarantee across worker processes
evidence: Surfaced as the first red 01 PR Check on main since DEPLOY-02's fix landed -- a push carrying only ledger JSON/CSV changes (commit 2f63af6, PR #43) could not have caused a real regression, so the failure was investigated rather than assumed to be unrelated noise. tests/test_websocket_cluster.py::test_shard_distribution failed with 'Shard 0 has 197 users, expected ~250' (tolerance +/-20% of 250, i.e. 200-300). Root-caused to backend_app/backend/websocket_cluster.py::ConnectionSharder.get_shard_for_user calling Python's built-in hash() on the user_id string -- CPython randomizes string hashing per process via PYTHONHASHSEED (on by default since 3.3, to resist hash-flooding DoS), so the exact same 1000 deterministic user_ids land in different shards on every process start; this run's seed happened to skew shard 0 outside tolerance. This is not merely a flaky test: the method's own docstring promises 'a user always connects to the same shard', which is false across any two processes with different hash seeds -- i.e. any two gunicorn workers in a real deployment. Confirmed ConnectionSharder has no other call site anywhere in backend_app/ (grepped the whole tree), so nothing live is currently mis-routed -- same 'built, tested, never wired in' pattern this ledger documents elsewhere (RT-11, HY-02) -- but the class exists and is tested as working correctness, not test-only scaffolding, so the gap is real for whenever it is wired in.
verification_level: Fixed by hashing with hashlib.sha256 instead of hash() -- stable across processes and interpreter restarts. Verified directly: the same two user_ids resolve to the same shard under PYTHONHASHSEED=1/2/3 after the fix (varied before it), and tests/test_websocket_cluster.py passes 12/12 under five different hash seeds (0-4), where it was previously seed-dependent.

title: Every ccxt websocket stream fails: ccxt 4.3.92 calls an aiohttp internal that aiohttp 3.11+ removed, and aiohttp cannot be downgraded because it is pinned for four CVEs
evidence: Found by deploying the market-data service and then DRIVING it, rather than by reading code. mds came up clean -- Redis connected on three databases, 'Listening to mds:commands...', health server on 8081 -- and then scripts/verify_mds_end_to_end.py published a real subscribe to mds:commands and waited for candles. Zero arrived in 90 seconds, and no mds:last_price key was written. The mds log says why, every five seconds: `ERROR - Error watching binance BTC/USDT: 'aiohttp._websocket.reader_c.WebSocketReader' object has no attribute 'parse_frame'`. REPRODUCED LOCALLY, which is what makes it a version fact rather than an environment quirk: with ccxt 4.3.92 and aiohttp 3.14.3, aiohttp._websocket.reader_c.WebSocketReader IS importable but `parse_frame` is absent from it (hasattr -> False), aiohttp.http_websocket.WebSocketReader has no parse_frame either, and a bare `ccxtpro.binance().watch_ohlcv('BTC/USDT','1m')` fails with the identical message. ccxt 4.3.92's websocket client reaches for an aiohttp internal that aiohttp restructured in 3.11; ccxt acknowledged this in ccxt/ccxt#24403 and advised pinning aiohttp 3.10.11. THE OBVIOUS FIX IS CLOSED. aiohttp is pinned at 3.14.4 for FOUR CVEs, each with its reasoning recorded in requirements-base.txt: CVE-2025-69223 (zip-bomb DoS via auto_decompress) and CVE-2026-69244 (out-of-bounds heap read in the C response parser's error path) are fixed by 3.14.3; CVE-2026-111063 and CVE-2026-111064 (GHSA-2g87-pp6c-29x5), found by CI's own pip-audit against 3.14.3, are fixed by 3.14.4. And .github/workflows/05-security.yml runs pip-audit WITH NO SUPPRESSIONS AT ALL -- that file's comment records the removal of its last --ignore-vuln flag. So downgrading aiohttp below 3.11 reintroduces four known vulnerabilities AND fails the security gate. It is not an option; the ccxt side has to move. WHAT IS BROKEN, which is the websocket half of the product. backend_app/mds/main.py's watch_ohlcv stream -- so no paper session can receive live candles, and PAPER-02's mds:last_price cache is never warmed. backend_app/backend/data_seeking_engine.py's stream_live_ohlcv, which relays that same channel. Its watch_my_trades generator, which is RT-16's private fill stream -- so implementing RT-16 on top of ccxt.pro today would produce a listener that cannot connect. And any live-trading order-update stream. WHAT IS NOT BROKEN, and the distinction matters for how much of the product is launchable: every REST path works. That is why DUP-01's Binance certification passed end to end on 2026-10-25 (create_order, fetch_order, find_order_by_client_order_id and a venue-side duplicate refusal, all REST), and why paper_trading_service.fetch_venue_quote can still price a manual market order from a ticker read. A REST-only platform is a smaller product than the one being launched, but it is not a broken one. WHY NOBODY HAD SEEN IT: no process in production had ever opened a ccxt websocket. mds was never deployed (INF-03), its image could not even be built (Dockerfile.mds's broken COPY), paper_sessions holds 0 rows, and RT-16's listener has no process entry point. The failure needed a running streamer to surface, and there was none until this session. A SECOND, SMALLER DEFECT OBSERVED IN THE SAME LOG: unsubscribing does NOT stop a failing stream task. The probe published `{'action':'unsubscribe', ...}` in a finally, and the five-second error loop continued afterwards (34 log events in the following 3 minutes), so a dead subscription retries forever and costs CloudWatch indefinitely. mds was scaled to desiredCount=0 for that reason. ||| FIXED IN SOURCE 2026-10-25 by upgrading ccxt 4.3.92 -> 4.5.90, with the aiohttp pin UNTOUCHED at 3.14.4. Verified directly: ccxt 4.5.90 + aiohttp 3.14.4 returns a real candle from watch_ohlcv('BTC/USDT','1m') -- [1792928580000, 80446.55, 80446.57, 80446.55, 80446.55, 0.09683] -- where 4.3.92 raised the parse_frame AttributeError on the identical call. So all four aiohttp CVEs stay fixed and the websockets work; ccxt/ccxt#24403's advice to pin aiohttp 3.10.11 was never usable here and did not need to be. The `[async]` extra went with the upgrade (4.5.90 warns it does not provide it; aiohttp is now a core ccxt dependency). BOTH MEASUREMENTS THIS ENTRY SAID WOULD NEED RE-RUNNING WERE RE-RUN, and both came back unchanged, which is the outcome that needed proving rather than assuming. SANDBOX_MECHANISMS under 4.5.90: binance URL_SWAP, bybit URL_SWAP, okx HEADER, coinbase/kraken/kucoin UNSUPPORTED, bitget still fails to leave production -- identical to the committed table, so no entry changes, EXCH-01's bitget block still stands, and DUP-01's permanently-blocked coinbase/kraken half is STILL blocked (the upgrade did not hand over new sandboxes). The has['fetchOrder'] audit: binance/okx/kraken/kucoin SUPPORTED on both halves, bybit and coinbase submit-OK/lookup-unclear -- materially unchanged. THE SANDBOX RE-MEASUREMENT NEEDED A PROBE FIX FIRST, and it is the third probe in this effort to report the opposite of the truth. staging/probe_exch01_sandbox_endpoints.py proved a url swap by comparing SERIALISED JSON for equality (`armed_api == test_url`), which held only because 4.3.92's set_sandbox_mode replaced urls['api'] wholesale. 4.5.90 MERGES instead -- swapping keys that have a testnet counterpart, keeping those that do not -- so the armed map is a SUPERSET of `test` and the strings differ although every swappable endpoint moved. The probe printed '*** NONE - ARMED BUT STILL ON PRODUCTION ***' for binance and bybit while its own armed_api line showed testnet.binancefuture.com. Believing it would have meant concluding that fixing the websockets removes binance's sandbox, which DUP-01's live certification disproves outright. The proof is now STRUCTURAL: for every endpoint `test` declares, does the armed map carry the test value rather than the production one -- true on both ccxt versions, and the same principle certify_venue_duplicate_protection.assert_pointed_at_sandbox applies to a live client. THREE TESTS FAILED AND ALL THREE WERE THE WORLD IMPROVING. (1) kraken NOW FORWARDS OUR CLIENT ORDER ID: its create path no longer mentions `userref` at all and reads safe_string_2(params, 'clientOrderId', 'cl_ord_id'), so it moved to FORWARDS_OUR_ID with NATIVE_FIELD 'cl_ord_id'. The SUBMIT half of DUP-01 is therefore now real on kraken -- the platform's deterministic execution_id reaches the venue -- while the CERTIFICATION half is unchanged, because kraken still has no sandbox in which to prove the venue refuses the repeat. Two different claims; only the first moved. (2) binance STILL invents an id when none is supplied, via generate_client_order_id(market) rather than uuid22(); the test had pinned an implementation detail one rename away from a false alarm. (3) THE OKX PRE-OPEN DEFECT IS FIXED UPSTREAM, which is a venue becoming usable rather than a test needing relaxing: on 4.3.92 okx.parse_market concatenated a None base and OKX's pre-open CT instrument made every OKX startup burn three attempts and six seconds of backoff before failing, so OKX markets did not load AT ALL. Measured on 4.5.90: okx.py carries the `weird preopen markets` guard and a real load_markets() returns 4705 markets INCLUDING CT/EUR, the exact instrument that used to break it. connection_engine's comment claiming 'OKX markets still do not load on this ccxt' is corrected, and its fail-fast branch is KEPT -- a library-internal parse fault is deterministic whatever venue caused it, so the branch is now a general guard with no known live instance rather than a workaround for one broken venue. ||| VERIFIED IN PRODUCTION 2026-10-26. The acceptance test this entry named passed against a real deployment, and it is the same script that FAILED against the old image, which is what makes the pass meaningful rather than vacuous. scripts/verify_mds_end_to_end.py published a real subscribe to mds:commands and observed: candles_received 2 (was 0); the first candle carrying transport='WEBSOCKET' -- the delivery path that was broken, not the REST fallback; and mds:last_price populated with {"price": 80134.11, "timestamp": 1793031960000, "transport": "WEBSOCKET"} at TTL 150 exactly (was null, TTL -2). So PAPER-02's durable last-price cache is live and paper_trading_service.get_fresh_market_price now has a measured price to fill a manual market order at. The five-second parse_frame error loop is gone: 0 occurrences in the four minutes after the roll, against 34 in three minutes before. HOW IT REACHED PRODUCTION WITHOUT THE PIPELINE, which matters because the pipeline could not do it. 03-deploy refused every run with 'REFUSING: 01 PR Check concluded failure for 77b71dbc' -- the pre-deployment gate working correctly, since the alias test and the drift baseline were red. And from 2026-10-26 GitHub Actions stopped running this repository's workflows at all: every run that day failed in 4-9 seconds with ZERO steps executed, including scheduled ones with no PR involved (04 Nightly Audit 07:16, 08 Secret History 08:10, 05 Security 09:50), and a Dependency Graph job sat queued for 12h42m. Runs the previous day took 12 minutes and produced real results. That is an account-level Actions cutoff, outside this repository. The image containing the fix had already been built before that happened (77b71dbc563ab703b8ff187b0797443d846aabd1, confirmed to contain the ccxt upgrade commit), so the services were rolled onto it directly with scripts/deploy_worker_services.py's new --image-tag and --update-existing flags: vyomquant-mds:3, and revision :2 for each of the four workers. ||| A FIFTH CONSEQUENCE OF THE UPGRADE, FOUND AND FIXED AFTER THIS ENTRY WAS CLOSED, AND IT WAS A MONEY-SAFETY CONTROL RATHER THAN A TEST. ccxt 4.5.90 also broke EXCH-01's verify_sandbox_endpoint, the check that proves a client asking for sandbox mode has actually left the production API. Its URL_SWAP branch required three conditions, and the third was `api != apiBackup`, which was true evidence on 4.3.92 because that version's set_sandbox_mode saved PRODUCTION into urls['apiBackup'] before swapping urls['test'] into urls['api']. MEASURED on 4.5.90: apiBackup comes out EQUAL TO THE TEST URLS -- apiBackup == test == armed api, all three identical, for binance, bybit and okx -- so the condition compared a value against itself and raised SandboxVerificationFailed on every client that had swapped CORRECTLY. It failed CLOSED, which is the one thing that went right: it refused to connect rather than quietly addressing production, so no order could have reached a live venue believing itself sandboxed. But it refused EVERY legitimate sandbox connection, which means testnet trading and DUP-01's certification harness were both dead from the moment the websockets started working. THE REPAIR compares against the venue's real production endpoint, read from a pristine instance of the same ccxt class (_pristine_production_endpoint), which is what the check always meant and does not depend on how ccxt chooses to use apiBackup. It is also strictly stronger than the old form: the old one proved only 'different from whatever apiBackup holds', this proves 'the declared sandbox endpoint is genuinely not the production one'. apiBackup is still required to be PRESENT, as evidence that ccxt ran its swap branch at all, but its value is no longer trusted. Pristine construction costs nothing and leaks nothing, measured rather than assumed: after cls({}) on ccxt 4.5.90 + aiohttp 3.14.4 both `session` and `tcp_connector` are still None, no 'Unclosed client session' warning is emitted at shutdown, no network call is made (ccxt fills urls from class data in the constructor) and the config is empty, so no credential is involved. A REGRESSION WAS INTRODUCED BY THE FIRST VERSION OF THIS REPAIR AND CAUGHT BY THE TEST SUITE SAYING 'DID NOT RAISE'. Reading production from a pristine client ONLY makes the refusal branch untestable: a FakeClient's https://api.example.com is not comparable to a real binance host, so 'a swap that lands back on production is refused' silently stopped exercising the branch it is named for -- the branch still existed and nothing reached it. verify_sandbox_endpoint therefore takes an optional keyword `production_endpoint`, defaulting to the pristine lookup, and the refusal test passes it explicitly. BOTH new refusal branches were then MUTATION-TESTED, because a refusal test that passes with the branch deleted is not a test: disabling `api == production` made exactly one test fail (DID NOT RAISE), and disabling the 'production could not be determined' refusal made exactly one other fail. Both mutations were reverted and the file re-checked for leftovers. The connect-path fakes now MODEL ccxt's swap -- production urls by default, the swap when options['sandbox'] is set -- instead of hardcoding the post-swap urls, because connect() has no independent knowledge of a production endpoint and legitimately reads it from a pristine instance of the same class; a fake that answers 'what is production?' with 'the sandbox' refuses every connection for a reason that exists only in the fake. VERIFIED IN BOTH DIRECTIONS AGAINST REAL ccxt 4.5.90 by the new scripts/verify_sandbox_control_still_refuses.py: binance and bybit VERIFY with sandbox != production, and the real bitget client RAISES both under its own id (the venue table is closed to unmeasured venues) and under a URL_SWAP declaration (the endpoint evidence itself is judged). The second bitget case was added because the first proves only that the table is closed and would stay green with the endpoint logic deleted outright. VERIFIED END TO END AGAINST THE REAL BINANCE SPOT TESTNET: certify_venue_duplicate_protection.py --venue binance --plan connected through the executor's own sandbox verification and resolved 7 URLs, every one a testnet host (testnet.binance.vision, testnet.binancefuture.com) -- the same script that the broken condition would have refused outright. Local tests: 29 passed in tests/test_exch01_sandbox_endpoint_verification.py (25 before, 4 of them red), 327 passed and 28 skipped across -k 'exch01 or sandbox or exch04', and 52 across the four other exchange-executor files. staging/exch01_sandbox_endpoint_evidence.json was re-measured under 4.5.90 in the same pass, which surfaced two further version-facts worth recording: arming sandbox mode on coinbase, kraken or kucoin now raises TypeError("'NoneType' object is not iterable") instead of ccxt's NotSupported, which is harmless here only because assert_sandbox_supported refuses those three BEFORE construction from their measured UNSUPPORTED declaration (and the constructor's catch-all would classify it as a refusal regardless); and bybit no longer sets options['sandboxMode'] at all, which is irrelevant to a verifier that reads urls rather than options.
verification_level: Verified in production by effect, with a test that had already failed against the previous image. Candles arrived on mds:data:* carrying transport='WEBSOCKET'; mds:last_price appeared with a real price and the documented 150s TTL; the error loop stopped (0 in 4 minutes, against 34 in 3). Every figure is from that run. The ccxt upgrade itself was verified before deployment by a real watch_ohlcv call returning a real candle, and both measurements the upgrade invalidated were re-run and came back unchanged. NOT verified by CI: GitHub Actions has been failing every workflow at the account level since 2026-10-26 (4-9s, zero steps, scheduled runs included), so the full suite has not run against this change. Targeted regression was run locally: 12 passed on the dup01 mapping, 15 on the connection_engine file, 22 on the capability registry, 466 across the capability/registry selection, 865 across exch/sandbox/executor/dup01/connection.
remaining_action: NOTHING FOR THIS FINDING. Websockets work in production and the acceptance test passes. Three things it uncovered belong elsewhere and are recorded rather than carried here: (1) THE RETRY LEAK, NOW FIXED: unsubscribing does not cancel a failing stream task, so a dead subscription retried every five seconds indefinitely. It is harmless while streams succeed, and it is what made the broken state expensive rather than merely broken. An unsubscribe should cancel the task for that (exchange, symbol), and a stream failing N times consecutively should stop and report. BOTH ARE NOW IMPLEMENTED. `unsubscribe` was literally `pass`, under the comment 'Memory optimization / cleanup is omitted for this implementation' -- it is not a memory optimization, it is why a dead subscription kept retrying. It now cancels the task for that (exchange, symbol) and AWAITS the cancellation, because returning as soon as cancel() is called would report the stream stopped while its next watch_ohlcv was still in flight, so an unsubscribe immediately followed by a subscribe could end up with two tasks on one symbol. The websocket loop now counts CONSECUTIVE failures (a successful candle resets the count, so a healthy long-lived stream cannot accumulate its way into a demotion) and at WS_CONSECUTIVE_FAILURE_CEILING=12 -- one minute at the existing five-second backoff -- it logs CRITICAL and FALLS BACK TO REST rather than giving up. That fallback choice is the one that matters for the product: this module already had a designed REST path reached on ccxt NotSupported, and every payload already carried a `transport` field so a subscriber could tell which path it was reading, so a websocket that has failed a dozen times running is the same condition learned by observation instead of declaration. HAD THIS CEILING EXISTED, WS-03 WOULD HAVE BEEN A DEGRADED FEED RATHER THAN A TOTAL OUTAGE -- REST candles, correctly labelled, instead of paper sessions receiving nothing at all. The REST path has its own ceiling of 30, after which the stream STOPS, because there is nothing left to fall back to and a symbol that can never poll (delisted, or a typo in a subscribe command) otherwise retries for the life of the container. A THIRD DEFECT WAS FOUND IN THE SAME CODE WHILE FIXING THESE: `subscribe` tested `key not in active_streams`, so a task that had ENDED left an entry behind that could never be replaced -- every later subscribe for that pair matched the dead entry and silently did nothing, and the health endpoint's active_streams count drifted upward forever. Streams now deregister themselves on completion via a done-callback guarded on task identity, so a late callback for a finished task cannot deregister a live replacement. VERIFIED BY 10 TESTS in tests/test_ws03_mds_stream_lifecycle.py, including the WS-03 error verbatim as the failure mode, and MUTATION-TESTED: restoring `unsubscribe` to `pass` fails exactly one test, and shifting the ceiling by two fails the two tests that assert the exact attempt count. (2) dag_worker's un-awaited redis_manager.sadd is NOW FIXED. It called `redis_manager.sadd(...)` from the SYNCHRONOUS `__init__`, and sadd is an async def, so the call built a coroutine and dropped it -- `RuntimeWarning: coroutine 'SharedRedisManager.sadd' was never awaited`, observed verbatim in the dag worker's own startup log -- while the very next line logged 'Worker registered'. The registry was never written, so anything reading dag:workers:registry saw an empty set however many workers were running. `cleanup()` had the same bug in the other direction (an un-awaited srem) and THE TWO CONCEALED EACH OTHER: deregistering a worker that had never been registered left a set that looked correct by being empty. A constructor cannot await, which is the whole reason the bug was possible there, so registration moved to `start()` -- before `super().start()`, because a worker claiming and executing DAG tasks while absent from the registry is the state that ordering prevents -- and cleanup's srem is awaited. VERIFIED BY 4 TESTS in tests/test_ws03_dag_worker_registry_is_written.py which assert on the RuntimeWarning ITSELF, not on a call count: a count-based test would have passed against the broken code, because the broken code did call sadd, it just never awaited the result. Mutation-tested by dropping the await again, which fails three of the four. (3) A STARTUP RACE in the cache manager: the dag worker logged 'Redis is unavailable and this is not a development environment' twice, then 'Connected to 3 databases' 106ms later. It fails CLOSED (refusing locks rather than silently succeeding per-process), so it is safe, but it means anything consulting the cache in the first fraction of a second gets a refusal on a healthy deployment. (4) THE SANDBOX VERIFIER REGRESSION THIS UPGRADE CAUSED IS FIXED, NOT OUTSTANDING: verify_sandbox_endpoint's third URL_SWAP condition rested on 4.3.92 keeping production in urls['apiBackup'], which 4.5.90 stopped doing, so it refused every correctly-swapped sandbox client. It now compares against a pristine client's real production endpoint, is verified in both directions against real ccxt and against the live Binance spot testnet, and both of its refusal branches are mutation-tested. See this entry's evidence. THE GENERAL LESSON, which applies to the next ccxt bump: a dependency upgrade can invalidate the FACT A SAFETY CHECK RESTS ON without touching the check, and this one failed closed only by luck of how it was written. DO NOT DOWNGRADE aiohttp if a future ccxt problem appears. That path reintroduces four CVEs and fails 05-security.yml's unsuppressed pip-audit; the answer is a different ccxt version.

title: process_referral_commission's installed signature does not match what backend_app/routers/billing.py calls it with, so every Stripe referral commission RPC call has been failing silently
evidence: Found while adapting migration 024 (MONEY-01's double-commission race fix) to the real production schema. The real installed function's signature, read directly off pg_proc, is process_referral_commission(p_payment_id varchar, p_referred_user_id uuid, p_subscription_tier varchar, p_payment_amount_usd numeric) -- note the second parameter is named p_referred_user_id. backend_app/routers/billing.py:2757-2764 calls it via supabase-py's .rpc('process_referral_commission', {...}) with the key 'p_referred_id' (not 'p_referred_user_id'). PostgREST resolves a dict-based .rpc() call by parameter NAME, so this mismatch means the call could never resolve to the installed function -- PostgREST would answer 'function not found', caught by billing.py's bare except and logged as an error, never raised. Zero 'Referral commission processed' log lines appear anywhere in 7 days of production logs (checked directly), consistent with every Stripe referral-commission credit having silently failed for at least that long. FIXED TWO WAYS, NEITHER REQUIRING A DROP (which this session's tooling could not execute -- see DEPLOY-04): (1) backend_app/routers/billing.py's RPC call was changed to pass 'p_referred_user_id' (the real, installed parameter name) instead of 'p_referred_id'. (2) The function's BODY (not its signature/parameter names, which CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION cannot change without DROP FUNCTION first) was replaced via CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION to add the atomic MONEY-01 guard: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (payment_id) WHERE payment_id IS NOT NULL DO NOTHING, with the referral_wallets upsert made conditional on the insert having actually happened, using the REAL wallet columns (balance_usd, total_earned_usd -- confirmed via information_schema, NOT migration 024's assumed pending_balance_usd/lifetime_earnings_usd) and preserving the installed version's referral_relationships.status='active' filter that 024's own replacement would have silently dropped. title: 35 PostgreSQL-gated test files are named in no PostgreSQL lane, so 432 tests -- including a P0's own regression suite -- skip in every lane and assert nothing against a real server

A file that gates itself on AERORA_TEST_DATABASE_URL and is named in neither list therefore runs against a real server NOWHERE, while still looking accounted for: the unit-tests lane has no DATABASE_URL by design so the file SKIPS there, and a skip is not a failure, so a fully green run reports nothing wrong. CLOSED: PR #52 merged to main as 611708c2, and the post-merge 01-pr-check.yml run 39731822360 on that exact commit is green on ALL 8 jobs. The new step -- 'Run every remaining PostgreSQL-gated test file' inside Provisioning, Privilege Hardening & Tenant Isolation -- reports 626 passed, 11 skipped, 0 failed in 42.38s against the postgres:17-alpine service, with the job's other steps unchanged (233 passed, 7 skipped for the original lane; 22 passed, 13 deselected for the production verifiers) and scripts/verify_schema_drift.py still reporting RESULT: NO DRIFT. verification_level: code+test; verified on main in GitHub Actions against real PostgreSQL 17
remaining_action: None for CI-11 itself: the gap is closed, the guard prevents it reopening, and the lane is green on main (611708c2). TWO RESIDUALS, both recorded rather than closed, neither caused by this change: (1) PAPER-05's 10 atomicity tests still SKIP inside the new step, for a reason that contradicts the same job's own provisioning log -- tracked under PAPER-05, needs a live PostgreSQL session to diagnose, and the lane now provides one. title: A module-level PostgreSQL gate placed below six database-independent tests discarded them in every lane, so AUD-01's signal-audit writers had no running test while the suite looked green
evidence: tests/test_aud01_signal_audit_log.py defines nine tests. Collection reported '0 items / 1 skipped'. Six of the nine are the fake-PostgREST unit tests the module's own docstring describes as proving 'every writer calls it correctly and that a failure to record the audit row never breaks the write it is recording'; they need no database. They sit ABOVE a module-level pytest.skip(..., allow_module_level=True) (itself preceded by a module-level pytest.importorskip('psycopg2')), and both forms abort collection of the WHOLE file, so those six went with it. They therefore ran in NO lane and nothing reported it: neither PostgreSQL job lists this file so the gate never opened, and the SQLite lane skipped the module BEFORE collecting them, so they never appeared even as a skip. Confirmed against the real log of run 39695784610: this file contributes no line at all to that run's 14,652 passed / 790 skipped. FIX (d95c8c7f): scoped the gate to the class that needs it, following this suite's own existing convention -- tests/test_production_security_probe_rolls_back_postgres.py already gates per-test with a pytest.mark.skipif named _needs_pg, which is exactly why its six source-inspection tests DO run in the SQLite lane -- and moved the psycopg2 import into the db fixture so a missing driver cannot delete database-independent tests either. NEW GUARD tests/test_module_level_gates_discard_no_tests.py fails if any module places a collection-aborting gate below tests defined above it, with a negative control (the detector must flag the pre-fix shape) and a positive control (a gate above every test is correct and must not be flagged). NEGATIVE CONTROL run against the original file text read from `git show HEAD:<path>` with the working tree untouched: the detector reports gate line 212 and names all six discarded AUD-01 tests, and gate line 262 with six for the probe file, and reports nothing for either post-fix version. Regression slice -k 'aud01 or aud02 or signal_audit or audit_trail or module_level_gates or security_probe': 53 passed, 25 skipped, 0 failed. Test-only change; no production code touched.

The file's three real-PostgreSQL migration tests still need a server; they are wired into the provisioning lane under CI-11 and pass there (run 39728990457). title: Migration 032 declares itself 'NOT APPLIED, PREPARED FOR APPROVAL' but provision_database.py applies it unconditionally, so two tests now disagree about the same file
evidence: Surfaced by CI-11 wiring test_p10d_referral_settlement_lifecycle_postgres.py into a PostgreSQL lane for the first time. backend_app/migrations/032_referral_payouts_terminal_evidence.sql carries a header banner reading 'NOT APPLIED. PREPARED FOR THE MIGRATION OWNER'S APPROVAL. This file alters a SHARED table...', and a test (test_the_proposed_migration_exists_and_is_not_silently_applied) asserts that the string 'NOT APPLIED' is still present. But the file lives in backend_app/migrations/, which scripts/provision_database.py applies wholesale: run 39728990457, job 119660118669 logs 'migrations/032_referral_payouts_terminal_evidence.sql: applied' and then 'skipped (already applied)' on the idempotency re-run. So every database provisioned from repository source DOES carry chk_referral_payouts_terminal_evidence, and the sibling test asserting the safe invariant XPASSed under strict mode and failed the job (fixed in de87b620 by removing that stale marker). Net effect: the repository now contains one test asserting the migration is unapplied and another relying on it being applied, both passing, because they measure different things (file text vs. live schema). NOTE: this is a consistency and governance defect, not a live exposure -- the constraint being PRESENT is the safe direction, and the ledger's own DEPLOY-04 entry records migrations 019-046 being closed out against the real production database. ||| CLOSED (Kiro, 2026-10-24). MEASURED FIRST, AND THE FILE WAS THE THING THAT WAS WRONG. Read from production's pg_constraint: chk_referral_payouts_terminal_evidence CHECK (((status)::text <> 'completed'::text) OR (processed_at IS NOT NULL)) is PRESENT on public.referral_payouts. So the banner 'NOT APPLIED. PREPARED FOR THE MIGRATION OWNER'S APPROVAL' was false, and this entry's question -- 'decide which statement is true for the PRODUCTION database' -- is answered: it is applied. It is applied because the file lives in backend_app/migrations/, which scripts/provision_database.py applies WHOLESALE (the directory is the unit, not the file), so 'prepared but not executed' was never a state that location could hold; the intent and the mechanism disagreed from the moment it was committed. The corrected header says so, keeps the superseded rule verbatim for the record, and names where a deliberately-manual migration actually belongs (migrations/hardening/ or an explicit applier under scripts/). THE STATED BLOCKER WAS WRONG IN BOTH HALVES, and checking it rather than inheriting it is what made this closeable. (1) The remaining_action said editing the file would red the drift gate. `recorded_migrations` is in verify_schema_drift.ADVISORY_DIMENSIONS -- a changed checksum is reported as a WARNING and does not fail the run, and that module's own docstring explains why bookkeeping is held to a different standard than schema shape. (2) It said the provisioner would refuse. provision_database._apply_sql does sys.exit(4) on 'applied previously with a different checksum', but production has NO public.schema_migrations table at all (only a 4-row recorded_migrations, which tracks something else), so there is no prior row to disagree with; and in CI the database is provisioned fresh every run. The edit was never gated by either mechanism. The baseline entry was updated anyway -- a stale digest whose correct value is computable would emit a spurious advisory warning on every future drift run -- and it was COMPUTED rather than measured against a server: sha256(file text) is a pure function of the bytes (provision_database.py:340-341, 473-474), and the script reproduced the OLD digest from the pre-edit file first to prove it had the algorithm right. Exactly one line of staging/provisioning_snapshot.json changes. THE TESTS NO LONGER CONTRADICT EACH OTHER. test_the_proposed_migration_exists_and_is_not_silently_applied (which asserted the string 'NOT APPLIED' was still in the file) is replaced by two: test_migration_032_is_present_in_the_live_schema reads pg_constraint and requires the constraint with 'completed' related to processed_at -- the answer lives in the database, not in the file -- and test_migration_032_no_longer_declares_itself_unapplied checks the one property text can establish. The second is deliberately NOT '"NOT APPLIED" not in text': the corrected header QUOTES the superseded banner verbatim, which is what makes the correction legible to someone who read the old file, so a bare substring check would fail on the quotation and teach the next person to delete the history instead of recording it. Matching raw strings is how this contradiction survived in the first place. Two stale docstrings went with it: the module docstring still described the strict xfail that de87b620 removed, and test_a_payout_cannot_be_completed_without_a_processed_at still carried the checksum explanation disproved above. VERIFIED against a real PostgreSQL provisioned from repository source exactly the way .github/workflows/01-pr-check.yml's provisioning job does (provision_database.py --apply --create-substrate): provisioning exits 0 and logs 032 as applied, all 11 tests in the suite pass with neither new test skipped, and the drift gate's own output shows 032's baseline digest equal to the live digest (the one 'modified' entry it reports is 003_create_exchange_keys_table.sql, not 032). FOUND WHILE VERIFYING, REPORTED NOT BUNDLED: the same drift run shows the committed baseline missing everything 059_mkt06_creator_payout_atomic.sql creates -- 3 tables, 4 check constraints, 8 indexes, 3 RLS flags, 4 policies, 45 privileges -- plus the stale 003 digest. That is a baseline regeneration owed by the MKT-06 change (merged in PR #117) and it is why `01 PR Check` is currently RED on main, independently of this fix.
verification_level: production READ (pg_constraint: the constraint is present) + a real PostgreSQL provisioned from repository source the way CI's provisioning job does (provision exits 0, 11/11 tests pass, neither new test skipped, drift gate confirms 032's baseline digest now equals the live digest)

Separately reported, pre-existing on main and NOT part of this fix: the committed drift baseline is missing everything 059_mkt06_creator_payout_atomic.sql creates and carries a stale digest for 003_create_exchange_keys_table.sql, which is why 01 PR Check is red on main.
