title: One kill-switch toggle issued TWO PUT /api/risk/settings requests: saveRiskConfig was called from inside a React state updater, which StrictMode double-invokes
evidence: RECLASSIFIED from P2/Medium 'flaky frontend test' to P1/High. The flake was a SYMPTOM; the cause is a product defect in a risk-control write path, found by doing the instrumented local run this entry's own remaining_action asked for rather than leaving it labelled flaky. ORIGINAL OBSERVATION (unchanged, still accurate): algo22-terminal/tests/unit/pages/riskSettingsKillSwitch.test.jsx failed on three CI runs across two commits -- runs 39731286176 (both attempts) and 39755298417 on main, where every other job passed -- with 'expected "vi.fn()" to be called 1 times, but got 2 times', a DIFFERENT test case each time because they share one helper. THE CAUSE: RiskSettings.handleToggleSwitch called saveRiskConfig -- an async PUT /api/risk/settings -- from INSIDE the setKillSwitches updater, alongside a second setState. A React state updater must be pure, and src/main.jsx wraps the app in <React.StrictMode>, which DELIBERATELY double-invokes updaters to surface exactly this impurity. So every kill-switch toggle in the real application issued two writes. React also re-invokes updaters when rebasing during concurrent rendering, so a production build is not safe from it either, merely less reliably unsafe. MEASURED, not inferred -- reverting the handler and running the new test gives, every time: 'expected 1 times, but got 2 times' on the pointer path, the same on the keyboard path, and 'expected 2 times, but got 4 times' for two toggles. WHY THE DUPLICATE WAS NOT HARMLESS: the second PUT races the first's response handler, which writes res.data's limits back into the form via setMaxLoss/setMaxPos/setLeverage, so two in-flight writes can land out of order and leave the form AND the server holding something other than the user's last action -- on a kill switch. WHY IT PRESENTED AS FLAKE: that test file asserts the count with 'await waitFor(() => expect(risk.updateConfig).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1))'. An exact-count assertion inside a RETRYING waitFor is only safe while a second call is impossible, because waitFor polls until the callback stops throwing -- so whether it sees 1 or 2 depends on whether the first poll lands between the two calls. That file also mounts with plain render(), without StrictMode, so it never got the deterministic double invocation. THE FIX (commit 81b7823f): the payload is computed from the current committed state OUTSIDE the updater and the state is set to that value, so no updater function remains to be double-invoked. The request BODY is unchanged by construction, which is what task 7.1's strongest assertion (keyboard body deep-equals pointer body) pins -- and that assertion still passes untouched. NOTABLY this is the exact fix the page's own file header had DEFERRED, calling the shape 'an antipattern ... deliberately not fixed here' because the correction changes when the write happens relative to the state change and that commit's subject was typography and colour. That was a correct deferral; the header is now updated so it no longer tells a future reader the shape is still deliberate. NEW tests/unit/pages/riskSettingsStrictModeSingleWrite.test.jsx (5 tests) mounts under <React.StrictMode>, which is how the real app renders, making the double invocation DETERMINISTIC rather than a race; and asserts the count OUTSIDE waitFor (awaiting the write's observable settled effect first), so an extra call fails every time instead of racing a poll. It carries a positive control (two toggles must give exactly two writes, not zero and not four), a payload assertion proving the surviving write is the RIGHT one and still leaves the three unenforced guards as the server reported them (RISK-02), and a check that nothing is written on mount, since StrictMode double-invokes effects too. VERIFICATION: 5 passed alone; 24 passed with the existing kill-switch file, three runs in a row. Negative control run TWICE -- once on the first draft and again on the finalised file after adding explicit settle timeouts, specifically to prove the timeouts did not weaken detection -- failing deterministically both times with the counts above. eslint clean on both changed files (one pre-existing unused-React warning; CI's threshold is 226).
verification_level: code+test; the defect was reproduced deterministically under StrictMode and the fix verified locally with a negative control run twice
remaining_action: None for the defect. Two notes for whoever reads this next. (1) THE SAME SHAPE MAY EXIST ELSEWHERE: handleStrategyAllocationChange and handleSliderChange in the same file were NOT audited for impure updaters in this pass -- the slider path debounces through a ref, which changes the reasoning, and it was out of scope for a fix whose subject was the toggle. A sweep for 'side effect inside a setState updater' across the frontend would be the systemic version of this finding and is not done. (2) THE RACY ASSERTION PATTERN REMAINS in riskSettingsKillSwitch.test.jsx's soleUpdateBody helper: now that the product issues one write, it can no longer observe 2 and the flake is gone at the source, but an exact-count assertion inside a retrying waitFor is still a latent trap if a future change reintroduces a second call -- it would flake again rather than fail. Left alone deliberately rather than rewritten: that file's assertions are about request CONTENT and accessibility and are not this finding's subject, and the new file now covers cardinality deterministically. VERIFIED ONLY LOCALLY so far -- CI has not yet run this change.

title: The Tauri desktop app's Rust dependency tree is scanned by nothing: there is no cargo-audit step anywhere in CI
evidence: Found while reconciling GitHub's 42 open Dependabot alerts against the blocking dependency gate for DEP-01. Four of the 42 are Rust advisories in algo22-terminal/src-tauri/Cargo.lock: tauri (GHSA-7gmj-67g7-phm9, MODERATE), glib (GHSA-wrw7-89jp-8q8g, MODERATE), serde_with (GHSA-7gcf-g7xr-8hxj, MODERATE) and rand (GHSA-cq8v-f236-94qc, LOW). Read every job in 05-security.yml and 01-pr-check.yml: the gates are pip-audit (Python), npm audit (the frontend's package-lock.json), Bandit (Python SAST), and three Trivy scans (container image, terraform IaC, repository secrets). NONE of them reads Cargo.lock -- Trivy can scan Rust lockfiles but the container scan's input is the backend image, which does not contain the desktop app, and the IaC scan is scoped to terraform/. So the only thing reporting these four is Dependabot, which is advisory and blocks nothing. Severity kept at MEDIUM rather than higher: the desktop app is a separately-built Tauri artifact (07-desktop-build.yml), not part of the SaaS runtime, and the four advisories are 3 MODERATE + 1 LOW with no critical among them. But the GAP is categorical -- an entire language ecosystem in this repository has no blocking vulnerability gate, so a future CRITICAL there would also be reported by nothing that fails a build. ||| CLOSED (Kiro, 2026-10-24). THE PREMISE WAS FALSE AND THE REAL GAP WAS NARROWER -- then the gate's own first run showed the gap was WORSE than either reading. (1) THE PREMISE. This entry says "there is no cargo-audit step anywhere in CI". There is one: `04-nightly-audit.yml` has run `cargo audit` since that workflow was written, and `07-desktop-build.yml`'s header refers to it by name. This entry's own evidence explains the miss -- it records reading "every job in 05-security.yml and 01-pr-check.yml" and never opened 04-nightly-audit.yml. (2) THE SUBSTANCE STILL HELD, for two reasons the entry did not name. That workflow triggers on `schedule` (02:00 UTC) and `workflow_dispatch` ONLY -- no push, no pull_request -- so it cannot fail a pull request, which is the only moment a gate changes an outcome. And the step carries `continue-on-error: true`, so it cannot fail the nightly run either; its JSON goes to `reports/cargo_audit.json` and is uploaded as an artifact. Which made it precisely what this entry said Dependabot was: reporting, not gating. (3) THE GATE. A new `rust-dependency-audit` job in 05-security.yml, which runs on `pull_request`. No `continue-on-error` -- that is the entire difference from the nightly step. Uses `dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable` and the pinned actions/cache + upload-artifact SHAs 07-desktop-build.yml already uses, so it adds no supply-chain surface the repository has not already accepted; the cache is keyed on the cargo-audit BINARY rather than Cargo.lock, because what is expensive is compiling the scanner. The nightly step is left alone deliberately: it feeds scripts/generate_reports.py, and tolerating a scanner outage is the right shape for a report. This job is the gate; that one is the record. (4) WHAT IT FOUND, WHICH IS THE POINT. It landed with NO suppressions on purpose, because this entry required that whoever added it "confirm the step actually reports the four known advisories before adding the ignore list, so the list is proven to be doing something". Its first run read Cargo.lock against 1378 advisories over 517 crate dependencies and did NOT report the four Dependabot names (tauri 2.10.3, glib 0.18.5, serde_with 3.18.0, rand 0.8.5). It reported TWO 7.5 HIGH VULNERABILITIES that appear in neither Dependabot's four nor this entry's list: RUSTSEC-2026-0195 (quick-xml 0.38.4 -- unbounded namespace-declaration allocation in NsReader enabling a memory-exhaustion denial of service) and RUSTSEC-2026-0194 (quick-xml 0.38.4 -- quadratic run time when checking a start tag for duplicate attribute names), both with solution "upgrade to >=0.41.0". So this entry's severity assessment -- "3 MODERATE + 1 LOW with no critical among them" -- was understated by the only measurement that has ever been taken of this lockfile, and the gate's justification is now made by the gate itself rather than argued. (5) CALIBRATION, FROM THE MEASUREMENT RATHER THAN FROM TASTE. The two HIGH ids are now ignored with the reason and the named follow-up -- the ratchet-from-a-known-baseline shape this entry asked for, with ids proven from the step's own output rather than guessed. `--deny warnings` was in the first draft and the first run removed it: it also fails on `unmaintained`, and this lockfile carries about ten such crates, every one transitive and none of them ours (fxhash, proc-macro-error, five unic-* crates, zbus_names, zvariant and more), all arriving through Tauri's own dependency tree so that no change to this repository can clear them. Ten --ignore lines for crates we do not control is exactly the list that stops being read, which is the failure mode the pip-audit gate above describes in its own words. They are still captured by the report step, which runs `if: always()` so the advisory ids and dependency paths do not require re-running the job to read. Cargo.lock is deliberately untouched: resolving the advisories moves the lockfile and nothing available here could compile the result -- `cargo install cargo-audit --locked` itself failed locally with `error: linker 'link.exe' not found`, the same MSVC environment gap 07-desktop-build.yml's own header documents. Shipping an unverifiable lockfile bump to a desktop application to quiet an advisory is the trade this gate exists to make VISIBLE, not to make silently. The desktop app is a separately-built artifact and not part of the SaaS runtime, so none of these reaches production today.
verification_level: measured in CI by the gate itself -- its first run read Cargo.lock against 1378 advisories over 517 crate dependencies and reported two 7.5 HIGH vulnerabilities, which is what the ignore list is derived from; the calibrated run is green
remaining_action: CLEAR THE TWO HIGH ADVISORIES, which the gate now holds at a known baseline rather than leaves unreported. RUSTSEC-2026-0194 and RUSTSEC-2026-0195 are both quick-xml 0.38.4 (7.5 HIGH: quadratic run time on duplicate attribute names, and unbounded namespace-declaration allocation enabling a memory-exhaustion DoS), solution `upgrade to >=0.41.0`. quick-xml is TRANSITIVE to the Tauri tree and appears in no Cargo.toml in this repository, so the fix is `cargo update` in algo22-terminal/src-tauri followed by a three-OS build proof from 07-desktop-build.yml -- which is why it was not done in the same commit as the gate: nothing available to the author could compile the result (no MSVC linker; `cargo install cargo-audit` itself failed locally with `error: linker 'link.exe' not found`, the same environment gap 07-desktop-build.yml's header documents). Whoever does it should drop both --ignore lines in the same commit, so the suppression goes with the pin. Separately and lower: ~10 unmaintained transitive crates (fxhash RUSTSEC-2025-0057, proc-macro-error RUSTSEC-2024-0370, unic-char-property/-range/-common/-ucd-ident/-ucd-version RUSTSEC-2025-0081/-0075/-0080/-0100/-0098, zbus_names RUSTSEC-2026-0371, zvariant) all arrive through Tauri's own tree; they are captured in the uploaded report and deliberately do not block, since no change to this repository can clear them.

title: Browser roles held INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/TRUNCATE on ten platform-owned tables in production, including orders and execution_records
evidence: Found by generalising SEC-07's check past `profiles` once that turned out to be live. SEC-07 was ONE INSTANCE of a systemic misconfiguration. scripts/check_production_privileges.py, run against production, reported 64 violations across all ten platform-owned tables checked: `anon` and `authenticated` each held INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and TRUNCATE on profiles, fee_records, execution_records, orders, referral_wallets, referral_commissions, referral_payouts, billing_invoices, payment_methods and subscriptions. `orders` and `execution_records` are the order and execution ledgers; `anon` is the UNAUTHENTICATED role whose key ships in the public JS bundle by design. RLS limited which ROWS were visible for UPDATE/DELETE, but TRUNCATE is not subject to RLS at all, and INSERT was unconstrained for tables whose policies did not cover it. REMEDIATED in one transaction, verified before commit: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, REFERENCES and TRIGGER revoked from anon and authenticated on all ten; SELECT retained (RLS scopes it per caller); service_role and postgres untouched, with the transaction asserting service_role retains SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE on every table before committing. SAFE because the frontend writes exactly TWO tables through Supabase REST -- grepped every .js/.jsx under algo22-terminal/src for `.from('<table>')` and found only `waitlist` and `download_analytics`, neither a platform table. Every platform write goes through the FastAPI backend as service_role. A FIRST ATTEMPT ROLLED BACK ON ITS OWN SAFETY ASSERTION, which is worth recording: it asserted `anon` holds INSERT on `waitlist` and that is false, so the guard fired and production was left untouched. The assertion was rewritten as a measured before/after comparison rather than an assumed grant set. AFTER: the standing check reports 'no browser role holds a write privilege on any checked table', 0 violations across 10 tables, and the ECS service stayed healthy throughout (1/1 running, 0 pending).
verification_level: applied and independently re-verified against production; service health confirmed
remaining_action: None for the ten tables checked. NOT EXHAUSTIVE, and deliberately stated as such: the table list in scripts/check_production_privileges.py is the set judged platform-owned, not every table in the database. A full sweep of all ~94 tables for browser-role writes is the obvious follow-up and was not done -- it needs a per-table judgement about which are user-owned, which is a design decision rather than a mechanical one. Also unaddressed: RLS is enabled but NOT FORCED on profiles (relforcerowsecurity = false), so a table owner bypasses it; worth a separate decision. And the root cause is organisational, not technical -- nothing was checking production, which is what let SEC-07 sit misrecorded. Wire scripts/check_production_privileges.py into a schedule.

title: Production schema diverges from repository source and has no migration ledger, so DEPLOY-04's close-out claim cannot be true as written
evidence: Observed while remediating SEC-07 against the real production database. (1) `public.recorded_migrations` DOES NOT EXIST in production, so there is no in-database record of which migrations have been applied -- which makes DEPLOY-04's recorded claim that 'migrations 019 through 046 were closed out against production' unverifiable from the database itself, and inconsistent with migration 033 demonstrably not being applied (its privilege guard was absent; see SEC-07). (2) public.profiles in production has 25 columns and LACKS five that repository migrations reference: plan_limit_overrides, referred_by_user_id, role, is_admin, api_calls_limit. The first is named directly in the frontend's own pricing copy (components/landing/Pricing.jsx: 'recorded per agreement in profiles.plan_limit_overrides') and in backend entitlement logic, so an Enterprise override has nowhere to be stored in production. (3) public.download_analytics does not exist, yet src/lib/downloadAnalyticsApi.js inserts into it on every download -- that write has always failed. (4) public.waitlist exists but `anon` holds NO privileges on it and `authenticated` lacks INSERT, while src/lib/waitlistApi.js inserts as the public (anon) client -- so the public waitlist signup cannot work either. These are four independent symptoms of the same thing: the deployed database was never reconciled against repository source, and the provisioning tests that pass in CI run against a freshly provisioned schema rather than this one. *** RE-MEASURED AND RE-CHARACTERISED (Kiro, 2026-10-22). Two of the four symptoms above are WRONG and are retracted; the other two are worse than stated. *** RETRACTED -- symptom (4), the waitlist. The missing anon INSERT grant and policy are DELIBERATE, not drift. backend_app/migrations/018_copilot_and_waitlist_tables.sql -- which IS applied (production has public.waitlist with the corrected app_metadata-based admin policies and the trader_type/monthly_volume columns) -- omits the public INSERT policy under a header titled 'WHY THERE IS NO PUBLIC INSERT POLICY -- read this before adding one'. Its reason: the archived original granted `FOR INSERT TO anon, authenticated WITH CHECK (true)`, i.e. a world-writable production table, and the public signup form is UNMOUNTED, so that would be pure spam surface with no consumer. VERIFIED rather than taken on trust: algo22-terminal/src/components/waitlist/WaitlistForm.jsx is imported by NOTHING outside tests, and LandingPage.jsx's own header records its removal ('WaitlistForm.jsx and the /admin/waitlist route are untouched and remain available for a future campaign'). tests/test_schema_table_reference_drift.py fails the moment the form is re-mounted without the policy, so the two cannot drift apart. There is nothing to fix. RETRACTED -- symptom (3), download_analytics. The claim that src/lib/downloadAnalyticsApi.js 'inserts into it on every download' so 'that write has always failed' is wrong in its premise: `track()`, the only INSERT, is called from NOWHERE. components/download/DownloadPage.jsx carries an explicit comment that it deliberately does not import the module ('an artifact nobody can fetch has no download to count'), and the sole importer -- components/admin/AdminDashboard.jsx -- calls only `getStats()`, which is a SELECT. So the live break is the opposite of the one recorded: the ADMIN download-stats panel reads a relation that does not exist, and nothing has ever written to it. The table also has NO DECLARATION anywhere in the repository (no CREATE TABLE in any .sql), so it is not schema drift at all -- it is a vestigial feature referencing a table that was never designed. That needs a build-or-remove decision, not a reconciliation. I had repeated symptom (3) myself in SEC-21's work, pre-authorising `download_analytics: {INSERT}` for the anon role in scripts/check_production_privileges.py on the strength of this finding's description without checking it. Corrected in the same change as this note -- the allowlist is now empty, which is the right state, because an entry there would have pre-approved a grant nothing needs. WORSE THAN STATED -- symptom (2). It is not five missing columns on profiles. TWO WHOLE MIGRATIONS NEVER RAN, and only two of the five named columns are actually wanted. Measured against production: backend_app/migrations/017_plan_entitlements.sql is entirely absent -- profiles.billing_interval ABSENT, profiles.plan_limit_overrides ABSENT, table public.plan_usage_ledger ABSENT, constraint chk_profiles_plan_limit_overrides_object ABSENT. migrations/referral_system_redesign.sql is entirely absent too -- profiles.referral_code ABSENT, profiles.referred_by_user_id ABSENT, constraint fk_profiles_referred_by ABSENT. Seven declared objects, none of them present. AND THE ORDERING IS PROVABLY BROKEN, which is the real point: production DOES have profiles.payment_provider and profiles.next_billing_date, which core/subscription_dependencies.py records as arriving with migration 037. So 037 was applied and 017 was not. Migrations have been applied out of order and out of band, which is precisely what a ledger would have caught. OF THE FIVE COLUMNS NAMED, ONLY TWO ARE WANTED, and the finding should not have asked for the other three. `plan_limit_overrides` is real and needed: it is the contracted capacity of the custom Enterprise tier, read by SubscriptionEngine.get_effective_quotas, and its absence is silent because subscription_dependencies.py carries a column-set fallback ladder (_PROFILE_COLUMN_SETS) that retries with fewer columns when PostgREST rejects an unknown one -- so an Enterprise override simply never applies and nothing errors. `referred_by_user_id` is real and needed: routers/auth.py:233 writes it with a service-role client on referral signup, so that write currently fails (the relationship is still recorded in referral_relationships, so the column is a denormalised copy). `is_admin` and `api_calls_limit` have ZERO references anywhere in backend_app -- adding them would be adding columns nothing reads. `role` is not needed either: admin authority comes from the JWT (`app_metadata.role`, which is what routers/admin.py, the waitlist policies and the frontend's AdminGuard all read), and routers/user.py's get_profile already treats a profiles-side role as optional with the token as the source of truth. For those three the DATABASE is right and the migration is aspirational. SHARPENED -- symptom (1). `public.recorded_migrations` does not exist, but neither does any declaration of it: grepping every .sql in the repository for `recorded_migrations` returns NOTHING. So this is not drift between source and production -- the ledger DEPLOY-04 claimed to have written to was never designed. What does exist: `public.alembic_version` holds exactly one row (d97ffff9c3bb, the execution schema rebuild) and `supabase_migrations.schema_migrations` holds exactly ONE row (20261017160919), against 50+ migration files in the repository. Building a migration ledger is a design decision, not a reconciliation, and improvising a schema-tracking mechanism at the end of a session is how the next DEPLOY-04-style claim gets made. *** THE TWO NEVER-APPLIED MIGRATIONS ARE NOW APPLIED AND VERIFIED IN PRODUCTION (Kiro, 2026-10-23). *** 017_plan_entitlements.sql applied in full: profiles.billing_interval (text), profiles.plan_limit_overrides (jsonb), public.plan_usage_ledger (with its 2 indexes, RLS enabled and the pul_owner_select policy), chk_profiles_billing_interval and chk_profiles_plan_limit_overrides_object. So Enterprise/custom-tier contractual overrides finally have somewhere to be stored instead of silently never applying -- the degradation was invisible because core/subscription_dependencies.py's _PROFILE_COLUMN_SETS ladder retries the read with fewer columns when PostgREST rejects an unknown one. HOW IT WAS APPLIED, because applying a migration blind is what this finding is about. A new tool, scripts/apply_migration_to_production.py, strips only the file's own bare BEGIN;/COMMIT; so IT owns the transaction boundary, which buys a --trial mode that executes the ENTIRE migration including its own postcondition blocks and then ROLLS BACK. Both migrations were trialled first and only applied after the trial reached 'postconditions passed' and rolled back cleanly. That mattered concretely for 017: plan_usage_ledger.user_id is REFERENCES auth.users(id), and auth.users is Supabase-managed, so creating that foreign key needed REFERENCES on a table this `postgres` role might not hold it on -- a failure that would have landed part-way through DDL, which is precisely why applying migration 033 blind was declined earlier. The trial proved the grant exists before anything was committed. The tool also enforces an invariant the migration files cannot enforce themselves: it diffs the ENTIRE browser-role write surface across public before and after, and refuses to commit if it grew. SEC-20/SEC-21 closed that surface; a migration can still GRANT explicitly, so every apply re-checks it. Reported unchanged at 143 grants for both. 051_deploy05_profiles_referral_columns.sql added, trialled and applied: profiles.referral_code (varchar(20)), profiles.referred_by_user_id (uuid), fk_profiles_referred_by (REFERENCES profiles(id) ON DELETE SET NULL) and uq_profiles_referral_code. routers/auth.py:233 writes referred_by_user_id with a service-role client on referral signup and that write was failing. WHY A NEW FILE RATHER THAN RUNNING THE ONE THAT DECLARES THEM: migrations/referral_system_redesign.sql declares both columns, but it is a REDESIGN -- it also drops and recreates functions that 006_reconcile_production_database.sql declares with DIFFERENT SIGNATURES (create_referral_code_for_user RETURNS VARCHAR vs RETURNS VOID; process_referral_commission with different parameters -- its own header documents the collision). Running it whole would have replaced live function definitions as a side effect of adding two columns. The two column declarations and their constraints were reproduced verbatim and nothing else from that file was applied. DELIBERATELY NOT ADDED, as recorded earlier: profiles.role, profiles.is_admin and profiles.api_calls_limit. The latter two have zero references anywhere in backend_app, and admin authority comes from the JWT's app_metadata.role. For those three the database is right and the migration is aspirational; 051's header records that so the question is not reopened. VERIFIED AFTER COMMIT, on a fresh connection: scripts/check_production_schema_drift.py reports 'OK: every declared object in the inventory is present in production' (was 7 of 7 absent across both migrations); scripts/check_production_privileges.py still reports all blocking invariants holding, now across 82 tables rather than 81; ECS vyomquant-api-service 1/1 running, rollout COMPLETED. AN INCIDENTAL CONFIRMATION OF SEC-20: public.plan_usage_ledger is a table created TODAY, and `anon`/`authenticated` received SELECT only on it automatically. Before SEC-20 revoked the default ACL, Supabase's stock default would have granted both roles every privilege on it the moment it was created -- so the root-cause fix demonstrably held on the first new table to test it. ||| CLOSED (Kiro). BOTH REMAINING ITEMS WERE DECISIONS, AND BOTH ARE TAKEN. ITEM (1), THE LEDGER. This entry asked: 'Decide whether to adopt the Supabase table, adopt Alembic properly, or build something -- and then backfill from EVIDENCE by probing'. NOT ALEMBIC, and the reason is the design rather than a preference. `alembic_version` holds ONE revision pointer, and that shape carries a specific claim: the applied set is a PREFIX of the revision sequence. Production disproves it -- this entry's own item (3) records 037 applied while 017 was not. A single pointer is structurally incapable of expressing a non-prefix reality, so adopting it would mean recording something false or abandoning the only semantics that give the pointer meaning. Left pointing at d97ffff9c3bb, untouched. NOT supabase_migrations.schema_migrations: it is the Supabase CLI's own bookkeeping and holds 1 row against 50+ files precisely because the CLI is not what applies these. Writing rows the CLI did not write would make a later `db push` reason from entries it has no basis for, and would couple this platform's deploy record to another tool's internal schema. Untouched. SO: migration 055 creates public.recorded_migrations, ONE ROW PER MIGRATION, the only shape that can say '037 yes, 017 no'. The name is not invented -- DEPLOY-04 already claimed to write to it, which is how its close-out claim came to be unverifiable. THREE PROPERTIES ANSWER THIS ENTRY'S OWN WARNING ('a half-working SQL parser that silently missed a declaration would restore exactly the false confidence this replaces'), and two are enforced by the schema rather than by whoever writes: (a) a row records EVIDENCE, not intent -- `verification` (closed vocabulary: EVIDENCE_PROBED | APPLIED_BY_TOOL) and `evidence` are both NOT NULL with a non-blank CHECK, so 'we ran it' and 'we confirmed it' can never be recorded as the same claim; (b) ABSENCE OF A ROW MEANS NOBODY CHECKED, never 'not applied' -- the inventory does not cover all 50+ files, and that reading is what keeps the next 'migrations N through M are closed out' claim falsifiable; (c) there is NO applied_at column, because that is unknown for a file applied out of band and a column for it would be filled with a guess. RLS enabled with NO policy plus REVOKE from anon/authenticated: deploy bookkeeping no tenant owns and nothing in the request path reads. scripts/record_migration_evidence.py backfills by PROBING the hand-maintained inventory in check_production_schema_drift.py::DECLARED_OBJECTS -- deliberately not a SQL parser, for this entry's own stated reason. It is tested for what it REFUSES: it never enumerates the migrations directory (no glob/iterdir/listdir/rglob), because 'the files up to N exist, therefore N is applied' is the inference that broke DEPLOY-04; it never records a partially-applied migration, which is the most dangerous state to mark applied; it writes EVIDENCE_PROBED only, since it looked rather than applied; and --apply requires --recorded-by, because a row with blank provenance is the record this exists to stop. APPLIED AND VERIFIED AGAINST PRODUCTION: 055 applied (6 NOT NULL columns, 4 constraints -- pk + the verification vocabulary + non-blank evidence + non-negative count -- RLS enabled, 0 policies). Then backfilled: 3 rows, all EVIDENCE_PROBED -- 017_plan_entitlements.sql (4 objects), referral_system_redesign.sql (3), and 055_deploy05_migration_ledger.sql itself (3), because the thing that records evidence is subject to the same check. check_production_schema_drift.py now reports 'public.recorded_migrations present' and 10/10 declared objects present, where before it reported 'ABSENT (and declared nowhere in the repository)' against 7. ITEM (2), download_analytics: REMOVED. The build-or-remove decision, taken as remove on the evidence already recorded here -- no declaration in any .sql, no writer (downloadAnalyticsApi.track() called from nowhere; DownloadPage deliberately did not import it), the admin dashboard's getStats() read the only live caller. The fact that DECIDED it, found while reading the code: getStats ends `if (error) throw new Error(error.message)` and the dashboard puts that into setError -- so the Downloads tab did not render an empty panel, it rendered a raw missing-relation error to an admin, and had done for every person who ever opened it. Building instead would have meant a table, an RLS policy, a writer on the public download page, and a retention position for behaviour-tracking data on EU/UK visitors that LEGAL-01's ROPA would need a new purpose entry for -- a product decision with privacy consequences that nobody asked for. Deleted algo22-terminal/src/lib/downloadAnalyticsApi.js; removed the tab, its two state hooks, its fetcher and its panel (AdminDashboard 301 -> 241 lines); dropped the two lucide imports it was the only user of; corrected two stale comments naming the deleted module. Frontend builds clean (vite, 36.8s) and eslint reports 0 errors. The drift inventory now records the resolution so a reader who finds the name in git history does not re-open it. ITEM (3), the general lesson, is now ENFORCEABLE rather than only stated: a future 'migrations N through M were closed out' claim is checkable against recorded_migrations, and a migration with no row reads as unverified rather than as applied. 20 new tests (tests/test_deploy05_migration_ledger.py).
verification_level: PRODUCTION-VERIFIED for the ledger: migration 055 was applied to the production database and its shape read back (columns, constraints, RLS state, policy count), then 3 evidence-probed rows were written and the drift checker re-run against production, which now reports the table present and 10/10 declared objects present. The frontend removal is build-verified but NOT production-verified: the running bundle predates it, so the broken Downloads tab is still live until the frontend is redeployed. NOT claimed: that the ledger covers all 50+ migration files. It covers the three whose declared objects are in the hand-maintained inventory, and the absence of a row is defined to mean unverified.
remaining_action: NONE blocking. Two standing, additive follow-ups, both of which the design anticipates: (1) extend check_production_schema_drift.py::DECLARED_OBJECTS as migrations are confirmed and re-run record_migration_evidence.py -- that is how coverage grows from 3 files toward 50+, and it is deliberately incremental because the inventory is hand-maintained; (2) have the deploy pipeline write APPLIED_BY_TOOL rows when it runs a file, which is the stronger provenance the vocabulary already reserves and which no backfill can produce. Also: redeploy the frontend so the removed Downloads tab stops showing an admin a database error.

title: Supabase default privileges granted ALL on every newly created public table to anon and authenticated -- the generator of SEC-07 and SEC-19
fix_commit: applied directly to production 2026-10-22; recorded in ce3df4b
evidence: Found by asking why SEC-07 and SEC-19 looked like the same defect 11 times. pg_default_acl carried, for schema public, from TWO grantors: grantor=postgres TABLES anon=arwdDxtm authenticated=arwdDxtm, and grantor=supabase_admin TABLES anon=arwdDxtm authenticated=arwdDxtm. `arwdDxtm` is every privilege (a=INSERT w=UPDATE d=DELETE D=TRUNCATE r=SELECT x=REFERENCES t=TRIGGER m=MAINTAIN). That is Supabase's stock default for the public schema, and it means every table created in public is automatically granted full write to both browser roles. So SEC-07 (profiles) and SEC-19 (ten platform tables) were not 11 separate mistakes -- they were 11 instances of one rule, and the next migration that created a table would have silently reopened the hole, undoing both fixes. This is the root cause; the earlier per-table REVOKEs treated symptoms. REMEDIATED: ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE postgres IN SCHEMA public REVOKE INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, REFERENCES, TRIGGER ON TABLES FROM anon, authenticated -- applied inside the same verified transaction as SEC-21. Confirmed afterwards: the default ACL now reads anon=rm, authenticated=rm (SELECT + MAINTAIN only), service_role and postgres unchanged at arwdDxtm. Migrations run as postgres, so application tables are covered.
verification_level: production (pg_default_acl re-queried on a fresh connection after commit, not inferred from absence of error)
remaining_action: PARTIAL BY NECESSITY, and deliberately left visible rather than closed: the grantor=supabase_admin default ACL is NOT fixed and cannot be fixed from this role. Verified by dry-run inside a rolled-back transaction: ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE supabase_admin is refused with 'permission denied to change default privileges' because current_user postgres is not a member of supabase_admin (which is a superuser; postgres here is rolcreaterole + rolbypassrls but NOT rolsuper). Its scope is objects created BY supabase_admin in public -- extensions and Supabase-managed objects, not application tables from migrations -- so the practical exposure is small, but it is real. Needs the Supabase dashboard or Supabase support. scripts/check_production_privileges.py reports it under 'NOT FIXABLE FROM THIS ROLE' on every run so it cannot be forgotten, and deliberately does not fail on it: a permanently red check is a check nobody reads, which is how SEC-07 came to sit at VERIFIED_FIXED while live.

title: The unauthenticated `anon` role held writes on 60 public tables, and could TRUNCATE user exchange credentials despite RLS being enabled
fix_commit: applied directly to production 2026-10-22; recorded in ce3df4b
evidence: Found by sweeping all 82 tables in public instead of SEC-19's curated list of ten. 60 of 82 carried browser-role write grants. RLS was enabled on all 60, which is why this was not a second SEC-19: for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE the policies did constrain the caller, and that was verified rather than assumed -- acting as a real user with 27 own strategies, UPDATE and DELETE against OTHER users' rows in public.strategies both affected 0 rows, SELECT returned 27 of 187, and anon SELECT returned 0 of 187 and 0 of 2 exchange_keys. Tenant isolation holds. (An earlier probe of mine reported those cross-tenant writes as 'PERMITTED' and was WRONG: it treated 'no exception raised' as success, but RLS filters rows rather than raising, so an UPDATE matching nothing succeeds affecting zero rows. Re-run with rowcount, the finding retracted itself.) THE REAL DEFECT IS TRUNCATE. PostgreSQL has no TRUNCATE row-security policy command, so RLS cannot filter it -- a role holding TRUNCATE empties the whole table regardless of policy. Measured in production inside rolled-back transactions, counting as `postgres` (rolbypassrls) on both sides of an `anon` TRUNCATE so the counts were not themselves RLS-filtered: anon emptied public.exchange_keys (2 rows of USER EXCHANGE API CREDENTIALS), public.alembic_version (1), public.risk_settings (1), public.referral_profiles (2), public.notification_settings (1) and public.ticket_comments (2). public.strategies (187 rows) was spared only by an incidental foreign-key constraint, not by any security control. `anon` is the UNAUTHENTICATED role whose key ships in the public JS bundle by design. EXPLOITABILITY, STATED HONESTLY: not reachable through the public API today. PostgREST exposes no TRUNCATE verb, and 0 of the 33 anon-executable functions in public contain a TRUNCATE (checked via pg_get_functiondef). So this was a latent hole, not an exploited one -- recorded P1 rather than P0 for that reason. It was fixed anyway because 'no route happens to exist' is not a control. REMEDIATED in one transaction that committed only after 14 postflight assertions passed: INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE revoked from `anon` on all 82 tables; TRUNCATE, REFERENCES and TRIGGER revoked from BOTH browser roles on all 82. SELECT retained (RLS scopes it per caller; removing it breaks the UI). service_role untouched -- asserted by diffing its full 82-entry grant matrix before and after. Zero functional risk established first: no application code issues TRUNCATE (grep of backend_app finds only the word in a comment about float indexes), and REFERENCES/TRIGGER are schema-modification rights no API client needs. Also dropped public.__probe_xyz, a 1-column/0-row/0-byte probe artefact with no inbound foreign keys left in production, DDL captured first.
verification_level: production (exploit reproduced against the real database in a rolled-back transaction, then re-attempted after the fix and refused; all grants re-queried on a fresh connection; ECS health confirmed after)
remaining_action: None for anon or for TRUNCATE/REFERENCES/TRIGGER -- those invariants are now enforced by scripts/check_production_privileges.py, which exits non-zero on drift. The remaining `authenticated` write surface is tracked separately as SEC-22.

title: `authenticated` retains write grants on ~51 backend-owned tables beyond any known application need (least-privilege backlog)
evidence: After SEC-21, `authenticated` still holds 106 write grants across 51 tables that no identified code path writes -- transaction_records/checkpoints/rollbacks, the paper_* family, library_*/marketplace_*, referral_profiles, strategy_limits, positions, fills, security_logs, risk_settings_audit, idempotency_keys, alembic_version, dag_tasks and others. NOT A BLOCKING FINDING, and not an open door: every one of these tables has RLS enabled with per-user policies, and after SEC-21 `anon` holds no write at all, so reaching any of them requires a valid signed-in JWT and confines the caller to their own rows. It is a defence-in-depth gap. DELIBERATELY NOT SWEPT, and this is the substance of the finding: the backend reaches PostgREST through two clients that map to two different database roles -- the anon key plus the end user's JWT (role `authenticated`) and the service-role key (role `service_role`) -- and revoking `authenticated` writes on a table the first kind writes takes a production feature OFFLINE. Deriving that inventory from source proved unreliable three times running, because the routers wrap the two client factories in local helpers (_sb, _get_supabase, _client) so the call sites do not grep as factory names. Two full passes over the backend produced a list missing `strategies` DELETE (backend/strategy_service.py:2502 -- strategy deletion, reached from the UI), `strategy_backtests` (backend/backtest_service.py:776), `training_jobs` and `training_governance_decisions` (backend/training_status.py:573) and `model_versions` (backend/model_versioning.py:1963). Each omission, had it driven a REVOKE, would have broken a working feature. A blanket sweep would additionally have taken out strategy create/rename/edit/clone/archive/pause/resume/stop, all strategy version persistence, risk-settings saves, notifications, support tickets, profile editing and exchange-key deletion.
verification_level: observed directly against production (read-only) and cross-checked against backend source; not fixed, by decision
remaining_action: Drain it one table at a time, each revoke paired with that feature's integration test, then enable the ratchet: `python scripts/check_production_privileges.py --strict` already fails on this backlog and is the gate to turn on once it is empty. The 16-table path-(A) allowlist in that script, with the writing call site recorded against each entry, is the working document. Do not sweep.

title: User-supplied max_daily_loss and max_positions are enforced with no server-side ceiling, so a user can disable their own circuit breakers
evidence: Found while assessing whether `authenticated` UPDATE on public.risk_settings was a privilege-escalation path. It is NOT a privilege finding -- the same values are settable through the legitimate UI (PUT /api/risk/settings -> routers/risk.py:227 upsert), so writing them directly via PostgREST gains a user nothing they cannot already do. The actual defect is the missing clamp. core/risk_manager.py:111 _load_user_risk_settings reads the row with the SERVICE-ROLE key, explicitly bypassing RLS (its own docstring says so), and validate_trade_request at :556 assigns the values straight into the order-time circuit breakers: effective_max_daily_loss and effective_max_positions are used as-is, with no min(), no tier cross-check and no ceiling, overriding the hardcoded RiskThresholds defaults (max_daily_loss_pct=0.05, max_open_trades=5) that then gate the order via REJECT_DAILY_LOSS and REJECT_MAX_OPEN_TRADES. A user who sets max_daily_loss to 1e12 and max_positions to 99999 makes both breakers unreachable. The asymmetry is what makes this a defect rather than a design choice: max_leverage in the same struct IS clamped, at risk_manager.py:~646, via min(self.thresholds.drawdown_tier_1_max_leverage, effective_max_leverage), so writing max_leverage=1000 yields at most 10.0. The clamping is incomplete, not absent. The same values also feed the paper engine (backend/paper_trading_service.py:1344-1390) through the in-memory store that routers/risk.py:165 populates from this table. Separately noted: risk_settings.max_position_size_usd and daily_loss_limit_pct are read by NO backend code at all -- a grep across backend_app returns zero hits for either -- so two of the limits the UI presents are not enforced anywhere. ||| CLOSED (Kiro, 2026-10-24). THE CLAMP: `min(platform_threshold, requested)` on all three limits in validate_trade_request, applied where the effective value is DERIVED rather than at each use site -- one place to read, one to get wrong, and a future check that reads effective_max_positions inherits the clamp instead of having to remember it. max_daily_loss is stored in account currency and compared as a fraction of capital, so it is converted before being clamped; a non-positive total_capital leaves the platform threshold standing alone, the pre-existing behaviour, unchanged. WHICH CEILING -- NOT THE PLAN TIER, AND THE REASON WAS MEASURED, NOT REASONED. This entry's own remaining_action proposed clamping against the account's plan tier. TenantQuota.for_plan does carry one (FREE 5 positions / 1.0x leverage, BASIC 20 / 1.0x, PROFESSIONAL 100 / 3.0x, ENTERPRISE 500 / 10.0x) and it is the WRONG ceiling: it is a fair-use resource table, not a risk policy, and its only enforcer (core/hard_quota_enforcer) is deprecated, raises a DeprecationWarning on construction and is carried by no route -- those figures have never been in force. The only in-production consequence is that one row's 10 concurrent positions is held to 5; its 3x leverage and $250 daily loss are already inside the ceilings and are unchanged. THE API BOUNDARY CLAMPS RATHER THAN REFUSES. The remaining_action asked for 'reject or clamp' at the boundary. The first draft REJECTED with a 400 and three existing tests caught that this rejects the endpoint's OWN DEFAULT of 10 positions -- it would have broken the settings page for every free user, i.e. everyone. Applied to the assembled `updated_record` and not to `body`: that record is the single thing that reaches the in-memory store, the risk_settings upsert, the WebSocket broadcast, the notification and the response, so clamping it where it is built is what makes all six agree -- clamping `body` would have left the current_settings fall-through unclamped, so a value already stored above the ceiling would survive a save that did not mention it. The response now carries `limit_adjustments` (empty on every ordinary save) and `platform_ceilings`, so a clamp is never silent, and POST /api/risk/validate reports the ceilings too -- additive, and the point of asking: a value can be `valid` against the API's declared 1..100 range and still be clamped on save, which a caller that cannot see the ceiling has no way to show. Both read the figures from RiskThresholds rather than restating them, so the boundary and the order path cannot drift apart. max_daily_loss is deliberately NOT clamped at the boundary: it is a currency amount enforced as a fraction of capital, and capital is not known there -- clamping it would compare dollars to a percentage. THE PAGE SAYS SO. RiskSettings.saveRiskConfig already adopted the server's returned values, so the control already snapped to the clamped number -- which is the half that reads as a bug: a slider jumping from 100 back to 5 under 'Risk parameters updated successfully.' It now reports the server's own sentence at `warning`, one of ds/Alert's five severities (not a new one) and the polite role='status' one, because the save SUCCEEDED. One case drives the real PUT end to end. Plus algo22-terminal/tests/unit/pages/riskSettingsClampedLimitNotice.test.jsx, 4 cases. Both are the same question -- a UI presenting a limit nothing enforces -- and both are a product decision (lower the default, or enforce the fields, or remove them from the page) rather than an engineering one, so neither is decided here. title: CVE-2026-114603 in opentelemetry-api failed the blocking pip-audit gate; the eleven opentelemetry packages were unused and are removed
evidence: Surfaced on a real CI run (39845453588, job 120057408416): pip-audit reported 'Found 1 known vulnerability' -- opentelemetry-api 1.25.0, CVE-2026-114603, fix 1.45.1. NOT caused by the change under test; main's own 05 Security run on 0bb637e2 passed this job about two hours earlier. pip-audit queries live advisory data, so an unchanged manifest flips from pass to fail when an advisory is published -- main was latently red too. Advisory detail from OSV: GHSA-xcq7-p3pf-p88h, 'OpenTelemetry Python: Unbounded tracestate parsing in opentelemetry-api', CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L -- availability only, no confidentiality or integrity impact. All versions below 1.45.1 affected. NOT REACHABLE IN THIS APPLICATION, established before deciding what to do. Only two files under backend_app import opentelemetry at all (backend/observability/opentelemetry_tracing.py and optimized_tracing.py), and an AST walk of every .py in backend_app found ZERO unguarded imports -- both sit inside try/except ImportError setting OPENTELEMETRY_AVAILABLE=False. Neither module's TracingManager is ever constructed: grepping main.py, core/, routers/ and api_ws/ for TracingManager / initialize_tracing / optimized_tracing / get_tracing_manager returns nothing, so FastAPIInstrumentor().instrument() is never called and no global text-map propagator is installed. With no instrumentation and no propagator, nothing parses an inbound tracestate header, which is the vulnerable path. REMOVED RATHER THAN UPGRADED, because upgrading is not possible here: opentelemetry-proto 1.45.1 requires protobuf>=5.0,<8.0 while tensorflow==2.16.1 requires protobuf!=4.21.0-4.21.5,<5.0.0dev,>=3.20.3 -- a direct conflict, and escaping it by upgrading tensorflow was already attempted and reverted under DEP-02. The old pin had the mirror-image problem: opentelemetry-proto 1.25.0's protobuf<5.0 ceiling is DEP-02's recorded blocker, so removing it clears that constraint instead of entrenching it. SAFETY VERIFIED BY EXECUTION, not by reading the guard: a sys.meta_path finder was installed to make every `opentelemetry*` import raise ModuleNotFoundError, reproducing the uninstalled state. Both modules then imported successfully with OPENTELEMETRY_AVAILABLE=False, TracingManager constructed without raising, get_tracer() returned a NoOpTracer, and NoOpTracer.start_as_current_span worked as a context manager whose span accepts set_attribute/is_recording. TRANSITIVE CHECK: every name==version pin across requirements-base.txt, requirements.txt and requirements-cpu.txt was resolved against PyPI metadata; no remaining package ACTIVELY requires opentelemetry, so removing the explicit pins removes the packages outright rather than leaving them to be resolved transitively at an unpinned version. sentry-sdk==2.11.0 does declare 48 opentelemetry requirements, but every one is gated behind extra == 'opentelemetry' or 'opentelemetry-experimental', and the manifest pins sentry-sdk[fastapi] -- so they are inert. (A first version of that check ignored extras markers and reported sentry-sdk as a blocker; it was wrong and was corrected to evaluate the markers.) VERIFIED ON A REAL CI RUN: PR #64 went green on all 14 checks, including the job that raised this -- 'Blocking Dependency Vulnerability Audit (pip-audit + npm audit)' SUCCESS -- plus Database Tests (PostgreSQL), Unit & Integration Tests, Execution Tests (production posture), Docker Build Validation and Provisioning, Privilege Hardening & Tenant Isolation, so the removal broke no test lane. Merged to main as 97dae06. One follow-up surfaced during that run and is part of this fix: the repository's OWN guard, scripts/dependency_audit.py, then failed with 'imported but not declared: opentelemetry' -- correctly, since the pins were gone while the two guarded import sites remained. Resolved using the mechanism that script already carries for this case, OPTIONAL_DEPENDENCIES (filtered at line 227, already holding torch for the same class of reason), with a comment requiring the entry be removed at the same time as any future re-add so the audit goes back to demanding the pins.
verification_level: root-caused against a real GitHub Actions job log; non-reachability established by AST analysis plus a grep of every wiring site; removability proven by executing the degraded path with the package blocked at import; transitive impact checked against PyPI metadata for all 54 pins; cleared on a real CI run (PR #64, 14/14 green) and merged
remaining_action: None for the CVE. Two notes for later: (1) if tracing is ever wanted, re-add opentelemetry-api/sdk at >=1.45.1 AND the instrumentation packages at >=0.66b1 (the two version tracks move in lockstep) TOGETHER with a tensorflow release whose protobuf floor is >=5.0 -- they cannot move independently -- remove the OPTIONAL_DEPENDENCIES entry from scripts/dependency_audit.py, and actually wire TracingManager into main.py's lifespan, which has never been done. (2) DEP-02 should be revisited: opentelemetry-proto's protobuf<5.0 ceiling was its recorded blocker and that package is now gone, so the protobuf/tensorflow upgrade it reverted may now be reachable.

title: The observability readiness check resolved PyPI distribution names through __import__, so three of its four dependency checks could never pass
evidence: Found while removing the opentelemetry pins for DEP-04. backend/observability/validation_checklist.py::_check_dependencies_installed held dependencies = ['prometheus-client', 'opentelemetry-api', 'opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-grpc', 'psutil'] and resolved each with __import__(dep). Those are DISTRIBUTION names, and a hyphen is not legal in a Python module name, so the call raises ModuleNotFoundError even when the package is installed and working. Measured in an environment where all four were installed: prometheus-client, opentelemetry-api and opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-grpc each reported ImportError; only psutil succeeded, and only because its distribution name and module name are identical. So the check reported success=False with three missing dependencies on every run, in every environment, since it was written -- it could not distinguish a broken deployment from a healthy one, which is the whole purpose of a readiness check. FIXED by querying importlib.metadata.version(), which is keyed by distribution name, instead of the import system, which is keyed by module name; the result now also reports the resolved versions. The two opentelemetry entries were dropped from the required list because DEP-04 removes those packages deliberately -- requiring them here would assert the opposite of the manifest.
verification_level: code+test (the failure reproduced directly against an environment where all four packages were installed, and the fix confirmed to resolve prometheus-client 0.20.0 and psutil 6.0.0)

title: redis_manager.hset passed its arguments to redis-py wrongly, so every hash write through it failed silently -- including every worker health heartbeat
evidence: Surfaced the instant INF-03's workers were first deployed. All four services logged, every 10 seconds: `HSET failed for 'worker:health:<worker>': HashCommands.hset() got multiple values for argument 'name'`. THE BUG, in backend_app/core/cache/redis_manager.py's SharedRedisManager.hset: the wrapper's signature is `hset(self, key, name=None, value=None, mapping=None)` and it called `await client.hset(key, name=name, value=value, mapping=mapping)`. redis-py's signature, confirmed by introspection rather than memory, is `hset(self, name, key=None, value=None, mapping=None, items=None)` -- ITS `name` IS THE REDIS KEY AND ITS `key` IS THE HASH FIELD, the exact opposite of this wrapper's parameter names. So `key` bound positionally to redis-py's `name` and `name=name` bound to the same parameter again, raising TypeError before any command was issued. The wrapper's own `except Exception` then logged it at WARNING and returned 0, so every caller saw a successful-looking no-op. WHAT WAS SILENTLY NEVER WRITTEN, by caller: backend_app/core/worker_base.py's heartbeat (`worker:health:*`) -- so WorkerBase's "publish status=unhealthy after three consecutive failures" mechanism, which Requirement 26.5 relies on and which marketplace_expiry_worker's own docstring names as one of its two independent failure signals, has never written a byte, and any liveness probe reading those keys reads an empty hash; backend_app/core/dag_task_queue.py's task data, status and result hashes; distributed_execution's worker_registry, lease_manager and heartbeat_manager state; and strategies.py's walk-forward job status. WHY IT WENT UNNOTICED FOR SO LONG: the loudest caller is the worker heartbeat, and until INF-03 no worker process had ever run in production. The other heavy callers sit in distributed_execution, which RT-11 unmounted. So the failure had almost no live caller to be noticed by, and the one it did have logged at WARNING rather than raising. A SECOND, SEPARATE BUG FOUND IN THE SAME SWEEP, and it is why the one-line fix was not safe on its own: three call sites in backend_app/routers/strategies.py passed a DICT as the second positional argument -- `hset(_status_key(job_id), {...})` -- which binds to the wrapper's `name`, the hash FIELD. While hset was broken those were harmless no-ops. With the call fixed and nothing else changed, they would have issued `HSET <key> "{'status': 'running', ...}" None`: a stringified dict as a field name, which is WORSE than the failure it replaced because it writes and succeeds. Fixed at source (mapping=), and the wrapper now also detects a mapping arriving in the field position, uses it as the mapping, and logs that it did so rather than silently reinterpreting it. ||| VERIFIED IN PRODUCTION 2026-10-26, and verified by the PRESENCE OF THE KEY rather than by the absence of the warning -- which matters, because this wrapper swallowed its own error, so a missing warning could equally have meant the call was no longer being made. scripts/verify_worker_health_keys.py scanned Redis from inside the VPC and found FOUR worker:health:* keys where there had never been any: worker:health:bt-9d7872e5, worker:health:command_worker-ip-10-0-154-216.ap-southeast-1.compute.internal-7, worker:health:dag-1 and worker:health:marketplace_expiry_worker. Each carries the fields WorkerBase writes -- status='healthy', consecutive_failures='0', last_heartbeat as an ISO instant, running='True' -- under a live TTL. So Requirement 26.5's 'publish status=unhealthy after three consecutive failures' now has somewhere to appear, and a liveness probe reading those keys sees real state instead of an empty hash.
verification_level: The diagnosis is confirmed three ways: the production log line itself; introspection of redis.asyncio.Redis.hset's real parameter order ('name','key','value','mapping','items'); and a reproduction that calls a signature-identical double the old way and raises the identical TypeError, then the new way and asserts the arguments land as redis key / field / value. The corrected positional call was also checked against the in-memory MockRedisClient, whose own parameter order is (key, name, value, mapping), so both backends accept it. Regression run: 225 passed / 23 skipped for the redis, worker_base, heartbeat and health selection, and 1503 passed for the strategies selection (the single error, test_route_contract.py::TestTheFourInstancesWave4Owns, is a known pre-existing failure on main and unrelated). NOT PRODUCTION-VERIFIED, which is why this is FIXED_UNVERIFIED and not VERIFIED_FIXED: the fix is in source only. The four running worker services use image d306bc7b..., which still contains the broken call, so they continue to log the warning every 10 seconds and worker:health:* remains empty until a new image is built and rolled out. ||| NOW PRODUCTION-VERIFIED: four worker:health:* keys exist with the fields WorkerBase writes and live TTLs, read from Redis inside the VPC. Deliberately evidenced by the key's presence and contents rather than by the warning's disappearance, since the wrapper's own except clause made absence of a warning ambiguous.
remaining_action: NOTHING FOR THE BUG ITSELF. One judgement call is left on the file and is worth making deliberately rather than by default: this wrapper's `except Exception: logger.warning(...); return 0` is what turned a TypeError -- a programming error that could never succeed -- into an invisible no-op for every caller for the life of the deployment. Fail-soft is right for a Redis outage and wrong for a signature mismatch. The same pattern sits on hget, hgetall and the neighbouring proxies, so it is a decision about the file rather than one method. A REGRESSION GUARD IS STILL ABSENT: no test calls this wrapper against a redis-py-shaped double, which is exactly the gap that let an argument-order bug live in shared infrastructure. A test asserting that a field/value write and a mapping write both reach the client with the redis key FIRST would have caught it, and would catch the next person who tidies the parameter names.

title: The whole-window outlier rejection makes Requirement 19.11's >=10,000-bar correctness floor unreachable at any threshold, so no market-data source can ever be admitted
evidence: MEASURED AGAINST LIVE BINANCE DATA (12,000 real BTC/USDT 1m bars, 11,999 log-returns, fetched 2026-10-23). This is the recalibration `market_data_validation.Z_SCORE_THRESHOLD_DEFAULT`'s own comment says is still owed: it concedes the 5.0 default is 'a principled default, not a result of fitting real market data, which this sandbox has none of'. HOW IT WAS FOUND: not by reading the code. RT-04's operator tool was run with a 60-second window as a smoke test before starting a multi-day one, and Candidate B came back NOT_MEASURED with 'DATA_QUALITY: ... Found 1 outliers in close log-returns using z_score for UNKNOWN. Dataset rejected - no synthetic data allowed.' The exchange was reachable and healthy (4,697 markets loaded; a direct klines fetch returns bars normally) -- the platform's own validator refused real exchange data. (1) THE NORMAL MODEL THE DEFAULT RESTS ON IS WRONG BY ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE. The comment computes per-point P(|Z|>5) ~ 5.7e-7. Measured on real data the rate is 3.667e-3 -- understated 6,396x. Crypto log-returns are fat-tailed; the observed max |z| was 12.13, and 44 of 11,999 returns exceeded 5 sigma. Measured understatement at other thresholds: 4.0 by 99x, 6.0 by ~1.0e6x, 8.0 by ~6.0e11x. (2) BUT RECALIBRATING THE THRESHOLD CANNOT FIX IT, AND THAT IS THE ACTUAL FINDING. `OutlierDetector._z_score_filter` raises on `outliers.any()` -- the ENTIRE window is rejected if ANY single bar exceeds. So the quantity that matters is per-WINDOW, not per-point: P(reject) = 1 - (1-p)^n, which tends to 1 as n grows for any p > 0. Measured by sliding over the real series, the share of windows rejected at the 10,000-bar size Requirement 19.11 demands is 100% at every threshold tested from 3.0 through 10.0, and still 50% at 12.0 -- a threshold above the largest z-score present in the sample. Smaller windows degrade gracefully (500 bars: 46.5% rejected at 5.0; 900 bars: 69.4%), which is why this never surfaced in shorter-horizon use. THE WHOLE-WINDOW REJECTION RULE AND THE >=10,000-BAR FLOOR ARE THEREFORE INCOMPATIBLE BY CONSTRUCTION. No value of MARKET_DATA_Z_SCORE_THRESHOLD makes RT-04 measurable. The codebase already half-knew this and recorded it as a tolerated strictness rather than an impossibility: `backend/training_worker.py:118` states '`_z_score_filter` REJECTS a window containing any close beyond 3 sigma, and a real multi-thousand-bar market series is near-certain to contain one. That component is REUSED AS-IS and its threshold is not relaxed', and `routers/strategy_operations.py:5882` records mapping it to a classified DATA_QUALITY block 'rather than loosening the threshold'. Both describe the symptom accurately. Neither connects it to Requirement 19.11's floor, which it makes unsatisfiable -- so RT-04 was recorded as needing a week of wall-clock measurement when in fact the measurement cannot succeed at all. Measurement script: kiro-session-artifacts/measure_zscore_reality.py (read-only; fetches live klines, computes the platform's own log-return z-scores, and reports per-point exceedance against the normal model plus per-window rejection rates by sliding over the real series). ||| RESOLVED AS A+C ON THE OWNER'S DECISION (Kiro). A+C is the only coherent pair, and this entry already said so: (C) alone leaves P(reject) -> 1, so it helps only combined with (A). Option (B) -- keep whole-window rejection and restate Requirement 19.11's floor -- was NOT taken: the floor is a correctness requirement, and weakening it to accommodate a detector defect would have made the requirement describe the bug. (A) OutlierPolicy.FLAG_AND_ADMIT, now the default. Detection and response were fused -- every detector raised on the first exceedance -- so 'this window contains an extreme bar' and 'this window is unusable' were one statement, and the quantity deciding admission was per-WINDOW rather than per-point. Now: flag the extreme bars, report how many, admit the window AS OBSERVED, refuse only when the flagged FRACTION exceeds max_outlier_fraction. The guarantee becomes BOUNDED contamination instead of ZERO contamination, which is a promise real market data can keep. (C) OutlierMethod.ROBUST_Z_SCORE, now the default: median/MAD, not mean/std. This is a CORRECTNESS fix rather than a threshold tweak, and the measurement is the argument. std / (1.4826*MAD) = 1.49 (BTC), 1.38 (ETH), 1.46 (DOGE) over 12,000 live 1m bars each -- so a few extreme returns inflate the scale and thereby DEFLATE every ordinary point's z-score, the textbook masking effect. max|robust z| (15.60/15.57/14.99) EXCEEDS max|classic z| (10.47/11.31/10.27): the classic rule was hiding its own most extreme points, because stats.zscore divides by a quantity computed from the very points it is judging. NO BAR IS MODIFIED, EXCLUDED OR WINSORISED, and the measurement is why: what this rule calls an 'outlier' in real crypto data is overwhelmingly an ORDINARY LARGE MOVE, so the bar is the venue's own true observation and replacing it would be the fabrication. Winsorising a close manufactures a price that never traded, which this module forbids everywhere else (_synthetic_fill, GapHandler's refusal). Excluding the bar would punch a hole GapHandler then refuses on the next step -- trading one unsatisfiable gate for another. TWO GUARDS, NOT ONE, which is what reconciles this with DATA-02. A fraction budget cannot catch a single bad tick: one corrupt bar in 10,000 is 0.01% contamination, far inside any usable budget, and DATA-02 requires that a genuine single-bar spike still rejects the window. So the budget answers 'are there too many extreme points?' (fat tails, ordinary) and a new MAGNITUDE CEILING answers 'is any single point impossible?' (bad ticks, never ordinary). The pre-DATA-03 rule had ONE threshold for both, which is exactly why it could not catch the second without rejecting all real data for the first; DATA-02's own spike fixtures pass unchanged against the new default as a result. The ceiling is an ABSOLUTE single-bar log-return bound, not a robust-z multiple, because a robust-z ceiling moves with the window's own dispersion -- a quiet market shrinks MAD and an ordinary move would breach it, the same self-referential defect that made the classic z-score wrong. Price columns only; volume routinely doubles. CONSTANTS FITTED, NOT ASSERTED -- the recalibration Z_SCORE_THRESHOLD_DEFAULT's own comment conceded was owed -- reproducible via `scripts/measure_market_data_outlier_reality.py --robust`, which this change added: robust-z 5.0 -> per-point 8.5e-3..1.1e-2, worst 10,000-bar contamination 1.07%; 8.0 -> 2.3e-3..3.0e-3, 0.35%; 10.0 -> 1.2e-3..1.4e-3, 0.16% (CHOSEN); 12.0 -> 5.0e-4..6.7e-4, 0.07%; 20.0 -> 0, 0.00%. 10.0 is where the rule still DETECTS something real (~1 bar in 850) while the worst case sits ~6x inside the 1% budget; a higher threshold trends towards the classic rule's own failure mode at 12.0, where it passed every window only because 12.0 exceeded the largest z-score present -- a detector that detects nothing is not a safety control. The ceiling, log(2) = 0.6931 (2.00x), sits 82x above the largest real single-bar move measured (0.0048..0.0084) and 5.6x below DATA-02's smallest spike fixture (3.9116; the sine-pool fixture is 7.0457). ACCEPTANCE, against the LIVE venue through the REAL validator (MarketDataValidator.validate, not a reimplementation): all three instruments ADMITTED at 12,000 bars, quality score 95.0 EXCELLENT, 12000 bars in and 12000 out (unmodified), contamination 0.117%/0.142%/0.125%. The SAME bars under the legacy policy: REFUSED, all three. With a 0% budget: REFUSED, so the budget is enforced rather than decorative. REQUIREMENT 19.11's >=10,000-BAR FLOOR IS NOW SATISFIABLE ON REAL DATA. Also fixed in passing: DataQualityReport.outliers_detected counted ISSUE RECORDS, not outliers (`sum(1 for i in issues ...)`), so a field named for a count of outliers could only ever report 0 or 1 per column. NEGATIVE CONTROL, behavioural, against HEAD's own detector: a 10,000-bar fat-tailed window is REFUSED at HEAD ('Found 38 outliers') and ADMITTED with the fix, while the 50x spike is refused BOTH ways -- so the fix flips the defect and preserves DATA-02's requirement. At HEAD the two cases were indistinguishable in the logs (both 'Found N outliers'); they now carry different messages. Regression: 19 new tests (tests/test_data03_outlier_policy_and_robust_scale.py); 302 passed across the five affected suites; 4375 passed / 135 skipped across the whole market-data/validation/paper/training/feed/contract/indicator/backtest selection. The 5 pre-existing errors in test_route_contract.py's Wave-4 class are identical at HEAD. ||| OPEN ON PR #85, NOT MERGED, AND NOT CLAIMED AS PASSING CI. The 'Unit & Integration Tests' job fails on that branch with exactly one failure, tests/property/test_protected_logic_containment.py::test_trace_and_export_surfaces_contain_no_protected_logic, while the same job SUCCEEDS on main (run 39987240090, commit ac11d030) -- so it is this branch, not flake: reproduced on a re-run of the identical commit. Everything else on the PR is green except 'Provisioning, Privilege Hardening & Tenant Isolation', which fails identically on main and is pre-existing. WHAT IS KNOWN. The reported error is NOT an assertion from the test: it is `ValueError: 48 is not in list` raised inside Hypothesis itself, at `internal/intervalsets.py:107` via `index_from_char_in_shrink_order` (48 is ord('0')), reached from `engine.shrink_interesting_test_cases` -> `greedy_shrink` -> `minimize_individual_choices`. Two consequences: (1) Hypothesis DID find a failing example -- shrinking only runs on an interesting case -- and (2) the shrinker's own crash MASKS whatever that example asserted, so the actual defect is still unseen. The crash signature is a library bug class: the collection shrinker's `short_circuit` tries `[zero] * min_size` for a text draw whose alphabet does not contain the zero character. WHAT WAS RULED OUT. Not reproducible locally: 5 consecutive whole-file runs, 3 explicit --hypothesis-seed values, then a 24-seed sweep with the shrink phase disabled -- all passed. Local Python is 3.12.10; CI is 3.11.17, with hypothesis pinned to the SAME 6.165.10 in both, so a version skew is excluded and the difference is the interpreter or the environment. A first hypothesis -- that the new autouse `_no_on_demand_venue_quotes` guard in tests/conftest.py was function-scoped and therefore wrapped every Hypothesis `@given` test -- was WRONG: it was changed to session scope (commit 49f29660, which is better engineering regardless: one substitution instead of fifteen thousand) and CI failed again identically. A temporary no-shrink profile was pushed to make CI print the real assertion; GitHub Actions never scheduled a run for that commit, so it yielded nothing and was reverted rather than left in. WHY A CAUSAL LINK TO THIS SESSION'S CHANGES IS NOT ESTABLISHED. The failing test exercises `strategy_operations.preview_node` and `compare_versions` for a NON-OWNER, NON-ENTITLED caller, whose authorisation refusal is reached before any market-data work; `_preview_data_quality` is called at strategy_operations.py:5030, downstream of that refusal. Neither the outlier policy nor the paper price path is reachable there. The likelier mechanism is indirect: two new test modules change collection, which changes Hypothesis's example stream, which surfaces a LATENT counterexample main's stream happened to miss. That is a hypothesis, NOT a measurement, and it is recorded as such. NEXT STEP, cheapest first: get the real assertion rather than the shrinker's crash -- either run that one test under Python 3.11 locally, or land a no-shrink profile that CI actually schedules, then read the falsifying example. Do not merge #85 until the underlying failure is identified; a protected-logic containment property (Requirements 1.19, 2.19) is not something to merge past on the assumption that it is noise.
verification_level: Measured against the live venue through the real validator, test-pinned, with a behavioural negative control against HEAD. NOT production_verified: the running image predates these constants, so production still evaluates windows with whole-window rejection until it is rebuilt. Note this does NOT hold paper sessions shut -- the per-candle feed path (paper_market_feed._validate_candle) deliberately runs only the structural and candle-integrity validators, never OutlierDetector, so the outlier rule governs WINDOW validation (validated_window, training, backtest) rather than a live session's bar-by-bar ingest.
