Until the image is rebuilt, re-running the RT-04 measurement harness against the DEPLOYED image would refuse again for the original reason, even though the measurement already recorded is valid evidence about the venue data and the current validator.

title: Every stored exchange credential is encrypted under a master key that no longer exists, so all of them are permanently unreadable
evidence: Found 2026-10-23 by the safety guard in scripts/rotate_master_encryption_keys.py --plan, which refuses to rotate when ciphertext decrypts under no available key. MEASURED AGAINST PRODUCTION: exchange_keys holds 2 rows (users d97d59c5.../85f4b896..., both exchange_id='binance', created 2026-06-21T09:00:44Z and 2026-06-21T09:18:01Z) carrying 4 non-NULL ciphertext values across encrypted_api_key/encrypted_secret_key (encrypted_password is NULL on both). ALL 4 ARE GENUINE FERNET TOKENS -- they are valid urlsafe-base64, 100 and 120 characters, and begin 'gAAAAAB' with version byte 128, which is Fernet's own format. So this is not placeholder or garbage data; a real key really did encrypt them. NONE OF THEM DECRYPT. Tested against: (1) the current MASTER_ENCRYPTION_KEYS as the MultiFernet api_key_vault.py:96-99 builds -- 0/4; (2) the PBKDF2(master key, CREDENTIAL_VAULT_SALT) derivation core/credential_vault.py:285 uses, in case the rows were written by that vault instead -- 0/4; (3) EVERY Fernet-shaped key recoverable from the entire git history -- 265 structurally valid candidates harvested by regex from `git log --all -p`, each tried against all 4 values -- 0 hits. The key that encrypted these rows exists in neither Secrets Manager nor git history, so the credentials are unrecoverable rather than merely misplaced. WHAT THIS MEANS OPERATIONALLY: api_key_vault._decrypt raises ValueError('Decryption failed. Key rotation issue or corrupted data.') on InvalidToken, so any attempt to use these credentials already fails -- these two users cannot trade live and could not have at any point since the key was lost. It is masked today only because live trading is hard-gated off by RT-15, so nothing exercises the path. THE ONE PIECE OF GOOD NEWS, and it materially narrows SEC-01: because no key in public git history opens these values, the leaked master_encryption_keys exposes NO customer exchange credential. That part of SEC-01 is a much smaller exposure than its CRITICAL classification implied, and the correction is recorded in SEC-01 as well. RECOVERY QUESTION CLOSED 2026-10-24, and this entry's own open item answered. The entry asked: 'whether the lost key is recoverable from anywhere outside this repository and this AWS account ... AWSPREVIOUS on master_encryption_keys was not examined for this and should be.' It has now been examined, and the answer is NO, for a structural reason rather than a failed brute force. (a) EVERY retained version of master_encryption_keys was read, including the deprecated pre-rotation version 10de1985-ac83-4865-a032-d50ab21c3d70 created 2026-07-29T19:18:20, which carries no stage at all and predates the rotation this effort performed. It does not open the rows. A first attempt failed on a bug in the probe rather than on the data -- it passed 8-character VersionId prefixes, and AWS requires >= 32 -- so the question was briefly and wrongly treated as answered; the corrected run passed full UUIDs. (b) A DELETED secret from the older UPPERCASE naming generation, /vyomquant/production/MASTER_ENCRYPTION_KEYS created 2026-07-22T01:06:38, was found in pending-deletion (deleted by this effort's own SEC-01 orphan sweep), RESTORED specifically to read it, and then re-deleted with a 30-day window so SEC-01 is not regressed. It holds the SAME key as the lowercase secret's pre-rotation version -- so Secrets Manager has held exactly TWO distinct master keys in its entire history, and neither opens the rows. (c) THE DECISIVE FACT: the rows were encrypted 2026-06-21T09:00:44Z and 2026-06-21T09:18:01Z, and the earliest master key material in this account dates from 2026-07-22 -- 31 days later. The key that encrypted them never lived in this account's secret store, so no amount of version history could ever have contained it. Combined with the 265 git-history candidates already tried, the four values are unrecoverable and the question is closed rather than open. A SEPARATE AND LARGER DEFECT WAS FOUND WHILE IMPLEMENTING THE REQUIRED CHECK, and it was not about the vault at all. dashboard_aggregation_service._fetch_exchange_credentials tries two projections, widest first, and the narrow one is the documented fallback for a schema that predates the validity columns: _EXCHANGE_KEY_VALIDITY_COLUMNS = 'is_active, validation_status, last_validated_at, can_trade' over _EXCHANGE_KEY_BASE_COLUMNS = 'exchange_id, updated_at'. exchange_keys has never had updated_at either -- 001 created it with user_id/exchange_id/encrypted_api_key/encrypted_secret_key/encrypted_password/created_at and nothing since added it. So the FALLBACK named a missing column too and BOTH projections were rejected. Measured against production PostgREST: select=exchange_id,updated_at,is_active,... -> HTTP 400 42703 'column exchange_keys.updated_at does not exist'; select=exchange_id,updated_at -> the same 400; select=exchange_id,created_at -> HTTP 200 with 2 rows. _fetch_exchange_credentials therefore returned [] for EVERY user, and get_exchange_data reported total_exchanges=0, connected_exchanges=0, exchanges=[], can_trade=false to every account that had connected a venue -- not a degraded reading, an empty venue list for everybody. That also made this finding's own requirement unreachable on its own terms: a credential state 'the UI can act on' cannot be acted on while the read that would surface it returns nothing.
remaining_action: NONE. Both halves are done and verified against production 2026-10-24. (1) THE AFFECTED ROWS now carry an explicit state instead of raising at use time. Migration 056_vault01_credential_validity_state.sql adds updated_at (backfilled from created_at, not now(), so a stale row does not claim it just synced) plus the four validity columns dashboard_aggregation_service has been asking for -- its own comment reads 'the moment a migration records validity the dashboard reads it without a change here', and this is that migration. can_trade is nullable with NO default on purpose: credential_validity() reads True/False/None and None means 'nobody checked', so DEFAULT false would record a negative finding nobody measured. scripts/quarantine_undecryptable_exchange_keys.py then marked the 2 rows validation_status='unreadable', can_trade=false. FLAGGED RATHER THAN DELETED: deleting destroys the only record that the user ever connected the venue and makes an unreadable row indistinguishable from one that never existed; flagging keeps the audit trail, is reversible, and leaves deletion available as an informed choice. is_active is deliberately untouched -- it means 'the user enabled this key', and the user did; we lost the ability to read it. The script never writes an affirmative, because being able to DECRYPT a credential says nothing about whether the VENUE accepts it. MEASURED AFTER APPLYING: the widened projection returns 2 rows where it previously returned HTTP 400, and both read credential_validity=False and venue_status='invalid_credentials' -- a known negative the UI can act on, distinct from the unknown. (2) THE CAUSE IS NOW DETECTED AT BOOT, which was the half this entry called 'the real risk'. core/credential_key_integrity.py decrypts a bounded sample (50 rows) of exchange_keys and reports one of five verdicts; main.py's lifespan calls it after the configuration checks and before any port is bound. It builds the cipher straight from MASTER_ENCRYPTION_KEYS rather than from app_state.vault, because core/state._safe_init swallows a vault construction failure into a MockEngine and a check running against a mock would report success for every possible key. ONLY ONE VERDICT REFUSES THE BOOT -- rows read, at least one in scope, and every one failed. That converts a wrong key into a FAILED DEPLOYMENT: ECS keeps the previous task definition, which by definition holds the key that works, so the rollout is rejected and nothing is lost. UNDETERMINED (sample unreadable) and DEGRADED (some rows fail) are logged loudly and allowed through, because refusing to start on a database blip or on one poisoned row would be a self-inflicted outage. An operator override, ALLOW_UNREADABLE_EXCHANGE_CREDENTIALS, exists for the emergency the check did not anticipate. A readiness probe reports the condition on the dependency surface but deliberately does NOT gate readiness: the remedy for an unreadable credential is for the user to RE-ENTER it through this API, so taking every pod out of rotation would remove the only route to the fix. QUARANTINE IS WHAT MAKES THE INVARIANT CHECKABLE, and the two halves are therefore one mechanism rather than two tasks: without somewhere to put the two dead rows, 'every row must decrypt' would be false in production forever and the check would have to be disabled to deploy -- and a check that always fails is a check nobody reads. A test pins that quarantine does not become a blanket amnesty: two quarantined rows plus one live row encrypted under an unconfigured key still reads KEY_MISMATCH. PRODUCTION VERIFICATION, all four measured against the live database after applying: a production boot with the real configuration PROCEEDS (verdict NO_SAMPLE, 2 rows quarantined); the same production rows with quarantine lifted in memory give KEY_MISMATCH naming both rows and REFUSE the boot, so the gate is not vacuously green; both quarantined rows read as invalid_credentials through the real PostgREST projection; and the quarantine script is idempotent on a second --apply. 39 regression tests in tests/test_vault01_master_key_decryptability_check.py, weighted toward the directions that must NOT block the boot, since that is where a boot-blocking check does its damage, plus a negative control. STILL TRUE AND NOT A BLOCKER: the two users must re-enter their exchange API keys; nothing can recover them. Both rows date from 2026-06-21 and are very likely the owner's own test accounts. They now present as 'reconnect this venue' rather than as an exception, which is what this finding asked for.

title: No live deployment can resolve an exchange account in production: exchange_keys has no id column and exchange_connections is empty
evidence: Found while wiring MKT-05's subscriber live-deploy UI, and it is not a marketplace problem -- it blocks the FIRST-PARTY live path identically. deployment_binding.load_owned_exchange_account (line ~960) resolves a deployment's exchange_account_id with .eq("id", exchange_account_id) against each of EXCHANGE_ACCOUNT_TABLES = ("exchange_keys", "exchange_connections"), and raises EXCHANGE_ACCOUNT_NOT_FOUND (404) if neither matches. MEASURED DIRECTLY AGAINST THE REAL PRODUCTION DATABASE (2026-10-24, read-only): (1) public.exchange_keys has 11 columns -- user_id, exchange_id, encrypted_api_key, encrypted_secret_key, encrypted_password, created_at, updated_at, is_active, validation_status, last_validated_at, can_trade -- and NO `id` column at all; its PRIMARY KEY is the COMPOSITE (user_id, exchange_id). So .eq("id", ...) against it raises 42703 'column exchange_keys.id does not exist', which that function's own except/continue -- written to tolerate a relation absent from a deployment -- swallows as 'table unavailable'. It holds 2 rows, i.e. real stored credentials. (2) public.exchange_connections DOES carry an `id` and is its primary key, but holds ZERO rows. So the only table that can answer the query has nothing in it, and the table with the credentials cannot answer it. Net effect: EVERY live deployment 404s. (3) A third mismatch in the same area, recorded because it will bite whoever fixes the first two: strategy_deployments.exchange_account_id is `uuid` while exchange_connections.id is `text`. HOW IT WAS FOUND, because the route matters: adding `id` to routers/exchange.py's _EXCHANGE_KEYS_PROJECTION so a UI could read a usable account id broke 9 tests in test_exchange_connections_read_regression.py, whose fake refuses any column outside the projection -- the fake was right and the change was wrong. Reverted, with the reason recorded at the constant so the next person does not retry it. Note also that GET /api/exchanges/ synthesises its `id` field as {user_id}_{exchange_id}, which is not any row's key and is not usable as an exchange_account_id either, so there is currently NO endpoint from which a client can obtain one. NOT A LIVE INCIDENT TODAY, and that is why this is P1 rather than P0: live trading is hard-off (ExecutionFlags.LIVE_TRADING_ENABLED is a hardcoded False, plus platform mode, enable flag and an empty tenant allowlist), so no live deployment is attempted in production. It is a launch blocker for live trading rather than an active fault. ||| CLOSED IN PRODUCTION (Kiro, 2026-10-24). THE FIX WAS DECIDED BY A FACT ABOUT HOW CREDENTIALS ARE ACTUALLY RESOLVED, not by preference between the three options this entry listed. `api_key_vault.load_decrypted_keys(user_id, exchange_id)` -- the call the execution process makes, and the one `deployment_binding.account_exchange_id` exists to feed by reading `exchange_id` back off the account row -- resolves credentials by the COMPOSITE, never by an account id. So `exchange_account_id` carries exactly one responsibility: a stable, single-column record of WHICH of a user's accounts a deployment was bound to. It is a HANDLE, not an identity. That is what `strategy_deployments.exchange_account_id uuid` (004e) is shaped for, and a composite natural key cannot be stored in one uuid column -- which rules out option (b), and would additionally make a binding ambiguous the moment a user holds two credentials for one venue. Option (c) (making exchange_connections authoritative) is the better-shaped end state and is NOT done, deliberately: it is the larger change, it is not what unblocks live deployment, and conflating 'stop the two tables disagreeing' with 'let a deployment name an account' would hold the second hostage to the first. FIX: backend_app/migrations/058_exch03_exchange_keys_stable_handle.sql adds `exchange_keys.id`, NOT NULL and UNIQUE, backfilled with gen_random_uuid(). THE PRIMARY KEY IS NOT TOUCHED: `(user_id, exchange_id)` is the real constraint -- one credential per user per venue -- and replacing the primary key of a table holding encrypted customer credentials to add a lookup handle would be a far larger risk than adding a column beside it. No FK from strategy_deployments, for the reason 004e gives for this exact column: it is a reference and never a credential, and a FK would make a credential's deletion unable to proceed while any historical deployment still names it. IT HANDLES BOTH LIVE SHAPES, which the first draft did not: migrations/003_create_exchange_keys_table.sql declares `id TEXT PRIMARY KEY`, so a database provisioned from repository source ALREADY has a handle (as text, as the primary key) while production's table -- never created by that migration -- had none. The migration therefore never retypes an existing id, skips the UNIQUE when the column is already the primary key, and its postflight accepts uuid OR text. The first draft asserted data_type='uuid' and would have failed on every CI run; that was caught by provisioning a from-source replica rather than by reasoning. APPLIED AND VERIFIED IN PRODUCTION: 2 exchange_keys rows, both carrying a unique uuid handle, and the postflight exercises the resolver's own lookup shape (`WHERE id = <handle>` returns exactly 1) rather than merely asserting the column exists -- the broken thing was the query, so proving the query works is what matters. Re-run is a clean no-op ('column already exists, skipping' / 'uq already present'). Row counts, 148 policies and 84 RLS-enabled tables all unchanged. ALSO WIRED, so a client can obtain the handle: `GET /api/exchanges/` now selects `id` and exposes it as `account_id` ALONGSIDE its existing synthesised `{user_id}_{exchange_id}` composite -- added beside rather than replacing, so nothing already consuming that response changes meaning underneath it. A row with no handle is passed through as null and filtered out by the UI rather than substituted, because a substituted value 404s at deploy time and reads as 'your account is missing' instead of 'this app asked for the wrong thing'. tests/test_exchange_connections_read_regression.py's column contract gained `id` and dropped it from COLUMNS_ABSENT_IN_PRODUCTION. NOTED WHILE THERE, not fixed: that fixture also claims production lacks `updated_at`, and a re-query found it present -- so that half of its premise is stale. It is kept out of the fixture's column set anyway, because making the pre-fix projection raise 42703 is the regression it exists to guard, and adding `updated_at` would retire that guard for a column no handler selects. Recorded rather than silently corrected.
verification_level: production (058 applied in a verified transaction; its postflight exercises the resolver's own lookup shape against real rows, not just column existence; re-run confirmed a clean no-op) + code+test (from-source replica provisioned to prove the migration handles the text-primary-key shape too)
remaining_action: NONE for the defect: a live deployment can now resolve the exchange account it was bound to, verified in production. Two standing items, both recorded rather than implied. (1) THE TWO TABLES STILL DISAGREE -- exchange_keys holds 2 rows and exchange_connections holds 0, while the resolver consults both. That is option (c) from this entry's original analysis and is still worth doing: exchange_connections should be populated whenever credentials are stored, so connection state and credentials stop being separately true. Nothing depends on it now that the handle exists. (2) exchange_connections.id is `text` while strategy_deployments.exchange_account_id is `uuid`; exchange_keys.id is uuid and matches, so the mismatch only bites a deployment bound to a connections row, of which there are none. Reconcile if (1) is ever done. Separately: migrations/003_create_exchange_keys_table.sql does not describe production's exchange_keys table at all (different primary key, and production carries columns 003 never declared), which is a schema-as-code gap of the same class as DEPLOY-05 and is not specific to this finding.

title: A marketplace deployment is recorded but never started: deploy_marketplace_strategy writes the row and starts no bot
evidence: Separated out of MKT-05 so it is not lost inside a closed finding. `routers/library.py::deploy_marketplace_strategy` ends at a single `.insert()` into `strategy_deployments` and returns the new id. It performs none of what the first-party path does after its own insert: no quota reservation, no `deployment_runtime.build_runtime_blueprint`, and no `fleet.start_bot`. `StrategyService.deploy_version` does all three. So a marketplace deployment's `status` stays at 'deploying' and nothing ever evaluates the strategy. THIS IS NOT NEW AND NOT SPECIFIC TO LIVE: it has been true of the PAPER marketplace path since that path was built, and MKT-05's live option inherited it rather than introducing it. It is recorded as its own finding because MKT-05's title -- a working UI path -- is satisfied by a deploy that is accepted, bound and correctly bounded, while 'the strategy actually runs' is a different claim that deserves its own entry rather than keeping a closed finding open. HARMLESS TODAY, which is why it is P2 and not higher: live trading is hard-off (ExecutionFlags.LIVE_TRADING_ENABLED is a hardcoded False, plus platform mode, an enable flag and an empty tenant allowlist), so a started live bot would place no orders anyway; and a paper marketplace deployment that never starts is a feature that silently does nothing rather than one that does something wrong.
verification_level: code (both handlers read in full: the marketplace path's single insert against StrategyService.deploy_version's quota reserve, blueprint build and fleet start)
remaining_action: Wire the marketplace deploy path to the same post-insert sequence the first-party path uses: reserve quota, build the runtime blueprint, start the bot, and roll the row back or mark it failed if the start does not take. Two things need deciding rather than copying: (a) whose quota a marketplace deployment consumes -- the subscriber's, almost certainly, but that is a product decision with billing consequences; and (b) what happens to a live marketplace bot when its authorization window closes mid-run, which MKT-05 already answers for the ORDER path (`master_executor.evaluate_authorization_window` refuses and requests a durable stop) but which has never been exercised against a bot that was actually started, because none ever has been.

title: OrderWatchdog runs its reconciliation loop in every gunicorn worker with no leader election, so N workers adjudicate the same open orders concurrently
evidence: Measured 2026-10-24 while closing RECON-01, because RECON-01's closure rests on 'OrderWatchdog already provides the capability' and that mitigation had to be checked rather than inherited. RECON-01's own evidence had already noted this and said it 'is not RECON-01's to fix'; filing it here is what stops RECON-01's closure from burying it. MEASURED: backend_app/main.py constructs OrderWatchdog and awaits .start() in the lifespan unconditionally (service_status['order_watchdog']='ACTIVE'), and startup.sh:102 runs `gunicorn --workers ${WORKERS:-2}` -- so the loop runs once per worker. OrderWatchdog._reconciliation_loop contains NO leadership guard: searched its own source for 'leader', 'lease', 'try_acquire', 'lock' and 'nx', all absent. The whole module contains ZERO occurrences of try_acquire_or_renew, leader_lease, LEADER, skip_locked or NOWAIT -- so unlike ExchangeReconciliationService and ReconciliationScheduler, which both delegate to core/leader_lease.try_acquire_or_renew, this one has no election at all. WHAT THAT MEANS: every worker queries the venue for the same open orders each interval, and each may adjudicate the same row. The protection against a double-applied position delta is the per-position `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` in the position-delta path, so correctness depends on that lock holding; this investigation did NOT establish that it fails, and the historical 'non-blocking fallback that proceeds unlocked' text in that module describes a defect recorded as already fixed. So the measured claim is duplicated venue queries and an unelected adjudication path, NOT demonstrated position corruption. IT CANNOT FIRE TODAY, which is why this is P2 rather than higher: public.execution_records holds 108 COMPLETED and 90 FAILED rows and ZERO in PENDING or EXECUTING, public.positions holds 0 rows, and live trading runs in paper mode -- so there is nothing for two workers to contend over. The condition becomes live the moment real orders exist, which is launch.
remaining_action: Decide and implement one of: (a) give _reconciliation_loop the same core/leader_lease.try_acquire_or_renew election ExchangeReconciliationService and ReconciliationScheduler already share, with its OWN key -- sharing a key would make whichever process won suppress the other subsystem entirely, which presents as 'the loop is running' while half the work silently never happens; or (b) prove the adjudication path is idempotent under concurrency and record WHY, which is a legitimate answer for a guarded UPDATE but has not been established for this path. (a) is cheap: the primitive exists, is tested, and has two callers already. BEFORE EITHER, confirm the position-delta `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` actually serialises, since that is the thing currently standing between two concurrent adjudications and a double-applied delta. NOT URGENT WHILE LIVE TRADING IS OFF and the PENDING/EXECUTING population is zero, but it should be closed before live trading is enabled, because the first real open order arms it.

title: ConnectionEngine announced 'Testnet/Sandbox ENABLED' without proving it, and the client pool could not tell a sandbox client from a live one
evidence: FOUND BY ASKING WHO CAN ACTUALLY REACH THE CONTROL, after repairing verify_sandbox_endpoint for WS-03's ccxt upgrade. Tracing every process that can construct a venue client turned up a SECOND client factory that never consulted the control at all -- and it is the one paper trading and live market data use. backend_app/backend/connection_engine.py's ConnectionEngine.connect read, verbatim: `if self.testnet: try: self.exchange.set_sandbox_mode(True); logger.info(f"[{...}] Testnet/Sandbox ENABLED.") except Exception: logger.warning(f"[{...}] Testnet requested but not supported by this exchange.")`. That is the EXCH-01 defect verbatim, in the factory EXCH-01 did not touch. TWO WAYS IT LIED. On bitget set_sandbox_mode neither raises nor moves the endpoint (its override does not call super() and bitget publishes no urls['test']), so 'Testnet/Sandbox ENABLED' was logged for a client addressing PRODUCTION. On a venue with no sandbox it RAISED, the bare except swallowed it, and execution continued with self.testnet still True and the client still on production -- a warning, not a refusal. On ccxt 4.5.90 that raise is TypeError("'NoneType' object is not iterable") rather than ccxt's NotSupported, measured while re-recording staging/exch01_sandbox_endpoint_evidence.json, so a fix matching on the exception type would have missed it. A THIRD DEFECT IN THE SAME PATH, AND THE MORE SUBTLE ONE: the client pool could not distinguish the two environments. _pool_key is sha256([user_id, exchange_id]) and nothing recorded which environment a pooled client addressed, so a caller asking for testnet could be handed the LIVE client that happened to be pooled first. Worse in combination with the pool's own credential rule, which is correct on its own terms: 'no credential supplied -> reuse whatever is pooled' is right for authentication (such a caller must not downgrade an authenticated client it did not build) and WRONG for the environment, so a credential-less testnet request was the exact shape that got a production client. exchange_executor's own cache had this right all along -- _executor_cache_key folds in 'sandbox' if sandbox else 'live' -- and this pool did not. SEVERITY IS BOUNDED BY A MEASURED FACT: NO CALLER ARMS IT. Every ConnectionEngine(...) and get_or_create_exchange(...) call site in backend_app/** omits `testnet`, so the default False applies everywhere and nothing in production has ever requested a sandbox through this factory. paper_trading_service.fetch_venue_quote passes none (it wants a public production ticker, which is correct); master_executor's market-data bridge passes none; routers/market.py, routers/orders.py and portfolio_cache_updater pass none. So this was a TRAP ARMED FOR THE NEXT CALLER rather than a live exposure -- which is exactly what makes it worth closing before launch, because the next caller is whoever wires the credential UI's testnet toggle (EXCH-06). ||| FIXED IN SOURCE. connect() now refuses a sandbox the venue cannot provide BEFORE constructing anything (assert_sandbox_supported, so no client and no aiohttp session is allocated for a connection that cannot exist), RAISES a classified SandboxVerificationFailed where it used to warn, and proves the routing with the control that already existed -- verify_sandbox_endpoint, which raises rather than returning a verdict precisely so a caller cannot drop it. On every refusal the client is closed and its reference nulled through this file's own disconnect() (FIX CE-3), the same teardown the AuthenticationError branch uses, so a refused sandbox leaks neither a session nor a reachable decrypted credential. The success log now names the MECHANISM and runs only after the proof. The pool records a per-entry sandbox flag alongside the existing credential identity and requires it to match UNCONDITIONALLY; it is tracked beside the entry rather than folded into _pool_key because changing the key would require every release_exchange caller (routers/exchange.py's store and delete paths) to know the environment too, and a one-sided edit there would make eviction silently miss -- CONN-01 again. THE PRODUCTION ENDPOINT IS INJECTED, NOT DEFAULTED, AND THAT IS THE SUBTLE PART. verify_sandbox_endpoint's default reads production from a pristine client it resolves out of ccxt.async_support, while this factory builds ccxt.PRO clients. MEASURED on 4.5.90: a pro client's urls['api'] carries an extra 'ws' key the REST client's does not, for binance, bybit and okx alike. So a pro endpoint can NEVER equal a REST one, and the 'did it leave production' comparison would come out true for a reason with nothing to do with routing -- it would pass VACUOUSLY, which is worse than failing because it looks like proof. connect() therefore constructs a pristine client of the same pro class and passes its endpoint explicitly, refusing outright if it cannot be read. That construction costs nothing and leaks nothing, measured not assumed: after exchange_class({}) on ccxt.pro 4.5.90, session and tcp_connector are both None and clients is empty, no network call is made, and the config is empty so no credential is involved. VERIFIED BY 14 NEW TESTS in tests/test_exch01_connection_engine_sandbox_proof.py over fake venue CLASSES that model ccxt's arming rather than hardcoding its result: a genuine swap verifies and proceeds; an arming failure raises where it used to warn; an arming no-op that stays on production is refused; an unmeasured venue and the three measured UNSUPPORTED venues are refused before a client exists; a live connection is untouched; and the pool refuses to serve a live client to a sandbox request and vice versa, in BOTH directions and with no credential supplied, while two identical sandbox requests still share one client so CE-4 is not sacrificed. THE INJECTION IS MUTATION-TESTED: dropping `production_endpoint=` makes test_production_must_come_from_a_pro_client_not_the_rest_default fail with DID NOT RAISE, i.e. the control verifies a client that never left production. That mutation check was run TWICE -- the first attempt put the edit, the test and the revert in one shell batch and the file was not mutated when pytest read it, so the 'caught' result was an artefact; re-run as three separate steps it genuinely fails. REGRESSION: 312 passed / 1 skipped across every test file that imports connection_engine, plus 494 passed / 7 skipped across the remaining paper, backtest and market-data consumers, plus 43 passed across the two EXCH-01 files together.
verification_level: Verified by test, NOT by production effect, and the distinction is the honest one: no caller in the deployed tree passes testnet=True, so there is no production behaviour to observe. The defect was latent and the fix is verified against fake venue classes that reproduce the three real shapes (genuine swap, silent no-op, raise-on-arm) plus the pool's two reuse directions. The ccxt facts the fix rests on ARE measured against real ccxt 4.5.90: the pro-vs-REST 'ws' key difference, the TypeError raised by venues with no sandbox, and the zero allocation cost of a pristine pro client. The one branch that cannot be exercised without a venue is unchanged by this work. NOT verified by CI: GitHub Actions has failed every workflow at the account level since 2026-10-26.
remaining_action: NOTHING FOR THE DEFECT. The second factory now proves what it claims and the pool keeps the two environments apart. ONE DEPENDENT ITEM, tracked as EXCH-06: the credential UI's 'Testnet / Sandbox Mode' toggle is the caller this fix was waiting for, and it is not wired to anything. Wiring it is what turns this control from a guard on an unused parameter into a guard on a real user choice -- and it must be wired to THIS parameter, not around it. ONE NOTE FOR WHOEVER DOES: arming sandbox on coinbase, kraken or kucoin is now a REFUSAL rather than a warning, because those three publish no sandbox endpoint on the installed ccxt. That is correct and it is a UX requirement -- the toggle must be unavailable for those venues rather than offered and then refused at connect time.

title: The credential UI offers a 'Testnet / Sandbox Mode' toggle that cannot be stored, is never read, and has no effect on any connection
evidence: A USER-FACING SAFETY LABEL THAT DOES NOTHING, and the chain is broken at every single link -- four of them, found by reading each in turn rather than inferring from one. (1) THE UI OFFERS IT. backend_app/core/exchange_connection_schema.py declares, for binance among others, an ExchangeCredentialField with field_id='sandbox', label='Testnet / Sandbox Mode', type=FieldType.BOOLEAN, description='Connect to Binance Testnet instead of Production.' (2) THE SCHEMA CANNOT HOLD IT. migrations/003_create_exchange_keys_table.sql is the only place exchange_keys is created, and its columns are id, user_id, exchange_id, encrypted_api_key, encrypted_secret_key, encrypted_password, created_at, updated_at. There is no sandbox or testnet column, in 003 or in 058. (3) THE WRITE PATH DROPS IT. APIKeyVault.store_exchange_keys builds its upsert dict with exactly six keys -- user_id, exchange_id and the three encrypted blobs -- so a submitted toggle has nowhere to land. (4) THE READ PATH NEVER RETURNS IT. APIKeyVault.load_decrypted_keys does select('*') but returns a dict of exactly three keys: api_key, secret_key, password. SO THE CONSUMER IS READING A FIELD THAT CANNOT EXIST. backend_app/backend/order_control.py's _executor_for -- the single per-tenant executor boundary, and the fan-in point for POST /api/orders/cancel/{id}, POST /api/orders/cancel-all, OrderWatchdog, ExchangeReconciliationService and PositionConsistencyChecker -- does `bool(keys.get("sandbox") or keys.get("testnet"))`. Against a vault that returns three fixed keys that expression is False unconditionally. It READS LIKE the sandbox intent is honoured on this path and it is structurally incapable of being anything but live. WHAT IS AND IS NOT AT RISK TODAY, stated precisely rather than alarmingly. These paths cancel and read; they do not open positions (order_control's own docstring: 'It never places an order', and flattening stays behind the live gates). Live trading is hard-gated off platform-wide (RT-15). And the only input that can arm the executor's sandbox verifier at all is a 'testnet': true key riding inside a strategy blueprint to master_executor.py's _recover_live_state -- nothing in backend_app/** ever writes that key. So no order is currently being placed on production under a sandbox label. WHAT IS WRONG IS THE PROMISE: a trader who ticks 'Testnet / Sandbox Mode' and connects gets a production connection, with no error and no warning, and the platform's own UI told them otherwise. For a venue where their real balance lives, that is the EXCH-01 defect class at the product surface instead of inside ccxt -- the label says sandbox, the socket says production.
verification_level: Not fixed. Every link above was read directly in the source named, not inferred: the UI field declaration, migration 003's column list, the vault's store and load dicts, and order_control's expression. The reachability claim (that nothing writes blueprint['testnet']) is from a repo-wide trace of the five deployed entrypoints and is the weakest of these -- it is an absence, and a strategy graph authored outside backend_app/** could carry the key.
remaining_action: A PRODUCT DECISION IS REQUIRED FIRST, which is why this is recorded rather than unilaterally fixed. Two honest endings, and the wrong move is a third one that silences the symptom. (A) WIRE IT. Add `sandbox boolean not null default false` to exchange_keys, carry it through store_exchange_keys and load_decrypted_keys, and let order_control's existing expression finally mean something. This is the ending the product clearly intends -- a trader needs testnet to try the platform before risking real money -- and EXCH-05 has already made the connection side safe for it: both factories now PROVE sandbox routing and refuse what they cannot prove. It needs a migration on the credentials table (a security-sensitive table whose primary key another author explicitly declined to retype, so it wants its own migration and its own backup), and it needs the UX consequence accepted: coinbase, kraken and kucoin publish NO sandbox on the installed ccxt, so the toggle must be unavailable for them rather than offered and then refused at connect time. (B) WITHDRAW THE PROMISE. Remove the field from the venue definitions until it is wired, so the UI stops offering a control the platform cannot honour. Smaller, honest, and it gives up a capability users will ask for. WHAT MUST NOT HAPPEN: deleting order_control's `keys.get("sandbox")` read on the grounds that it is always False. The expression is the only thing in the code that still says what was intended; removing it would make the gap invisible instead of closed.

title: There is no payout mechanism for marketplace creators to ever receive their earned revenue share
evidence: There was previously NO way for a marketplace strategy creator to ever receive their earned revenue share. routers/library.py::creator_analytics (via settlement_service.creator_earnings, lines ~1186-1293) already derived a creator's lifetime earnings correctly -- the exact integer sum of marketplace_settlements.owner_share_minor over non-reversal rows minus reversal rows, per currency -- but that function is READ-ONLY: nothing in this codebase ever marked any of it paid, and nothing ever created a payout. A prior pass's own comment in library.py (routers/library.py, the block above _CREATOR_ANALYTICS_LISTING_SELECT) named the gap directly: 'no payout mechanism exists in this system', after deleting a dashboard label that falsely claimed 'Monthly auto-transfer (Stripe Connect)'. That comment had never been given its own tracked finding; this is that finding, closed on the REF-01 template (backend_app/migrations/049_ref01_payout_atomic.sql, routers/referral.py::create_payout_request/settle_payout) for the structurally identical referral-payout problem, deliberately choosing the SAME manual, admin-attested settlement answer -- this sandbox has no live Razorpay/Stripe credentials to verify an automated outbound transfer against, and building a different answer here than REF-01 built for the same underlying problem needed a product reason this task did not have. DIFFERENCE FROM REF-01: creation is platform-initiated on a weekly cadence, not creator-requested -- backend_app/core/creator_payout_scheduler.py polls hourly (POLL_INTERVAL_SECONDS=3600) and checks a durable sweep log (marketplace_creator_payout_sweeps, MAX(finished_at)) for whether SWEEP_INTERVAL_SECONDS (7 days) have elapsed, rather than a bare asyncio.sleep(7*86400) that could never recover a missed cycle after a restart; a sweep that started and crashed leaves finished_at NULL, which the due-check correctly does not treat as a completion. Only one web worker runs a sweep per cycle: the scheduler reuses reconciliation_scheduler.py's own Redis leader-election primitive (_try_become_leader, a renewable SET key value NX EX lease) verbatim, under its own lease key (leader:creator_payout_scheduler) so the two schedulers' leaderships are independent. THE SCHEMA QUESTION THIS PASS HAD TO SETTLE FIRST, THE SAME WAY REF-01 DID FOR referral_wallets: confirmed against this session's own disposable, fully-provisioned Postgres replica (via pg_get_functiondef('marketplace_settlement_append_only_guard'::regproc), not assumed from the migration file's comments) that marketplace_settlements carries a trigger that RAISES on every UPDATE unconditionally, and refuses DELETE while its subscription_id still exists -- Requirement 10.8's 'never modify a persisted Settlement_Record', enforced at the database. The first version of this migration added a nullable claimed_by_payout_id column directly to marketplace_settlements and tried to UPDATE it; that failed on its very first real call in this session's own disposable replica (psycopg2.errors.CheckViolation, 'marketplace_settlements is append-only: UPDATE is not permitted'), caught by this session's own test run before being treated as correct, and the design was changed to a separate claims table before anything was committed. Added backend_app/migrations/051_mkt06_creator_payout_atomic.sql: two new tables -- marketplace_creator_payouts (id, owner_id, amount_minor BIGINT, currency, status pending/completed/rejected, period_start, period_end, reference, reason, created_at, updated_at, settled_at -- mirroring referral_payouts' column set with an integer Minor_Units amount instead of referral_payouts' DECIMAL(10,2), since Requirement 10.3's no-binary-floating-point-money rule does not stop applying for a new table) and marketplace_creator_payout_claims (payout_id, settlement_id UNIQUE, the idempotent 'already paid out' boundary: a settlement row's absence from this table means payable, its presence means claimed; INSERTed by create_creator_payout, DELETEd -- never UPDATEd -- by settle_creator_payout on a rejection) -- plus a marketplace_creator_payout_sweeps log table for the scheduler's durable due-check. Two SECURITY DEFINER functions: create_creator_payout (p_owner_id, p_period_start, p_period_end) computes, per currency, sum(CASE WHEN is_reversal THEN -owner_share_minor ELSE owner_share_minor END) over settlements with no existing claim row, serialised per owner_id via pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended(owner_id::text,0)) (a single-row SELECT...FOR UPDATE, REF-01's own mechanism, does not apply here because the thing being locked is a SUM over an unbounded row set, not one wallet row's balance column), and for every currency with a positive total, inserts one marketplace_creator_payouts row and claims exactly the settlement ids captured in the SAME query that computed the sum (no separate 'which rows to claim' re-query that could see a newer unclaimed set than the sum was based on). A currency whose unclaimed net is zero or negative gets no payout and its rows stay unclaimed, mirroring creator_earnings's own documented choice not to clamp a negative total. settle_creator_payout (p_payout_id, p_status, p_reference, p_reason) is the pending->completed/rejected step: 'completed' requires a non-blank reference and never touches the claims table; 'rejected' DELETEs every claim row this payout holds in the SAME transaction as the status flip, so those settlements are summed again by the next create_creator_payout call -- proved directly by test_rejecting_a_payout_unclaims_its_settlements_which_become_payable_next_cycle, the single test this task's own instructions called out as most important. PY001 invalid argument, PY002 not found, PY003 invalid status/missing reference, PY004 already terminal -- same vocabulary and status-code mapping as REF-01's RF00x codes. Both functions are REVOKEd from anon/authenticated and GRANTed only to service_role (postflight DO block asserts this), since creation is never creator-initiated (no POST endpoint exists for it, unlike referral's user-requested POST /referral/payouts) and settlement is operator-only. RLS: owner-read-only SELECT policy on marketplace_creator_payouts (owner_id = auth.uid()), service_role FOR ALL on both new tables, deliberately narrower than referral_payouts' own 'FOR ALL...USING(user_id=auth.uid())' policy since nothing in this design lets a creator write their own payout row directly. routers/library.py: GET /creator/payouts (literal_router, owner-scoped by predicate on the authenticated session exactly like creator_analytics, returns amount_minor/currency/status/period/reference/reason, no major-unit conversion for the same Requirement-10.3 reason _earnings_entry already documents) and PUT /creator-payouts/{payout_id}/settle (router, since it carries a path parameter -- registered after literal_router's routes are spliced in front, confirmed live via a route-table dump showing /creator/payouts ordered before /creator/{creator_id}), admin-gated via get_admin_user and the service-role client exactly like referral.py::settle_payout, with a docstring stating explicitly that it never itself moves money. backend_app/main.py: start_creator_payout_scheduler()/stop_creator_payout_scheduler() wired into lifespan startup/shutdown identically to ReconciliationScheduler's own wiring, plus a service_status['creator_payout_scheduler'] entry. TESTS: tests/test_mkt06_creator_payout_atomic_postgres.py (13, against this session's real disposable Postgres replica): both functions exist exactly once and are service_role-only; zero balance creates no payout; a positive balance creates exactly one payout and claims the settlement; running create_creator_payout twice in a row for the same creator does NOT double-count (the exact REF-01-style race); two different currencies for the same owner produce two separate payout rows (money never summed across currencies); a net-negative/fully-reversed currency balance creates no payout and leaves both rows unclaimed; two REAL THREADS calling create_creator_payout concurrently for the same creator produce exactly one payout (pg_advisory_xact_lock proven under real concurrency, mirroring REF-01's own two-thread test); completing records a reference and leaves claims intact; completing without a reference is refused (PY003) and changes nothing; rejecting releases claims and the NEXT create_creator_payout call creates a fresh payout for the same amount (the most-important property, its own dedicated test); an already-terminal payout cannot be settled again (PY004, both terminal states parametrized); settling a nonexistent payout raises PY002. tests/test_mkt06_creator_payout_scheduler.py (17): leader election reuses the identical INF-04 primitive under its own lease key (only one of two instances wins, the leader renews its lease, a challenger cannot steal an active lease, a crashed leader's lease expires and another takes over, fails closed when Redis is unreachable or errors, a non-leader cycle does not run the sweep); the durable due-check (due when no sweep has ever finished, not due within the interval of a recent completion, due again once the interval has elapsed, a crashed sweep with finished_at still NULL does not count as a completion, not due -- fails in the SAFE direction -- when no service client is available); the sweep calls create_creator_payout exactly once per DISTINCT owner_id (deduplicating a repeated owner_id across settlement rows), never inspects amounts or currencies itself (a zero-balance creator still gets exactly one RPC call, which itself returns nothing), records a finished sweep row, and one owner's RPC failure does not abort the sweep for the others. tests/test_mkt06_creator_payout_settlement.py (7, mirroring test_ref01_payout_settlement.py's own fake-RPC-double shape): non-admin refused with 403 before the database is touched; completing records the reference and leaves claims untouched; completing without a reference is refused (400); rejecting releases claims; an already-settled payout cannot be re-settled (409, both terminal states); a nonexistent payout is 404. tests/test_validation_sweep.py: registered the new PUT route in MUTATING_ROUTES (same admin-gated, body-never-inspected shape as referral.settle_payout). FULL REGRESSION (this session, confirmed nothing else disturbed): test_mkt06_creator_payout_atomic_postgres.py (13) + test_mkt06_creator_payout_scheduler.py (17) + test_mkt06_creator_payout_settlement.py (7) + test_ref01_payout_atomic_postgres.py (11) + test_ref01_payout_settlement.py (6) + test_creator_analytics_regression.py + test_settlement_service.py + test_marketplace_concurrency.py + property/test_settlement_ledger.py + property/test_settlement_idempotence.py + test_billing_e2e.py (196 passed) + test_validation_sweep.py (379 passed, 2 pre-existing unrelated skips) + test_library_route_resolution.py (35 passed, confirms /creator/payouts is not shadowed by /creator/{creator_id}) + test_router_registration_completeness.py -- all passed, zero failures, zero newly-introduced skips. Ported onto main (commit 9620ae9) after this branch was found to have diverged significantly from an independent work stream; migration renumbered 051 -> 059 to clear a collision with main own sequence (advanced to 058). Re-verified against main current head: tests/test_mkt06_creator_payout_atomic_postgres.py (13), tests/test_mkt06_creator_payout_scheduler.py (17), tests/test_mkt06_creator_payout_settlement.py (7), tests/test_validation_sweep.py all pass together (417 passed, 1 skipped, 0 failures).

remaining_action: NOT applied to the real production database -- deliberately, as a separate, later, carefully-reviewed step, exactly as REF-01's own remaining_action states for the identical reason: this touches real creator money-movement bookkeeping and this session has no production credentials. Apply backend_app/migrations/051_mkt06_creator_payout_atomic.sql to staging first, then production, and have an operator run a real settlement (a test creator payout, completed and rejected) against it before trusting it on real creator earnings. THIS HAS NEVER RUN AGAINST THE REAL PLATFORM'S LIVE CREATOR-EARNINGS DATA -- every test above runs against this session's own disposable, fully-provisioned Postgres replica (vyomquant_test), not production, and production_verified is correctly false. Two things this pass deliberately did NOT build, matching the task's own explicit scope: (1) no automated outbound payment-rail integration (RazorpayX Payouts, Stripe Connect, or anything that itself moves money) -- settlement stays a manual, admin-attested step, same as REF-01's referral payouts, and the operator still has to actually transfer money outside this system before marking a payout 'completed'; (2) no creator-facing request-a-payout endpoint -- unlike referral payouts, creation is entirely platform-initiated by the weekly scheduler, by design, so there is currently no way for a creator to ask for an out-of-cycle payout, which may or may not be a gap product wants closed separately. A third, smaller item: this scheduler's hourly due-check and weekly sweep have been exercised only with a fake/mocked service client and against a short-lived disposable Postgres replica in this session, never against a real long-running worker process over an actual multi-day interval -- the sweep-log-based restart recovery is proven by direct unit test of _sweep_is_due's logic, not by actually restarting a running worker mid-week and observing the real recovery.
